sens: To seize something and remove it, to drag it, to lift it
To attract, charm, seduce someone or something towards oneself
To stretch, extend, deploy a force or a weapon
To prolong, extend in time, delay, persist
To walk, advance, set in motion
H4900.detail:
1. To draw in the literal sense means to seize with force and remove, drag something. It is the image of Joseph being drawn out of the pit: "they drew and brought up Joseph out of the pit" (Genesis 37:28). It is also to draw iniquity with cords as one draws a heavy cart (Isaiah 5:18).
2. To attract in the figurative sense means to charm, seduce, bring towards oneself by attraction. Psalm 36:11 speaks of extending goodness, that is, making it shine as an attraction: "Extend your goodness to those who know you." Jeremiah 31:3 expresses God's love that "draws" (prolongs) His goodness: it is to attract by eternal love.
3. To draw can also mean to stretch or deploy a weapon or force with effort. It is to draw the bow of the warrior or to deploy power.
4. To prolong means to extend in time, to make last. The word expresses the idea of continuing, persisting, delaying. Proverbs 13:12: "Hope deferred makes the heart sick."
5. To walk, advance, set out. Judges 5:14 says that Benjamin "walked" behind: it is to move, progress with intention.
H4900.origine: The Hebrew root primarily expresses the physical gesture of drawing, dragging. It has generated derived images: to attract by seduction, to prolong in time, to advance with movement. The word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of action: to seize, to remove, to move. The same root in Aramaic retains these meanings.
H4900.emploi: The verb appears 36 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and poems. It primarily expresses the physical action of drawing or dragging (Joseph drawn from the pit, Jeremiah drawn from the well). In the Psalms, it becomes figurative: it is the extension of divine goodness (Psalms 36:11), the attraction of love (Jeremiah 31:3). In Job and Ecclesiastes, it takes on the meaning of prolonging, persisting. Isaiah uses it to "draw" sin as one draws a cart, an image of accumulated guilt. The verb can also mean to walk or advance in a group, like Benjamin following the troop (Judges 5:14).
H4900.portee: This word shows how God acts towards His people: not by constraint, but by the gentle and persistent attraction of His love. The image of drawing also reveals the strength of sin that pulls us away from God, like a rope that draws. For the believer, it is an invitation to understand that God continually draws us to Himself and prolongs His grace upon us, despite our unfaithfulness.

sens: That which is drawn, dragged, pulled
A trail of drops or grains that follows a movement
Comparison, parallelism of two things
H4901.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of an action of drawing or pulling something behind oneself. In Job 28:18, wisdom is worth more than pearls and coral: nothing can be compared to it, it has no equivalent in trail (that is, nothing walks alongside it, nothing is drawn by it in equivalence).
2. A trail can designate what is sown and follows the sower. In Psalms 126:6, the one who walks while sowing seed advances with it behind him, like a trail of grain: his work precedes and follows him at the same time.
3. By extension, the trail becomes a measure of proximity or relation: two things are one beside the other, one following the other, in a relationship of dependence or comparison.
H4901.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to draw" or "to drag." It evokes the concrete image of something being pulled behind oneself, like a rope, a trace, or a seed that is sown while advancing. This root is found in other Hebrew words designating the act of drawing or removing.
H4901.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a position of comparison or relation. In Job 28:18, it expresses the absence of comparison: wisdom has no trail, no equivalent. In Psalms 126:6, it designates the trail of the sower, what follows his act of sowing. In both cases, the word marks a relationship of succession or parallelism: something follows or accompanies the main action.
H4901.portee: This word shows us how true wisdom has no price; no wealth can even be put in trail with it. It also reminds us that faithful work (sowing the seed) bears fruit that follows the one who accomplishes it: the joy of the harvest returns to the one who acted with trust, even in tears.

sens: Son of Japheth and grandson of Noah
Ancestor of a northern people established near the Caucasus
H4902G.detail:
1. Meshech is one of the seven sons of Japheth, himself the son of Noah. He appears in the genealogy of the peoples that populate the earth after the Flood, listed alongside his brothers Gomer, Magog, Madai, Javan, Tubal, and Tiras (Genesis 10:2; 1 Chronicles 1:5). He is a figure from the primitive history of humanity.
2. His descendants are a northern people, often mentioned with the Tubals, Magogs, and other northern nations. The name evokes the Moschi, a people who inhabited the mountainous regions of the Caucasus, at the borders of Colchis and Armenia, far from the lands where the Israelites lived.
H4902G.origine: The name Meshech means "drawing" or "that which is drawn." Its Hebrew etymology refers to the idea of drawing, extracting. In the table of nations in Genesis, all the sons of Japheth receive names that mark their characteristics or geographical origins. Meshech designates the peoples who settled in the mountainous areas of the northeast, far from the cradle of civilization according to the biblical perspective.
H4902G.emploi: Meshech appears only twice in the Bible, both times in genealogical lists: in Genesis 10:2 and in 1 Chronicles 1:5, which repeat the same passage. He is listed in the table of nations that enumerates the descendants of Noah after the Flood, establishing the origins of the peoples known to the ancients. These passages do not tell anything particular about Meshech himself, but situate him as the ancestor of a northern people, often cited with Tubal and Magog, who are also northern and northeastern peoples.

sens: People or region of the ancient north
Descendants of a namesake ancestor
Commercial partner of Tyre
Nation associated with powers hostile to Israel
H4902H.detail:
1. Méschec refers to a people and a region located in the north, probably in ancient Caucasia, between Colchis and Armenia. The name often appears alongside Tubal and Magog, forming a trio of feared northern peoples.
2. According to tradition, Méschec was the son of Japheth and the father of a numerous lineage. This genealogy places the people among the distant and powerful nations known to the Israelites in the ancient world.
3. As a commercial partner, Méschec is among the peoples that traded with Tyre, the great trading city. The passage in Ezekiel 27:13 mentions it alongside Javan and Tubal, exchanging slaves and bronze utensils.
4. In the prophecies of Ezekiel, Méschec becomes a symbol of a hostile power: it is inseparable from Gog and Rosch, forming a war coalition directed against Israel. This people represents the threat from the north, the enemy of God and His people.
H4902H.origine: The name literally means "drawn" or "that which draws" (from the idea of "drawing out"), possibly evoking the action of extraction or traits in battle. In Genesis, Méschec is listed among the sons of Japheth, ancestors of the non-Semitic nations. Historically, this people may correspond to the Moschi, a population known in antiquity on the borders of the Caucasus.
H4902H.emploi: Méschec appears 5 times in the Bible, primarily in the book of Ezekiel (4 occurrences) and once in the Psalms. The psalmist uses it as a figure of exile or distance: "Woe is me that I dwell in Méschec" (Psalm 120:5), transforming this people into a symbol of distance from God. In Ezekiel, it is systematically associated with Tubal, Rosch, and Gog in the context of commercial exchanges (27:13) and especially in eschatological prophecies against a northern coalition threatening Israel (38:2-3; 39:1). Its role evolves from a mere commercial partner to a representative of hostile forces in the end times.
H4902H.portee: Méschec reminds the reader that the threat of evil often comes from the north, from where darkness and distance arise, and that even the most feared political and military powers remain under the sovereign control of God. The prophecies against Gog, prince of Méschec, assure God's people that their enemies, no matter how powerful, will be defeated. It is a call to trust in divine protection in the face of adversity.

sens: People or region of the north, at the borders of the known world
Descendants of a namesake ancestor, associated with warrior nations
H4902I.detail: 1. Méschec refers to an ancient people established in the north, likely around the Caucasus and Armenia. The name evokes the idea of "the one who draws" or "who stretches," perhaps in reference to an ancient leader or founder. 2. In the Bible, the Méschéciens are regularly associated with other distant northern peoples like Tubal and Magog, forming a bloc of warrior and pagan nations in the eyes of the Hebrews. Ezekiel 32:26 mentions them among the fallen powers, struck by the sword, symbolizing divine judgment on the enemies of Israel.
H4902I.origine: The name Méschec comes from a root meaning "to draw" or "to stretch." It is a collective name formed from a namesake ancestor, as many peoples of the ancient Near East: the people bears the name of its founder. The descendants of Méschec are mentioned alongside those of Tubal in the lists of northern peoples.
H4902I.emploi: Méschec appears only once in the Segond (Ezekiel 32:26). The context is that of a lamentation over the fallen nations in the realm of the dead. Ezekiel enumerates the defeated powers—Egypt, Assyria, Edom—and among them are the Méschéciens, described as uncircumcised who have caused terror. This passage reflects Israel's perspective on the distant northern nations: powerful, warlike, but ultimately subject to God's judgment.
H4902I.portee: This mention of Méschec reminds us that God's judgment extends to all peoples, even the most formidable and distant. It assures the reader that no earthly power, even a warrior nation established at the ends of the known world, escapes divine sovereignty.

sens: son of Aram and brother of Uz, Hul, and Geter
ancestor of the northern peoples, including the Moschi
figure from the patriarchal era, ancestor of distant nations
H4902J.detail:
1. Méschec is a son of Aram, himself a son of Shem and grandson of Noah (1 Chronicles 1:17). He has brothers Uz, Hul, and Geter, all mentioned in the genealogy of the peoples who dispersed after the flood.
2. His name means "the one who draws" or "the one who extracts," evoking an action of pulling or separation. In the genealogical text of 1 Chronicles 1:17, he represents a namesake ancestor, that is, the legendary founder of a people.
3. The descendants of Méschec are the peoples who inhabited the regions north of Israel, notably the Moschi, a people established on the borders of Colchis and Armenia. Genealogically, Méschec belongs to the lineage of Shem, not that of Japheth as is sometimes read.
H4902J.origine: The name Méschec (מֶשֶׁךְ) literally means "the one who draws" or "the one who draw out." It comes from a root that evokes the action of extracting or drawing. In the biblical genealogy, this name designates not only a historical or legendary person but also, by extension, the people or nation that comes from it. This naming system is common in the genealogical lists of Genesis and Chronicles, where namesake ancestors give their name to the groups that follow them.
H4902J.emploi: Méschec appears in the Bible within genealogies that enumerate the peoples descended from the sons of Noah after the flood. He is first mentioned in Genesis 10:23 as a son of Aram. The same character reappears in 1 Chronicles 1:17, which reproduces and updates the genealogy of Genesis. In prophetic texts, the descendants of Méschec (or Meshech) are often associated with powers from the distant north, particularly in oracles against Gog or Magog (Ezekiel 27:13; 32:26; 38:2-3; 39:1), where they appear among the allies of Israel's enemies. This association underscores the geographical remoteness and, from the biblical perspective, the potential hostility of these northern peoples.
H4902J.portee: The mention of Méschec in Noah's genealogy reminds readers that all nations of the world are descended from one man and are therefore part of the same divine creation. It also shows how the Bible integrates the known peoples of the ancient world into a global and ordered story. By situating Méschec in the north and among the potential enemies of Israel, it teaches that God knows and controls all nations, from the nearest to the farthest.

sens: Bed or surface on which one sleeps or rests
Place where thoughts and visions come, especially during sleep
H4903.detail:
1. The word designates the bed or couch on which a person physically rests. It is the piece of furniture where one lies down to sleep or rest. In the biblical context, it is an intimate and personal place, the one where King Nebuchadnezzar slept before having his visions (Daniel 2:28).
2. The word takes on a spiritual or mental meaning: the couch becomes the place where deep thoughts, dreams, and visions arise. It is on his couch that the king sees in a dream the giant tree that represents his reign (Daniel 4:10), and it is also while lying down that Daniel receives his own prophetic visions (Daniel 7:1). The couch is thus the setting where God communicates through dreams and revelations.
H4903.origine: The Aramaic word מִשְׁכַּב (mishkav) comes from the Hebrew root שׁכב (shakh) which means "to lie down, to be reclined." It is the same word as in biblical Hebrew (H4904), where the same root produces related forms designating the bed or place of rest. The image is that of the body lying down, motionless, vulnerable to sleep and the visions that visit it.
H4903.emploi: The word appears six times in the book of Daniel, always to designate the bed of King Nebuchadnezzar or that of Daniel during their prophetic dreams. In Daniel 2:28-29, it is on his couch that the king received the dream that troubled his spirit. In Daniel 4:5, 4:10, and 4:13, the word returns to situate the visions and frightening thoughts that overwhelm the king. In Daniel 7:1, it is on his couch that Daniel himself has the vision of the four beasts. In all cases, the couch is the privileged place where the doors of divine mystery open and where human thoughts confront heavenly revelations.
H4903.portee: This word reminds us that God speaks to His people in the intimacy of rest, away from the noise and agitation of the world. The couch is the place of vulnerability where the defenseless man meets the Eternal. For the believer, this invites us to see sleep and rest not as emptiness, but as a time when God can still instruct the soul, correct thoughts, and reveal His plans.

sens: Piece of furniture or surface on which one lies down to sleep or rest
Act of lying down, stretching out to sleep or rest
Intimate or sexual relationship between a man and a woman
Room or place where one sleeps
H4904.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the piece of furniture itself: a bed on which one rests (2 Samuel 13:5: "Lie down on the bed"). It is the physical object where one lies down.
2. It also signifies the act of lying down, the very action of stretching out to sleep or rest (Job 33:19: "man is chastened on his couch" during illness, referring to the moment when he lies in suffering).
3. In many passages in Leviticus and Numbers, "couch" has a very concrete meaning: that of a man and that of a woman designates the act or context of carnal intimacy (Leviticus 15:24: "any bed on which he lies will be unclean"). The "couch" of someone can also refer to their intimate partner.
4. By extension, the couch is the bedroom, the place of rest and intimacy, where one withdraws (Ecclesiastes 10:20: "in the room where you lie down").
H4904.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root "shkb" which means "to lie down, to stretch out." It is a very ancient term, common throughout the Old Testament to designate the action of lying down and its place. The equivalent Aramaic form is identical. The word is concrete: it paints the image of the body lying down, at rest or in intimacy, and the furniture that receives it.
H4904.emploi: This word appears 44 times in the Old Testament, particularly in the Pentateuch (Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers) and in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings). It is used in three main contexts: illness and rest (Job 33:19, Psalms 41:4), ritual purity (Leviticus 15: the couch is defiled by bodily fluids), and marital or illicit intimacy (Genesis 49:4: the father's couch, Leviticus 18:22). In the prophets, it can take on a figurative dimension: Isaiah 57:8 speaks of the "couch" in a context of religious infidelity. The word is simple and unambiguous: always a place or act of rest or intimacy.
H4904.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility of the body and the importance of rest. It also emphasizes that carnal intimacy is not a taboo subject in the Bible, but framed by God's Law: ritual and moral purity in marriage are essential. The "couch" of Psalm 4:5 ("Lie down in your hearts") invites introspection and repentance. In summary, this word helps the believer see that their life of rest and intimacy falls within the realm that God governs.

sens: Poem or song intended for the praise of God
Composition that expresses meditation or spiritual teaching
Musical piece entrusted to the chief musicians of the temple
H4905.detail:
1. The canticle is primarily a poem or song addressed to God in prayer and praise. It is a literary genre intended to be sung, as shown by the inscription of Psalm 47:8: "Sing a canticle!", where the action verb accompanies the mention of the canticle.
2. Beyond simple praise, the canticle is often a poem of contemplation or spiritual teaching: it invites reflection on moral life and the relationship with God. Psalm 78:1 begins with "A canticle of Asaph. My people, listen to my instructions!" — the canticle becomes a means of transmitting God's wisdom to the community.
3. In the temple liturgy, the canticle is an official musical composition, given to the chief musicians to be performed publicly. Almost all uses include the mention "To the chief musician," which shows its role in regular worship.
H4905.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "sakhel," which means "to be prudent, to have understanding, to meditate." The canticle is therefore originally a poem that bears the marks of reflection and wisdom. This is why many canticles are compositions of sages (Asaph in Psalm 78) or personal testimonies marked by spiritual understanding.
H4905.emploi: The word "canticle" appears 14 times in the Bible, exclusively in the titles of the Psalms. It designates poems attributed to recognized composers: David (Psalms 32, 53, 55, 142), the sons of Korah (Psalms 42, 44, 45), Asaph (Psalm 78). These canticles alternate between joyful praise (Psalm 47: "Sing a canticle!"), confession and penitence (Psalm 32 on the forgiveness of sin), and community instruction (Psalm 78 exposing God's actions in history). All are intended for the direction of the chief musicians, confirming that they are liturgical pieces performed regularly.
H4905.portee: The canticle invites the believer to express their faith not through empty words, but through meditation rooted in the wisdom of God. It teaches that sincere praise comes through reflection on who God is and how to live in His presence. The canticle calls to sing not only with the voice but also with the spirit, internalizing spiritual truth.

sens: Sculpture or carved statue, particularly an idol
Object or representation formed by the art of the sculptor or engraver
Thought, imagination, conception of the mind
Evil thought or guilty idea
H4906.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a sculpted or carved form in stone or wood, particularly an idol intended for worship: in Leviticus 26:1, God forbids Israel from making "carved idols," stone or metal statues that neighboring peoples will "erect" as places of worship (Numbers 33:52). 2. The word can also refer to a work of art that is chiseled, engraved, or crafted by hand — for example, the "chiseling" of silver on which golden apples are placed, symbolizing wise words (Proverbs 25:11). 3. By a natural shift, the word takes on the meaning of thought or imagination: the "thoughts" of the hearts of unjust men come from their mouths (Psalms 73:7), like the fruits of what they secretly imagine. 4. In the context of sin, it refers to an evil thought or hidden intention: the elders of Israel had filled their chambers with "figures" representing the idols to which they secretly devoted themselves, believing that the Lord would not see them (Ezekiel 8:12) — the word then designates both the idol and the thought of apostasy it expresses. It is also the imagination of pride: the rich see their wealth as a "high wall" in their "imagination," meaning in their intimate dream (Proverbs 18:11).
H4906.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to form" or "to shape" — hence the idea of giving form to something. The root also appears in other Hebrew words related to creation, shaping, and craftsmanship. The basic image is that of the hand of the sculptor or engraver creating a visible form. From there, the word naturally extends to what the mind "shapes" — the thoughts one forges in secret, the images one creates in imagination.
H4906.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in contexts of idolatrous worship or hidden thought. In Leviticus 26:1 and Numbers 33:52, it refers to the idol statues that the Canaanite peoples set up in the Promised Land and that the Israelites must destroy. In Ezekiel 8:12, the "figures" are the idolatrous images that the elders of Israel contemplate in secret, representing their hidden unfaithfulness. In Psalms 73:7 and Proverbs 18:11, the word applies to the thoughts of the heart — the evil intentions that spring from the unjust man, or the pride that the rich maintain in their hearts. Proverbs 25:11 offers a more neutral usage: the word simply designates a chiseled work of art, the decorative frame that highlights a wise word.
H4906.portee: This word reminds us that idolatry never begins with a mere statue: it begins with a "figure" that one creates in the heart, a thought, an imagination. The elders of Israel sculpted idols in stone, but they first carved images in their minds — and it is this secret thought that God saw. For the reader, it is a lesson on transparency: no hidden thought escapes God. It is also a warning: what one cultivates in their imagination easily becomes what one worships.

sens: The place where one lives, where one resides
The dwelling place of God, His habitation among His people
H4907.detail:
1. A dwelling is simply a place where someone lives, where they have their abode. It is the general term to describe the home or habitation of a person.
2. In the biblical text, this dwelling particularly refers to the dwelling of God in Jerusalem — the place where His presence resides, namely the temple. When the king of Ezra sends gold and silver to Jerusalem "to the dwelling" of the God of Israel, he acknowledges that God dwells there, that He has established His presence (Ezra 7:15).
H4907.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to dwell" or "to reside." It is closely related to its more well-known synonym, "tabernacle" (H4908 in Strong's numbering), which refers to the holy tent of God's presence in the wilderness. Both share the fundamental idea of a place where God "dwells" with His people — whether it be the portable tent in the desert or the permanent temple in Jerusalem.
H4907.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezra 7:15, where it refers to the dwelling of God in Jerusalem. In this context, the Persian king Artaxerxes publicly acknowledges that the God of Israel has a dwelling, a place of residence, in the holy city. The term emphasizes that God is not absent or distant, but that He truly dwells among His people, in a tangible and localized manner.
H4907.portee: This term reminds us of a profound truth at the heart of biblical faith: God does not remain far away in heaven, but establishes His dwelling among His own. It also shows how even foreign rulers could recognize and respect the God of Israel, and understand that He had a holy place, a habitation at the heart of His chosen people.

sens: Portable worship tent built by Israel in the desert, dwelling of God among the people
Structure made of frames, curtains, and carpets with the sacred furniture it houses
Set of utensils and objects of worship used in this tent
Place of divine presence, sanctuary where God dwells with His people
H4908.detail:
1. The tabernacle is primarily a large tent that the Israelites built in the desert according to God's instructions. Moses receives the precise plan for this dwelling from God (Exodus 25:9), and skilled artisans make it with ten fine linen curtains (Exodus 36:8). It is a removable structure that the people set up, transport, and reassemble as they move: after a month in the desert, the tabernacle is erected for the first time on the first day of the second month of the second year (Exodus 40:17).
2. Materially, the tabernacle includes several elements: a wooden frame (boards and crossbars), curtains and carpets that cover everything, and all the liturgical equipment inside. The sons of Gershon and the sons of Merari each had the responsibility of transporting certain parts during the marches in the desert (Numbers 10:17, Numbers 3:8).
3. The word also refers to all the sacred objects: the ark, the table, the lampstand, the altar of incense. This is why the translation sometimes uses "sanctuary" or "dwelling."
4. Theologically, the tabernacle is the place where God dwells among His people. It is the visible and portable manifestation of His blessing presence: the glory of the Lord fills the tabernacle after its completion (Exodus 40:34), and it then guides them (Exodus 40:36-38).
H4908.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to dwell" or "to reside." Its primary meaning is therefore "dwelling" or "place of habitation." In the Old Testament, it applies to God's residence, which, instead of remaining distant and transcendent, descends to dwell among His people in the form of a portable tent. This choice of a tent — and not a stone temple — says something about God's intention: to accompany His people in their movements and trials, rather than remaining confined to a single location.
H4908.emploi: The word tabernacle appears 129 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the books of Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers. In Exodus, it first describes the plan given by God (Exodus 25:9), then the meticulous construction by the artisans (Exodus 36:8), and finally its erection and possession by the divine glory (Exodus 40:17-38). In Numbers, the tabernacle is the center of everything: the tribes camp around it (Numbers 3), it is guarded by the Levites (Numbers 1:50-53), and it moves with the people on the march (Numbers 10:17). The word is also used metonymically to refer to the utensils of worship (Numbers 3:8). Only once in our references, in Job 18:21, does it take a figurative sense and refer to the "destiny" of the wicked — their "dwelling" or lot — which shows how the tabernacle, as a dwelling, can symbolize a person's state or fate.
H4908.portee: The tabernacle teaches the believer that God does not remain distant and abstract, but desires to dwell at the very heart of His people's lives. This portable tent, much more than a stationary temple, indicates that God accompanies His people in the desert and in exile. For the Christian, the tabernacle foreshadows Christ Himself: in Jesus, God pitched His tent among us and dwelt in our flesh (John 1:14 uses this same image of dwelling). Meditating on the tabernacle invites the believer to see in the Lord a benevolent and accessible presence, not distant behind veils, but close to those who seek Him.

sens: Payment in money or goods given in exchange for work
Reward, remuneration given by God for a faithful or just act
H4909.detail:
1. Salary is what one receives as payment for the work they have accomplished. Jacob asks Laban: "What will your wages be?" (Genesis 29:15) — it is the agreed price in advance for fourteen years of service to receive Rachel as a wife. It is a concrete exchange: work for compensation.
2. In a broader sense, the word refers to the reward that God grants to those who act with justice and faithfulness. Ruth, who showed kindness to Naomi, receives the blessing: "May your reward be full from the Lord" (Ruth 2:12). Here, it is God Himself who "pays" in blessings to those who do what is right.
H4909.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to keep" or "to observe." Salary is what is "kept" for you in return for your faithfulness — it is your due. In Hebrew as in French, salary links the idea of work accomplished and deserved compensation.
H4909.emploi: The word appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, three times for earthly wages and once for divine reward. The first three occurrences (Genesis 29:15; 31:7, 31:41) all concern Jacob and Laban: Jacob complains that Laban has "changed his wages ten times," showing that salary can be subject to negotiation or injustice. The last occurrence (Ruth 2:12) elevates the concept: the reward becomes God's blessing on those who practice charity. The word thus refers to both human payment and divine remuneration.
H4909.portee: This word reminds the reader of a fundamental biblical truth: work deserves just compensation, and the injustice of a master who changes the terms of payment is a transgression. More deeply, Ruth 2:12 opens the spiritual horizon: God does not forget those who act with justice and mercy. This promise of divine reward encourages the believer to faithfulness, knowing that God will "pay" what is just — not by calculation, but by grace.

sens: Exercer l'autorité, le pouvoir sur quelqu'un ou quelque chose
Régner, gouverner un peuple ou un royaume
Commander, diriger en tant que maître ou chef
S'imposer, prévaloir sur
Contrôler, maîtriser (ses passions, ses actes)
H4910.detail:
1. Exercer l'autorité, le pouvoir sur quelqu'un ou quelque chose : c'est avoir la mainmise, commander. Les astres sont placés dans le ciel « pour présider au jour et à la nuit » (Genesis 1:18) — ils règlent le temps comme un roi règle son royaume. Un serviteur peut « dominer » sur le maître si celui-ci est insensé (Proverbs 17:2) : l'ordre naturel s'inverse.
2. Régner, gouverner un peuple ou un royaume : c'est l'exercice du pouvoir politique et royal. Gédéon refuse de « dominer » sur Israël, reconnaissant que seul l'Éternel « dominera » sur eux (Judges 8:23). David établit son règne sur tout Israël (2 Samuel 23:3).
3. Commander, diriger en tant que maître ou chef : c'est occuper une position de responsabilité et d'autorité directe. Un roi envoie son intendant qui « dominera » sur ses biens (Genesis 24:2).
4. S'imposer, prévaloir sur : avoir le dessus, l'emporter. « La main des diligents dominera », tandis que la main lâche sera tributaire (Proverbs 12:24) : l'effort triomphe de la paresse.
5. Contrôler, maîtriser ses passions ou ses actes : c'est une domination intérieure. Le péché désire avoir le contrôle sur l'homme, mais celui-ci peut résister (Genesis 4:7).
H4910.origine: Le verbe vient d'une racine hébraïque exprimant l'idée de tenir fermement, de saisir avec force. Il renvoie au latin « dominari » (dominer), dont nous tenons « domination ». Dans l'Ancien Testament grec, on le traduit souvent par « arkho » (commander) ou « exousiazo » (exercer l'autorité). Le mot évoque l'image du berger qui tient son troupeau, ou du roi qui tient les rênes de son royaume.
H4910.emploi: Le verbe « dominer » apparaît 74 fois dans l'Ancien Testament. Il s'emploie d'abord pour décrire l'ordre créé : Dieu donne aux astres et à l'homme la charge de dominer (Genesis 1:18, Psalms 8:7). Il caractérise le pouvoir royal et politique : les rois « dominent » sur leurs royaumes (1 Kings 4:21), et les prophètes décrivent les rois étrangers qui doivent « dominer » Israël en châtiment (Isaiah 3:4, Ezekiel 19:11). Il s'applique aussi aux rapports humains quotidiens : un serviteur peut dominer, une main diligente domine (Proverbs 12:24). Le verbe peut exprimer l'autorité du péché sur l'homme (Genesis 4:7), mettant en lumière une forme de domination contre nature qui menace l'homme.
H4910.portee: Ce mot ouvre au lecteur la question du pouvoir et de l'ordre : d'où vient l'autorité ? Qui doit dominer ? Dieu seul possède une domination absolue et juste ; tout pouvoir humain en est une délégation responsable. Comprendre ce que signifie « dominer » aide le croyant à réfléchir à sa propre autorité — si peu soit-elle — et à reconnaître que le vrai pouvoir appartient à Dieu seul.

sens: Être similaire à quelque chose ou quelqu'un, avoir des traits communs
Devenir pareil à, égal à quelqu'un d'autre
Être comparé à, mis en parallèle avec
H4911A.detail:
1. Être similaire à quelque chose ou quelqu'un, avoir des traits communs : le mot décrit une ressemblance réelle entre deux choses. Quand Job dit « je ressemble à la poussière et à la cendre » (Job 30:19), il veut dire qu'il est devenu aussi misérable et insignifiant que de la poussière. C'est une ressemblance dans l'état ou la condition.

2. Devenir pareil à, égal à quelqu'un d'autre : le mot souligne parfois le passage d'un état à un autre, le fait de devenir comme. Quand on dit à quelqu'un dans son abaissement « tu es devenu semblable à nous » (Isaiah 14:10), cela signifie qu'il a perdu sa force et son honneur — il s'est réduit au même niveau que les faibles. C'est un changement, une chute.

3. Être comparé à, mis en parallèle avec : le mot peut aussi exprimer une simple comparaison établie entre deux réalités. Psalms 49:13 et 49:21 comparent l'homme sans intelligence aux bêtes qu'on égorge : il est placé sur le même plan qu'elles, dépourvu de ce qui le distinguerait.
H4911A.origine: Ce verbe vient d'une racine hébraïque exprimant l'idée de ressemblance et de parité. Il est lié au nom hébreu משַׁל (mashal), qui signifie « proverbe » ou « parabole » — ce parallèle étymologique est révélateur : une parabole fonctionne en comparant une chose à une autre, en établissant une ressemblance instructive. Le verbe décrit donc le mouvement même d'une comparaison : montrer que deux choses se ressemblent.
H4911A.emploi: Ce verbe apparaît sept fois dans l'Ancien Testament, surtout dans les Psaumes et les prophètes. Il exprime généralement comment une personne dans le malheur ressemble à quelque chose d'abaissé ou de sans valeur : la poussière, la cendre, les bêtes à l'abattage, ou les morts qui descendent dans la fosse. C'est un mot des lamentations et de l'humiliation. Dans Isaiah 14:10, il décrit aussi comment les puissants déchus se trouvent ramenés à l'égalité des faibles. Le sens ne varie guère : partout, il s'agit de constater qu'on est devenu pareil à quelque chose d'inférieur ou de déshonorant.
H4911A.portee: Ce mot montre comment la Bible parle de l'abaissement et de la dégradation : quand une personne « ressemble » à la poussière ou aux bêtes, c'est que sa condition s'est effondrée, qu'elle a perdu ce qui lui donnait dignité et valeur. Cela aide le lecteur à saisir le désespoir des psalmistes qui crient vers Dieu : ils se sentent réduits à néant. C'est aussi un appel à la miséricorde divine : comment supporter d'être assimilé à la mort et au néant ?

sens: To pronounce a concise word that contains a general truth or moral lesson
To express a thought in the form of poetry, riddle, or parable
To formulate a saying, a maxim that everyone knows and repeats
To apply to someone a well-known saying or proverbial formula
H4911B.detail:
1. To say a proverb means to express in few words a truth recognized by the wise that can be applied to many cases. It is the short and grave word that strikes the mind. In Ezekiel 18:2, the people of Israel say, "Say this proverb": "The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge" — everyone repeats it to complain.
2. The word also applies to one who speaks in riddles or parables, that is, in veiled, mysterious language that requires reflection. Ezekiel 17:2: "Propose a riddle, speak a parable to the house of Israel!" — the prophet must wrap his message in a striking image.
3. To say a proverb is also to circulate a ready-made phrase, a formula that everyone uses. The mocking speeches mentioned in Ezekiel 12:23 are sayings that people repeat at will.
4. To apply a proverb to someone is to use a known word to judge or criticize them. In Ezekiel 16:44, those who say proverbs "will apply this proverb" to Jerusalem: "Like mother, like daughter" — meaning she resembles her mother in her guilt.
H4911B.origine: The Hebrew verb mashal comes from a root that evokes the idea of "similarity" or "parallel." A proverb brings two things together to draw a lesson: it says "it is like...", establishing a similarity. The noun mashal (proverb, parable, saying) is very ancient in Hebrew; it can be found in the Psalms and the wisdom books. The central notion is that of a word that enlightens by putting two realities in parallel.
H4911B.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost always in Ezekiel, the prophet who loves riddles and parables. Ezekiel 17:2 commands the prophet to "speak a parable" to teach. Ezekiel 18:2-3 reports a popular proverb that the people "say" or "hold" from mouth to ear, and God commands that it cease to be said. Ezekiel 16:44 shows how a known proverb is "applied" to someone. In Numbers 21:27, "the poets say," meaning they compose and recite a song-proverb. The verb shifts from the meaning "to express in parable" to the meaning "to compose a poetic formula" or "to circulate a saying." It is an act of speech: to say, to formulate, to compose, to transmit.
H4911B.portee: This word reminds us of the place that the Bible gives to wise and memorable words. A proverb is a tool of transmission: it engraves a truth in minds. For the Christian, this shows the importance of poetic language and riddles in God's revelation — Jesus himself will often teach in parables. It is also a warning: the words we repeat, the sayings we "hold" from mouth to ear can be false or mocking; the Lord, in Ezekiel, commands the people to cease repeating a deceptive saying.

sens: A short and memorable formula expressing a truth, a moral maxim, or practical wisdom
A comparison or brief story that illustrates a lesson or hidden truth
An enigmatic word or prophetic oracle
A mocking discourse or derisive word that makes someone an object of ridicule
A poetic statement or ethical and sapiential saying
H4912.detail:
1. A proverb in the strict sense is a short and striking formula that states a truth about life: "As the legs of the lame are weak, so is a saying in the mouth of fools" (Proverbs 26:7). It is a practical teaching intended to guide behavior.
2. The proverb can also be a comparison or a parable that veils a lesson under an image: Ezekiel is commanded to pronounce enigmatic parables about Jerusalem (Ezekiel 17:2). The deep meaning requires interpretation.
3. A prophetic oracle bears this name when it is stated in a solemn and mysterious form: Balaam pronounces oracles against Moab and Israel (Numbers 23:7, Numbers 24:23). It is the powerful word of a seer.
4. The proverb becomes a word of mockery, a derisive word: one who transgresses the law becomes "a subject of sarcasm and ridicule among all the peoples" (2 Chronicles 7:20). It becomes an object of ridicule.
5. Finally, it is a general term for any form of wise or poetic speech: the book of Proverbs gathers "sayings of wisdom" (Proverbs 1:1, Proverbs 10:1), while Ecclesiastes 12:11 compares the words of the wise to nails firmly planted.
H4912.origine: The Hebrew word mashal comes from a root that means "to dominate" or "to govern" (compare with the word melek, king). The basic idea is that the spoken word dominates and imposes itself: a true wise or prophetic word exercises authority. From there comes the extension to any memorable formula that imposes itself on the mind and governs thought. The word may also have evolved towards the meaning of "comparison" (that which is placed in regard) and "mockery" (that which negatively imposes itself on someone).
H4912.emploi: The word mashal appears 39 times in the Old Testament and is especially prominent in three contexts: wisdom, prophecy, and mockery. In the wisdom books (Proverbs, Job, Ecclesiastes), it is the moral saying and aphorism: the Proverbs of Solomon are a collection of mashal (Proverbs 1:1). Among the prophets, particularly Ezekiel and Balaam, it is the oracle and prophetic parable: veiled words that require a key to interpretation (Ezekiel 17:2, Ezekiel 24:3). In the context of punishment, it is the word that makes someone an object of ridicule: Israel becomes a proverb, an object of mockery, if it violates the covenant (Deuteronomy 28:37, 1 Kings 9:7). Isaiah 14:4 and Habakkuk 2:6 testify to this: the tyrant becomes a byword, a word of derision over which one leans. The word thus covers all types of striking statements that impose themselves on memory and conscience.
H4912.portee: The proverb is not a literary decoration: it is wisdom that governs life. Studying the proverbs of the Bible is to allow oneself to be shaped by a wise word that imposes itself with authority on the disciple's path. Moreover, prophetic parables remind us that God continues to speak in mysterious images to probe the heart: listening to proverbs is to remain attentive to the voice of God. Finally, to become a proverb oneself is a serious threat: it invites the people of God to humility and faithfulness.

sens: City of Asher assigned to the Gershonite Levites
H4913.detail: Maschal is a city located in the territory of the tribe of Asher, in the land of Israel. It was assigned to the Levites of the family of Gershon, descendants of Levi responsible for the service of the tabernacle and later the temple. Its name appears in the list of Levitical cities, showing that Israel reserved certain urban centers for priests and Levites to allow them to carry out their religious ministry among the people (1 Chronicles 6:74).
H4913.origine: The name Maschal (מָשָׁל) literally means "entreaty" or request. It is a city in northern Galilee, in Asher, a fertile coastal region of the Israelite territory. It is sometimes also mentioned under the name of Mishal (מִשְׁאָל), with both forms possibly designating the same place.
H4913.emploi: Maschal appears only once in the Bible in French (Segond 1910), in the context of the distribution of Levitical cities among the families of the Levites. After the conquest of Canaan, the twelve tribes of Israel distributed cities to the Levites who had not received their own territory, since their inheritance was the service of the Lord. Maschal is included in this enumeration for the tribe of Asher, confirming its status as a Levitical city intended for the descendants of Gershon.

sens: Word or speech that has become proverbial and mocking
Proverb or saying ridiculed that circulates about someone
Person who becomes the subject of ridicule and derision
H4914.detail:
1. A fable is a discourse, an expression, or a saying that circulates among people and becomes a sort of mocking proverb — it is repeated, amplified, and mocked. This is why Job says he has become the fable of the peoples: everyone talks about him, but to ridicule him, not to honor him (Job 17:6).
2. It is also a person themselves who becomes, through their misfortune or infamy, a sort of negative legend — a living example spoken of as a story or a warning. Job has become "the fable of the peoples": he exists in the eyes of others only as a subject of gossip and contempt.
3. The word carries the idea of public disgrace: one who has become a fable has lost their honor, their integrity; they no longer count, they are pointed at, and they are cited as an example for criticism or amusement.
H4914.origine: The Hebrew word meshôl comes from a root that originally means "to resemble" or "to be similar." From there comes the idea of what is comparable, what illustrates an idea — hence "proverb," "parable," or "fable." Here, the word has taken on a pejorative color: a fable that is mocked, a word that resembles a despised story and that circulates from mouth to mouth.
H4914.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible in this precise sense (Job 17:6). It describes Job's condition: overwhelmed with suffering and abandoned by his friends, he has lost all dignity. He is no longer a respectable man, but a curious case, a subject of malicious conversation. What people repeat about him — his misfortunes, his degradation — has become a fable, that is, a public discourse where his name is attached to shame rather than honor. It is the painful echo of the isolation that Job complains of: he has become an object of contempt.
H4914.portee: This word evokes the cruelty of hasty judgment and gossip. When someone suffers or shipwrecks, they risk becoming a "fable" — a dark legend, a story told to mock. For the Christian reader, it is a call to compassion: before repeating or mocking the misfortune of another, one must remember that the fable we spread hides a human suffering, and that God hears our words and sees our hearts.

sens: No person, no being, in a comparison
No one who is equal or similar to someone
H4915A.detail:
1. The word expresses complete absence: there is no person or creature comparable to the one being spoken of. In Job 41:24, speaking of the Leviathan, the author declares that "there is none on earth" who is its master — that is, no creature equals its strength or can dominate it.
2. More broadly, it conveys the idea of a one-of-a-kind, an incomparable: no one resembles it, no one is of its rank. It is an assertion of absolute superiority.
H4915A.origine: The Hebrew word מֹשֶׁל (moshel) comes from a root that speaks of resemblance and comparison. It is related to words meaning "equal," "similar," or "one who is like." This root expresses the fundamental idea of parity or similarity: to say that there is no moshel is to affirm that there is no one like it.
H4915A.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 41:24, in the impressive description of the Leviathan — this sea monster that no human can master. The author uses this term to emphasize the absolute uniqueness of this creature: no equal exists on earth. Used in a poetic and rhetorical manner, it reinforces the image of a superhuman and incomparable power.
H4915A.portee: This word invites reflection on what has no equal. In the context of the Leviathan, it shows the limits of human power in the face of the formidable creatures that God has formed. For the believer, it also speaks of the uniqueness of God Himself: there is none who is comparable to Him, no equal among the gods or creatures.

sens: Power to rule, sovereign authority
Exercising control over a territory or people
State or condition of one who reigns
H4915B.detail:
1. The word designates the power of a king or sovereign — his right and ability to command. In Zechariah 9:10, the Messiah "will rule from sea to sea," which paints the extent of His future empire over all peoples.
2. It is also the action of reigning, of concretely exercising authority. The context of Daniel 11:4 shows a kingdom that loses its power and domination: the Messiah who succeeds Alexander will "not be as powerful as he was," for his empire will fragment.
3. By extension, it is the condition or status of one who possesses this power — the act of reigning, the established state of domination.
H4915B.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to reign" or "to be master." It evokes the image of a king sitting on his throne, commanding his people. The same verb in Hebrew produces this noun to designate the power itself. This term particularly applies to kings and empires that control territories and nations.
H4915B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in prophetic contexts. In Daniel 11:4, it describes the loss of domination of an empire that disintegrates after the death of a great conqueror. In Zechariah 9:10, it announces the future domination of the Messiah over all the earth, of a universal and definitive scope. These two uses contrast: one shows the collapse of human and earthly domination, the other affirms the establishment of a permanent and beneficial messianic domination.
H4915B.portee: This word reminds us that all human power is fragile and fleeting — empires break and fragment. But it also announces that Christ will reign with eternal and just authority, bringing peace to all nations. For the believer, it is an assurance: behind the upheavals of history, the Messiah is progressively establishing His unshakeable kingdom.

sens: Action of letting go, of releasing
Possession, wealth, riches
Project or work that one undertakes
H4916A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of letting go or releasing: in Isaiah 7:25, one will "let loose" the ox and the sheep in the abandoned mountains, meaning they will be allowed to graze freely. It is the act of releasing something or someone.
2. By extension, the word designates what one possesses, what one has in hand and can use or share: the "goods" that God gives to His people (Deuteronomy 12:7, 12:18). It is wealth or what one holds.
3. In a more abstract sense, an "enterprise" is a project, a work, or an endeavor that one carries out: God blesses all your "enterprises" (Deuteronomy 15:10, 28:8), meaning all your projects and works.
H4916A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to send" or "to let go." The same family produces the word "sending" or "mission." The basic image is that of extending the hand to send something far away, or to release what one was holding. This root also appears in the name of Passover: "Pesach" literally means "passage" or "crossing," because God "sent" the plagues and let them pass over the houses of the Hebrews.
H4916A.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Old Testament, mostly in Deuteronomy. It first designates possessions or goods that God grants (Deuteronomy 12:7, 12:18: the goods one can eat before the Lord with joy). It then takes on the meaning of "enterprise" or "project" in passages that speak of divine blessing on work and human affairs (Deuteronomy 15:10, 28:8: blessing on enterprises). In Isaiah 7:25, it regains the concrete sense of "letting go" or "releasing." The word conveys the idea of what one launches, possesses, or carries out successfully.
H4916A.portee: This word reminds the believer that all work, all possession, all project comes from God and depends on His blessing. When the Bible speaks of blessing the "enterprises," it invites seeking divine favor not only in prayer but in every daily action. It is an invitation to recognize that success is not solely due to human will, but to God's support.

sens: portion of food or goods sent to someone
what is seized, taken by force from an enemy
gesture of generosity or sharing
H4916B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a portion — of food, of goods — that is sent to another person. In the book of Esther, during the feast of Purim, the Jews send "portions to one another" (Esther 9:19, 9:22), meaning they share food as a sign of joy and brotherhood.
2. By extension, the word can mean "prey," what is conquered or taken by force from an enemy. Isaiah speaks of the "prey" that the descendants of Jacob will take from neighboring peoples (Isaiah 11:14), using the image of what falls into the hands of the victor.
3. Beyond the material object, the "sending" evokes an act of goodwill: sharing one's goods with others, whether through generosity towards a friend or by military obligation towards the victor.
H4916B.origine: The Hebrew word מִשְׁלוֹחַ (mishloach) comes from the verb שׁלַח (shlach), "to send, to release, to dispatch." The root evokes the idea of putting something in motion, extending it, or sending it far away. The "sending" is therefore what is launched towards someone, set in motion for their sake. Mishloach is a spelling variant of mishloach (מִשְׁלַח), primarily attested in later texts such as Esther.
H4916B.emploi: This word appears only three times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in the books of Esther and Isaiah. In Esther 9:19 and 9:22, it describes the custom of Purim: the Jews exchange "portions" of food and gifts in celebration of their deliverance. The "sending" here takes on a festive and communal dimension, sealing the covenant between the Jews and their regained joy. In Isaiah 11:14, the same word, translated as "prey," evokes the spoils of war: what the conquered peoples entrust to the hands of the victor. Despite this diversity of uses, the fundamental meaning remains: something that passes from one hand to another, that is given or sent.
H4916B.portee: This word reminds the reader of the beauty of sharing and generosity: in Esther, it symbolizes how a community celebrates its salvation by giving each other goods. It also invites reflection on solidarity — making a "sending" to one's brother or neighbor is to recognize their need and their right to enjoy the common blessing. For those who understand God's grace, it is a reflection of divine generosity itself.

sens: A group of people sent on a mission
A sending, an expedition
A deliverance, a release from a situation
H4917.detail:
1. A group is a collection of people gathered to accomplish a specific mission. In Psalms 78:49, God sends a "group of messengers of calamity": these are not armed soldiers, but angels or celestial beings tasked with executing divine judgment. It is the image of an organized sending.
2. The word can more broadly refer to a sending or an expedition: something that is launched or dispatched somewhere with a purpose. This is the meaning of the verb from which it comes: to send, to dispatch.
3. In the context of Ecclesiastes 8:8, "deliverance" translates the same word: it refers to the possibility of escaping from evil, of being freed from servitude. Man has no "deliverance" on the day of death — no means of being sent far from the fight, of escaping it.
H4917.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root שׁלח (shalah), which means "to send, to dispatch." It is very common in biblical Hebrew. The form used here is a feminine noun that designates the action of sending or the group sent. Related words: שָׁלִיחַ (shaliah, "sent one, messenger"), שִׁלּוּחַ (shiluah, "sending, repudiation").
H4917.emploi: This word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 78:49, in the account of the plagues of Egypt, it designates a group of celestial creatures or plagues sent by God. In Ecclesiastes 8:8, it takes on the meaning of "deliverance, escape," to express human powerlessness in the face of death. It is a poetic word, especially used in theological or reflective contexts, where it expresses either the divine action of sending His agents or the absence of an exit, of possible escape.
H4917.portee: This word reminds us that God is sovereign in the execution of His plans: He sends His messengers, His judgments. It also shows one of the great realities of the human condition — our inability to escape death. For the believer, this underscores their dependence on God and the importance of turning to Him rather than seeking an escape by oneself.

sens: Character from the divided monarchy period
Father of Ahaziah and grandfather of Shaphan the scribe
H4918G.detail: Meschullam is a man who lived during the period of the divided monarchy of Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible: as the father of Ahaziah and grandfather of Shaphan, the scribe of King Josiah who played an important role in the discovery of the Book of the Law in the temple (2 Kings 22:3).
H4918G.origine: The name Meschullam means "friend" in Hebrew, formed from a root evoking peace and friendship. This name appears several times in the Old Testament to designate different people, notably Levites and leaders of the people during the reconstruction after the exile.
H4918G.emploi: Meschullam appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Kings 22:3, where he is presented as the father of Ahaziah and the grandfather of Shaphan. Shaphan, his grandson, is the scribe of King Josiah and was one of the key figures during the rediscovery of the Book of the Law in the temple, a determining event for the religious reform of the kingdom of Judah.

sens: Man of the tribe of Gad during the divided monarchy
H4918I.detail: Meschullam is a man of the tribe of Gad mentioned in the genealogical register of the sons of Abihail. He lived during the time when the kingdoms of Israel and Judah were divided, and he is listed among the seven brothers descended from Gad.
H4918I.origine: The name Meschullam means "friend" in Hebrew, formed from a root expressing friendship or reconciliation. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by many important people: priests, Levites, restorers of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile. The name reflects the importance of friendship and peace in the community of Israel.
H4918I.emploi: Meschullam of the tribe of Gad is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 5:13, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Gad. He is presented there as one of the seven sons of Abihail, alongside Michael, Sheba, Jorai, Jaecan, Zia, and Eber. This passage simply archives his place in the genealogical history of Israel, without reporting any particular events of his life.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H4918J.detail: Meschullam is a proper name referring to a man of the tribe of Benjamin. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:17, where he is listed among the sons of Elpaal. The genealogical context shows that he lived during the time of the Divided Monarchy in Israel, when the kingdom was divided between Judah and Northern Israel.
H4918J.origine: The name Meschullam means "friend" in Hebrew, derived from the root שלם (shalôm) which evokes peace, wholeness, and friendship. This name reflects the value that ancient Israelites placed on harmonious relationships.
H4918J.emploi: Meschullam appears only once in the provided biblical usages, in 1 Chronicles 8:17, where he is presented as the son of Elpaal and brother to several other men of Benjamin. It is a simple genealogical mention intended to preserve the memory of the lineages of the tribe of Benjamin.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin living at the time of the return from exile after 586 B.C.
H4918K.detail: Meshullam is a name that appears several times in the Old Testament to designate different individuals, particularly during the period of exile and the return to Jerusalem. The text of 1 Chronicles 9:7 mentions him as an ancestor of Sallu, part of the genealogical lineage of the Benjamites who resettled in Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity. His name means "friend" in Hebrew, reflecting the importance of this person in the communal reconstruction of the people returned from exile.
H4918K.origine: The name Meshullam (משׁלם) literally means "friend" or "one who is a friend." It is formed from a Hebrew root expressing the notion of friendship and relational bond. This name was common in Israel, borne by many individuals from different tribes and roles (Benjamites, Levites, priests, scribes) throughout biblical history.
H4918K.emploi: Meshullam is a name borne by many individuals in the Old Testament, particularly during the period of exile and return (6th-5th centuries B.C.). In 1 Chronicles 9:7, he is mentioned as the father of Sallu and son of Hodaviah, in a genealogical list of the Benjamites who returned to settle in Jerusalem after the captivity. Other Meshullam of the same name or homonyms appear as priests, Levites, and leaders of the reconstruction of the temple and the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah's leadership. The name was quite common to designate important figures of this restoration period.

sens: Man of the Exile and Return period, mentioned only once in 1 Chronicles 9:8
H4918L.detail: Meshullam is a name borne by many individuals in Israel, especially during the time of the Exile in Babylon and the return of the exiles. The text of 1 Chronicles 9:8 designates him as the son of Schephathiah and a member of the tribe of Benjamin. He was among the Benjamites who settled in Jerusalem after the captivity.
H4918L.origine: The name Meshullam literally means "friend" or "one who is at peace," formed from the Hebrew root that expresses completeness and wholeness. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, carrying a positive connotation of reconciliation and harmony. Several Meshullam appear in the books of Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah, indicating that this name was very widespread, particularly among priestly, Levitical families and among the leaders of the people.
H4918L.emploi: The Meshullam mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:8 is a Benjamite living after the return from Exile. He is genealogically presented as the son of Schephathiah, in a list of Benjamite families established in Jerusalem after the captivity. sens: Figure from the time of the exile and the return to Judea

sens: man who lived during the exile and the return to Jerusalem

sens: Man who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the exile

sens: man of the exile and return period
one of the notable figures who stood beside Ezra during the reading of the Law

sens: Man of Israel at the time of the exile and return
Leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah

He serves as a porter, that is, a guardian at the entrance of the temple and the Tent of Meeting (1 Chronicles 26:1). His sons, including the eldest, Zechariah, follow the same vocation and also serve as porters at the gates of the house of God (1 Chronicles 26:2). Meschélémia and his family embody a lineage of servants dedicated to the service of the sanctuary: "Here are the divisions of the porters. Of the Korahites: Meschélémia, son of Korah" (1 Chronicles 26:1). This role of guardian of the temple entrances was responsible and prestigious in the organization of Israelite worship.
H4920.origine: The name Meschélémia (or Shelemiah, an alternative name) means "the one whom Jehovah repays" or "Jehovah repays." It is composed of the element yah (an abbreviation of Jehovah) and evokes the divine idea of reward and retribution. The name reflects a trust in God's providence. Meschélémia belongs to the lineage of Korah, a Levitical family dedicated to the service of the temple since the origins of Israelite worship.
H4920.emploi: Meschélémia appears four times in the book of Chronicles, always in relation to his role as a porter. He is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 9:21 as the father of Zechariah, a porter at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. He is then presented as the chief of a class of Korahite porters (1 Chronicles 26:1). The genealogical lists specify his sons and their number: eighteen valiant men in total, which underscores the importance of this family in the organization of temple service (1 Chronicles 26:2 and 26:9). Meschélémia thus embodies a stable and organized Levitical institution of temple worship.

sens: Levite from the tribe of Levi living during the time of the Exile and the Return

sens: Complete destruction of a place, which becomes barren and uninhabitable
Devastated land, reduced to a state of desert or ruin
Feeling of horror and fear in the face of ruin
Abomination, that which provokes disgust and dread
H4923.detail:
1. Desolation primarily describes the physical destruction of a territory: cities, fertile lands reduced to nothing. When Isaiah speaks of the waters of Nimrim "devastated" (15:6), the dried grass and the vanished greenery, he paints the image of a once-prosperous region now barren and dead.
2. The word also designates the state of solitude and abandonment that follows: a desert where no one lives or passes (Ezekiel 33:28-29). The entire land becomes like the desert of Dibla, empty and hostile.
3. But desolation also evokes the feeling experienced in the face of this ruin: the dread, the horror that seizes one who contemplates such annihilation (Ezekiel 5:15). It is a visceral reaction to the spectacle of destruction.
4. By extension, the word can designate that which provokes this feeling of horror: the abominations themselves (Ezekiel 33:29), the acts that deserve divine judgment and ruin.
H4923.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that means "to be desolate" or "to be horrified." It carries within it the idea of a violent contrast: where there was life and fertility suddenly emerges emptiness, absence, horror. It is a word of rupture and catastrophe, often linked to the action of divine judgment on sin.
H4923.emploi: This word appears seven times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the prophets Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel. It regularly describes the consequences of God's judgment on the nations and on Israel: the lands become desolation, the inhabitants disappear. The translations of the Segond 1910 oscillate between "desert," "devastated," "desolate," and "dread," depending on the context: physical when it concerns the destroyed landscape, emotional when it evokes the reaction of witnesses. It is a prophetic language of threat and warning.
H4923.portee: Desolation reminds the Christian reader that divine judgment is real and that sin has tangible consequences: ruins, death, absence. It invites one to take seriously the warnings of the prophets. But it also reveals the gravity of apostasy: when a people forsakes God, even their land becomes a desert. It is a call to repentance and faithfulness.

sens: Fertility of the soil, agricultural wealth of a territory
Abundance and material prosperity
Absence of fertility (in negative form)
H4924A.detail:
1. The "fat of the earth" refers to the fertility of soil, its richness in nutrients that allows crops to thrive. It is a poetic image for the most productive and generous land. In Genesis 27:28, Isaac blesses Jacob by invoking for him "the fat of the earth": he wishes for him to dwell in a fertile and abundant land.
2. This term extends to the abundance and material prosperity that a fertile land provides: wheat, wine, food in quantity. It is the concrete blessing that God grants to His people.
3. The same expression can be denied or removed to signify the opposite: poverty and barrenness. In Genesis 27:39, Isaac tells Esau that his dwelling will be "deprived of the fat of the earth": instead of wealth and blessing, it will be impoverishment.
H4924A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that primarily denotes animal fat, the rich and nourishing substance. Applied to the land, the image is clear: a "fat" land is fertile and productive, laden with resources, just as fat nourishes the body. This metaphor was natural in an agricultural context where wealth was measured by the productivity of the fields.
H4924A.emploi: The word appears twice in Genesis, both in the same passage of Isaac's blessings. In Genesis 27:28, it is a blessing: Jacob will receive "the fat of the earth," a symbol of divine prosperity. In Genesis 27:39, it is a curse or deprivation: Esau will be "deprived" of this same wealth. These two uses show how the term plays on abundance or lack of abundance, always linked to material well-being and God's favor toward a people or a person.
H4924A.portee: This expression reminds us that divine blessing manifests concretely in life: through fertile land, abundant harvests, material security. It invites the reader to see prosperity as a sign of God's favor and to recognize that all that nourishes us comes from His generous hand. It is also a call to gratitude for the goods received.

sens: The state of being fatty, rich in fat material
The fatty or fleshy part of the body, succulent meat
The strength and vigor that come from abundance and ease
Fatness, the gradual decline of strength
Fertile and prosperous regions
H4924B.detail:
1. Literally, fat is the fatty material accumulated in the animal or plant body. It is the substance that accompanies the richest and most flavorful meat — what was offered in sacrifice to God. For example, Isaiah 17:4 speaks of "the fat of his flesh" to evoke Jacob's physical and material wealth that is withering away.
2. By extension, fat denotes muscular strength and the power of the body: in Psalms 78:31, the "mighty ones" (literally "the fat ones") are the strong young men who are struck down by death, those who have well-nourished flesh and the energy of youth.
3. Fat also represents prosperity and abundance: a "fat" people or region is a flourishing people, overflowing with resources, whose land produces generously. Daniel 11:24 mentions "fertile places" as rich and well-supplied areas that can be plundered and exploited.
4. Conversely, the loss of fat signifies decline, the gradual weakening of strength. Isaiah 10:16 announces the "wasting away" of the robust warriors of the king of Assyria — their strength fades like fat melting in the fire.
5. Fertile regions are literally "fat places," meaning rich, well-irrigated lands, abundant in humus, which nourish those who inhabit or conquer them.
H4924B.origine: The Hebrew word מִשְׁמָן (mishman) comes from a root that means primarily "to be fat, to become fattened," and more broadly "to be abundant, prosperous." The central image is that of fat: a substance that fills the body when one has eaten to satisfaction, showing animal power, health, and ease. The same root produces words for oil (another form of fat), wealth, and abundant things. This is why the word easily transitions from physical meaning (body fat) to moral and economic meaning (prosperity, fertility, strength).
H4924B.emploi: The word mishman appears four times in the Hebrew Bible, first to designate the vigorous young men struck down by God's judgment (Psalms 78:31), then for physical and material strength in decline — notably the "wasting away" that strikes the warriors of Assyria (Isaiah 10:16) and the weakening of Jacob's "fatness" (Isaiah 17:4). The word is also used for naturally productive regions well-endowed with resources (Daniel 11:24). In each case, the meaning retains this idea of fullness, strength, tangible wealth — either as what one enjoys in abundance or as what one loses in famine or judgment.
H4924B.portee: This word reminds the believer that the strength, health, and material prosperity we see as durable are actually fragile and controlled by God. They can vanish in an instant like fat in the fire (Isaiah 17:4). Conversely, it invites us to recognize that our true stability does not rest on bodily or territorial wealth, but on divine grace. The passages where mishman appears often speak of judgment and decline: an invitation not to place our trust in the "fat" of human riches, but to seek the true strength that comes from God.

sens: Meat or food rich in fat, savory and abundant nourishment
What is tasty, succulent, prepared with care
Figuratively: what nourishes the soul, joy, and well-being
H4924C.detail:
1. The word literally designates fatty meat, the rich and fleshy portions of an animal prepared for eating. In Nehemiah 8:10, the people returning from captivity are instructed to eat "fat meats" — sumptuous dishes — as an expression of their liberation and new life.
2. More broadly, it refers to any rich and well-prepared food, the opposite of a lean meal or frugality. It conveys the idea of abundance and feasting.
3. The text of Nehemiah transposes this material meaning into spiritual joy: eating the fat is participating in celebration, tasting the goodness of God, and this nourishment of the heart becomes "strength" for life.
H4924C.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of richness, of dense and generous substance. In biblical thought, fat is not a defect but a sign of prosperity and abundance; that is why, in sacrifices, the fatty parts were offered to God (the most precious offering). The word is linked to the idea of what truly "fills" and "nourishes."
H4924C.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Nehemiah 8:10. It occurs during the great Feast of Restoration, when the walls of Jerusalem are rebuilt and the people celebrate their return from captivity. In this context, eating fat is not a matter of gluttony, but a religious and communal act: it is tasting divine mercy and manifesting the joy allowed after years of mourning and exile.
H4924C.portee: This passage reminds the Christian reader that joy is not unworthy of faith: rejoicing, feasting, tasting the good things that God gives is to honor God and recognize His goodness. Spiritual joy is also expressed in simple gestures, shared meals, and communion. It is an invitation not to confuse piety with gloominess, and to see in every generous food a gift from God that deserves gratitude and celebration.

sens: Gadite warrior during the time of David
H4925.detail: Mischmanna is a military leader from the tribe of Gad who joined David at Ziklag when he was fleeing from Saul (1 Chronicles 12:10). He appears in the list of mighty warriors who rallied to the future king.
H4925.origine: The name Mischmanna literally means "fat" or "plump" in Hebrew, derived from the root שׁמן (shaman) which evokes wealth and abundance. It was a name borne among the Gadites, an eastern tribe of the Jordan known for its valiant warriors.
H4925.emploi: Mischmanna appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 12:10. He is presented as the fourth in a list of Gadite leaders who provided military support to David. These warriors left their lands to join David at Ziklag, demonstrating their commitment to the future king of Israel.

sens: what is heard indirectly, by rumor rather than by direct knowledge
a report, second-hand information that is not verified by personal experience
H4926.detail:
1. The word literally refers to what has been heard — not what one has seen with their own eyes, but what is reported after being heard. It is rumor, information that circulates without guarantee of authenticity. In Isaiah 11:3, the text contrasts true judgment with that which would be based on hearsay: the Messiah will not judge "by hearsay," meaning without personal and direct investigation.
2. The image evokes the weakness of second-hand knowledge. Unlike what one perceives themselves, what is heard can be distorted, inaccurate, or even false. Hearsay does not have the solidity of knowledge acquired through direct experience or certain understanding of the truth.
H4926.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root שׁמע (shama), which means "to hear" or "to listen." The term מִשְׁמָע adds the prefix מִ (mi) and properly designates "that which is heard" — the audible thing or information received by hearing. This root is very common in biblical Hebrew to express the act of listening, obeying, or receiving a word.
H4926.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 11:3, where it describes the perfect judgment of the coming Messiah. The context is that of an ideal king who will judge with justice, not by outward appearance or rumor, but by true and penetrating knowledge. It is a rare word that emphasizes the importance of discernment and judgment based on truth, not on what is heard.
H4926.portee: This verse reminds us that true judgment requires personal and direct knowledge, not blind trust in hearsay. For the believer, it is an invitation not to judge others based on rumors or gossip, but to seek the truth with wisdom and discernment, as Christ does perfectly.

sens: One of the twelve sons of Ishmael
Descendant of Simeon, son of Mibsam
H4927G.detail: 1. Mischma is one of the twelve sons that Ishmael had according to Genesis. He appears in the genealogy of the ancient Arab peoples (Genesis 25:14), listed among his brothers Nebaioth, Kedar, and others. 2. Another Mischma, much later, is mentioned as the son of Mibsam and belonging to the family of Simeon (1 Chronicles 1:30), placing him in a different Israelite lineage.
H4927G.origine: The name Mischma comes from a Hebrew root that literally means "an audition" or "a listening." It evokes the idea of hearing or receiving what is said. This name fits within the biblical tradition of giving children names loaded with spiritual meaning or significant events.
H4927G.emploi: The name Mischma appears twice in the Bible. First in Genesis 25:14, where he is listed as a son of Ishmael among the ancestors of the Arab peoples of the desert. Then in 1 Chronicles 1:30, in the same genealogical list. A second Mischma, from the family of Simeon, is also mentioned in the genealogies of Israel. These genealogical lists aim to identify the peoples and families descended from great patriarchal ancestors.

sens: Son of Mibsam, from the family of Simeon, during the time of the divided monarchy
H4927H.detail: Mischma is a man from the tribe of Simeon mentioned in the genealogy of the descendants of Simeon during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel (after the reign of Solomon). He is the son of Mibsam and the father of Hammuel (1 Chronicles 4:25-26).
H4927H.origine: The name Mischma literally means "an audition" or "a listening," formed from the Hebrew root that evokes the action of hearing or receiving a word. This name belongs to the semantic family of terms designating the transmission of the word and the divine message, common in the Bible for naming people.
H4927H.emploi: Mischma appears twice in the Bible, only in the genealogical passage of 1 Chronicles 4:25-26, where the descendants of Simeon are listed. He is an ancestor of the people of Israel, recorded in one of the long lists of names that structure the family history of the tribes of Israel and ensure the continuity of the chosen people.

sens: what one is commanded to do
one who obeys an order, subject or servant
the whole of those who obey, the subjugated
the secret entrusted to those of trust
H4928.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is that of a command or order given: "David, son-in-law of the king, devoted to his orders" (1 Samuel 22:14). It is a directive, an instruction to follow.
2. By extension, it also refers to one who executes the order, the submissive subject who obeys. It is a way of naming the person by their relationship to power.
3. The word can also designate the whole of the subjects or the subjugated: in Isaiah 11:14, "the sons of Ammon will be subjugated to them" speaks of entire peoples placed under a yoke.
4. The word also takes on the meaning of secret counsel or trust: when David "admitted" someone "into his secret counsel" (2 Samuel 23:23), he entrusted them with his confidences, placing them in his intimate circle where internal orders are whispered.
H4928.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to keep" or "to observe." It conveys the idea of a guardian or one who keeps in memory and practice what is entrusted to them — a word, an order, a secret.
