The family of this word encompasses the idea of guarding, protection, a hierarchical chain where each keeps what has been entrusted to them.
H4928.emploi: This word appears only four times in the provided Hebrew Bible. In 1 Samuel 22:14 and in the parallel passages of 2 Samuel 23:23 and 1 Chronicles 11:25, it designates the order or directives of the king to which David was attached as a faithful servant. In these warrior contexts, it is the obedience of the warrior to their chief. In Isaiah 11:14, it takes on a broader political meaning: the conquered peoples become the subjugated, those who are under the authority of the new power. The word thus shifts between the individual order to execute and the collective status of those who are dominated.
H4928.portee: This word reminds the reader of the structure of authority established by God: all power, from the king to the subjects, implies order and obedience. It reflects submission to the divine will. For the believer, it also speaks to the integrity of David, recognized for his faithfulness to Saul — even as a servant, he remains worthy. Finally, in Isaiah, it is a promise: the subjugation of hostile peoples shows the final triumph of the one who keeps the covenant with God.

sens: Closed place where prisoners are confined
Group of people responsible for monitoring or guarding
Action or duty of monitoring, keeping watch
Observance, respect of a rule or commandment
H4929.detail:
1. The most direct meaning is a place of confinement: a prison, a dungeon, a cell where captives are held. It is the place where Joseph sees Pharaoh's servants imprisoned (Genesis 40:4), or where one is placed for gathering wood on the Sabbath (Numbers 15:34).

2. The word also refers to the men themselves who guard: a team of sentinels, a squad of guards. Nehemiah speaks of keeping watch at night with the servants, going together on the walls (Nehemiah 4:22).

3. By extension, it is the action of keeping watch, the service of surveillance, the duty of protection. The Levites are "charged with celebrating and praising the Lord, according to the order of David" (Nehemiah 12:24), which shows how the word shifts from the post of a sentinel to the entrusted service.

4. Finally, the word can mean the observance of a rule, the respect of an order: keeping a command, fulfilling a promise. It is to ensure that something does not escape, as Job asks God: "Why do You set guards around me?" (Job 7:12), an image of oppressive surveillance.
H4929.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to keep" or "to observe." The same root produces other words for one who guards, for a guardrail (the railing), for anything that "observes" or "watches." The basic image is that of vigilant attention: the one who guards must remain awake, alert, ready to intervene. The word thus encompasses both the place where one is held, the agent who watches, and the action of keeping watch.
H4929.emploi: The word appears about twenty times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical and wisdom narratives. It is very frequent in the cycle of Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 40-41), where several people are put "in prison." It is found in Nehemiah during the rebuilding of Jerusalem, where it designates both the guard posts on the walls and the duty of surveillance (Nehemiah 4 and 12). In other contexts, particularly poetic, the word signifies observance or respect for a rule (Proverbs 4:23, where keeping one's heart means watching it jealously). The usage is always linked to the idea of control and vigilance: one guards a place, one guards a person, one guards oneself.
H4929.portee: This word reminds the reader of two essential truths. On one hand, it shows that confinement and captivity exist: the Bible does not hide the reality of suffering and restriction. On the other hand, it invites vigilance and observance: taking care of one's heart, respecting God's commandments, is to exercise attentive guarding. The word suggests that spiritual life requires vigilance, like that of the guard on the walls of the city.

sens: Metal point driven into wood or stone
That which fixes or holds firmly
Word or teaching that sinks into the mind and remains engraved
H4930.detail:
1. A nail is a metal point that is driven into wood or stone to assemble or fix things together. It is the concrete object of construction or assembly.
2. Figuratively, a nail represents that which holds or fixes — what stands firm, what does not move. It is the image of solidity and permanence.
3. In Ecclesiastes 12:13, the "words of the wise" are compared to nails: just as a nail is driven deeply and remains planted, wise words sink into the mind and remain engraved, indelible. They are not forgotten; they remain and act long after being spoken.
H4930.origine: The Hebrew word masmerah comes from a root that means "to keep" or "to retain." A nail is that which keeps, that which holds together. This sense of fixing or retention explains why the Bible can use it figuratively to speak of what sinks into memory or the heart and remains attached.
H4930.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ecclesiastes 12:13. The wise man uses it to encourage his readers to respect the Word of God by comparing the words of the wise to nails: firmly driven, solid, memorable. It is a poetic image to show that true wisdom does not fade away but takes root deeply in the one who listens to it.
H4930.portee: This image of the nail speaks to us of the lasting power of God's Word and faithful teaching. Wise words are not sounds that vanish; they sink into our hearts and memories to act for a long time, transforming our lives. It is an invitation to listen with respect and to keep God's words as nails that anchor us.

sens: Surveillance of a place or person, watch post
Detention, confinement, captivity
Conservation, preservation of a entrusted thing
Order, command, obligation to respect
Function, assigned service, liturgical duty
H4931.detail:
1. The guard is primarily the active surveillance of a place or person: it is to remain awake, vigilant, at one's post. In Jerusalem, Nehemiah orders the inhabitants to "keep watch" at their gate (Nehemiah 7:3), each one watching in front of their house. It is the role of the lookout who scans the horizon.

2. The word also designates a place of detention, a prison: a place where someone is held. It is confinement, captivity.

3. To conserve is to entrust something to someone for them to keep it safe. When it is ordered to "keep" the ashes of the red heifer outside the camp (Numbers 19:9), it is to put it away for later use.

4. The guard is also what is required, the order: Abraham "observed" the orders, the "commandments" and statutes of the Lord (Genesis 26:5). It is the imposed duty, the rule to follow.

5. In the service of the tabernacle, the guard becomes a function, a specific charge: the Levites had the "care" of everything entrusted to their responsibility (Numbers 3:7), and they performed their "service" according to their assigned place.
H4931.origine: The word comes from the root "shamar," which means "to keep, observe, preserve." This root evokes the idea of watching over, maintaining something in a safe place, remaining vigilant. The same root appears in many biblical words related to guarding, observing, and protecting. In Hebrew, "mishméret" is the abstract noun that reinforces this idea of ongoing responsibility and constant vigilance.
H4931.emploi: This word appears 69 times in the Hebrew Bible, concentrated mainly in the Pentateuch and historical books. It primarily designates the cultic service of the Levites: they had the "guard" of the tabernacle and the sanctuary, divided into posts and specific tasks (Numbers 3-4, 1 Chronicles 23-26). It also evokes the observance of the laws and commandments of the Lord: observing His "commandments" is a form of spiritual guarding (Genesis 26:5, Deuteronomy 11:1). In historical narratives, the term encompasses military vigilance: the guards of kings watched over the security of the palace and the city (2 Kings 11:5-7, Nehemiah 7:3). The word is also used for the preservation of holy or important things: the manna was "kept" in a jar (Exodus 16:32-34).
H4931.portee: For the believer, this word teaches that serving God is not a vague aspiration, but a concrete and ongoing charge: "keeping" His commandments means practicing them with vigilance and faithfulness. It also reminds us that every task, no matter how modest in the service of the Church, is a sacred function deserving to be carried out with seriousness. Finally, it invites spiritual vigilance: guarding is an act of love towards the one whose interests one defends.

sens: Quarter of a city distinct from the first, either an administrative or geographical district
Old residential area, often fortified, located beyond the main city
H4932G.detail: 1. The word designates the second quarter or district of a city, meaning a part of the city that is well-defined and organized. In Jerusalem, the prophetess Huldah lived in this second quarter (2 Kings 22:14), which shows that it is a structured and identified urban area. 2. It is also a residential area that can refer to a fortified or remote part of the city, less central. Zephaniah mentions the lamentations that will rise from this quarter on the day of judgment (Zephaniah 1:10), emphasizing that it is a populated and distinct area where inhabitants lived.
H4932G.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root שנה (sh-n-h), which means "to repeat" or "to change," hence the idea of "second" or "other." Mish-neh adds the preposition "mi" (of) and the suffix "eh," forming a noun that specifically designates a second element or a double. In biblical Hebrew, this word precisely describes an administrative or geographical division that is "the second" or "the other" in relation to a first reference element.
H4932G.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament, exclusively to designate the second quarter of Jerusalem. In 2 Kings 22:14 and 2 Chronicles 34:22 (two parallel accounts), it precisely locates the home of the prophetess Huldah in this urban second quarter, showing that it was a recognized and named residential area. In Zephaniah 1:10, it appears in a judgment announcement where God declares that lamentations will rise from this quarter, indicating that it was a populated and significant area. The context always suggests a clear administrative division of the city.
H4932G.portee: This term reminds us that Jerusalem, like any large city, was structured into distinct zones, each with its own inhabitants and life. The mention of Huldah's home in this quarter emphasizes that God's wisdom and prophetic word could manifest outside the temple or central palace — in a simple woman's home, in a less prestigious neighborhood. It is an invitation to seek God's voice everywhere, not just at the heart of religious or political power.

sens: What comes in second position in a series or order
Twice the same amount, the double
A copy or reproduction of an original
A rank or function of second importance
A quarter or administrative division
H4932H.detail:
1. What comes in second position in a series or order: the word simply designates the one who occupies the next place after the first. For example, in 1 Samuel 17:13, the sons of Jesse are listed: "the firstborn of his three sons was Eliab, the second Abinadab, and the third Shammah."  
2. Twice the same amount, the double: when speaking of a doubled quantity, of an equivalent repetition. Thus in Job 42:10, after Job prayed for his friends, "the LORD gave him double of all that he had owned" — he received twice what he had lost.  
3. A copy or reproduction of an original: particularly in the legal or administrative field, a document that reproduces a prior text. In Deuteronomy 17:18, the king must make "a copy of this law."  
4. A rank or function of second importance, like a second command: in Genesis 41:43, Pharaoh places Joseph on "the chariot that followed his own," establishing his authority immediately after that of Pharaoh himself.  
5. A quarter or administrative division of a city: a specific section of a city, as in 2 Kings 23:4 where the text mentions divisions of Jerusalem.
H4932H.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root expressing the idea of duality or repetition. It is formed with a suffix that transforms the concept of "two" into an adjective or noun designating "the one who is second." It is found in other biblical contexts where it always designates what doubles, repeats, or follows in numerical order.
H4932H.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Old Testament, mainly to classify people according to their rank ("the second son," "the second priest"), quantities ("the double"), or territorial divisions ("the second quarter"). In 1 Chronicles 5:12 and 1 Samuel 17:13, it clearly identifies a position in a listing. In Deuteronomy 15:18 and Job 42:10, it expresses a doubled quantity. The context determines whether the word emphasizes a succession order, a numerical multiplication, or an official reproduction of a text.
H4932H.portee: This word reminds us that God orders all things with clarity and hierarchy. Seeing Joseph as "second" in Egypt (Genesis 41:43) shows how God elevates His servants to places of authority. The promise of the "double" to Job (Job 42:10) reveals that divine generosity exceeds what has been lost — it is not merely a restoration, but a superabundance from the Lord.

sens: What is taken by force from someone during a fight, conquest, or theft
Spoils seized by the victor or aggressor
State of one who is stripped, dispossessed of their goods
Object or person delivered to the destructive power of the enemy
H4933.detail:
1. The word primarily designates the goods that are forcibly taken during a battle or conquest. When Israel's enemies win the war, its riches become their plunder: this is expressed in 2 Kings 21:14, where Israel becomes "the spoil and prey of all their enemies."  
2. More generally, it is the act of pillaging, ravaging an area or city to remove everything of value. Isaiah 42:22 depicts a people where everyone is "put to plunder," stripped of everything, bound in caves — an image of total ruin.  
3. The word also describes the condition of one who is dispossessed, deprived of their goods. In Jeremiah 30:16, God promises that "those who plunder you will be plundered": the word then emphasizes the loss suffered, the miserable state resulting from theft.  
4. Sometimes the expression "delivered to plunder" means delivering someone to the power of the enemy, rendering them unable to defend themselves. In Zephaniah 1:13, the goods that the Judeans have built "will be for plunder": not only lost but abandoned to the destroyer.
H4933.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of tearing away or dispossession. Its feminine form (הָּה ש מְ ) emphasizes that it designates an action, a process of spoliation. The term meshussa (מְשׁוּסָה) is a variant of the same word with a slight vocal difference, but carries exactly the same meaning: both evoke this violent removal of what belongs to someone.
H4933.emploi: This word appears six times in the Old Testament, mainly in the prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Habakkuk, Zephaniah) and in the books of Kings. It always appears in a context of divine judgment or military defeat. In 2 Kings 21:14 and Zephaniah 1:13, it is the punishment of Israel: God abandons His people or city to plunder because they have disobeyed. In Isaiah 42:22-24, the prophet denounces the servitude of the people, "plundered and stripped," and reminds that it is the LORD Himself who has delivered them to their enemies because of their sins. In Jeremiah 30:16, God promises the opposite: the plunderers will be plundered in turn. The word reappears in promises of restoration (Habakkuk 2:7): the one who has exploited others will be dispossessed. Biblical usage shows that plunder is never presented as a morally neutral act, but always as a consequence — either of God's judgment or of the injustice of oppressors.
H4933.portee: This word reminds the Christian reader of an important biblical truth: God sees oppression and spoliation, and He does not tolerate them indefinitely. The one who plunders and dispossesses others provokes divine anger. Conversely, God's people may experience plunder as punishment for their unfaithfulness — but God promises that it will not be eternal and that He will restore justice. This term thus invites justice towards others and trust in God to protect our goods and dignity.

sens: Narrow and hollow way
Narrow passage between vineyards or fields
Pathway worn by use, enclosed
H4934.detail: 1. The path is a narrow and hollow way, traced by the repeated passage of pedestrians or animals that gradually compress the ground. It is a very confined route, often enclosed between natural or artificial walls — in this case, in Numbers 22:24, a path between two vineyards with a wall on each side, resembling a corridor. 2. It is also a passage worn by use, where one progresses while being surrounded: unlike a broad road, the path confines the traveler and limits lateral movements. This is precisely what traps Balaam's donkey, which cannot move forward or backward without touching the walls on both sides.
H4934.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that denotes the idea of digging or making a furrow. The path is literally a dug-out way, marked by the wear of passage. It is a term specifically agricultural or rural, speaking of daily life in the Holy Land, where country paths follow the topography and are hollowed out between crops.
H4934.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Numbers 22:24. In this account, the angel of the Lord stands in this narrow path between two vineyards to block the way of Balaam and his donkey. The narrowness of the passage emphasizes that the donkey is trapped: it cannot turn to the right or left, unlike what happens in the two previous appearances of the angel (verses 23 and 25). It is the image of a spiritual dead end for Balaam.
H4934.portee: This narrow path reminds us that sometimes God closes the widely accessible ways to force us to stop and reconsider our direction. The donkey, a mute and obedient creature, sees what the rebellious prophet does not see: the angel blocking the way. It is an invitation to humility and to listen to God, even — and especially — when we believe we are on the right path.

sens: the act of cleaning, washing, and making clean
the ritual care of the newborn: washing, salting, and wrapping
the preparation to receive care or dignity
H4935.detail:
1. The word denotes physical cleaning: washing with water to remove dirt and impurities. This is what is done to the newborn immediately after birth, as shown in the account of Ezekiel 16:4 where Jerusalem, presented as an abandoned child, has not received even the most basic care: no bath, no salt, no wrapping.
2. The word includes the gestures of care and dignity that accompany this cleaning: washing, rubbing with salt (which soothes and strengthens the skin), then wrapping the child in swaddling clothes. It is a set of gestures that shows that one is taking care of a person.
H4935.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes cleaning and washing. Its basic image is that of water that washes and purifies. In Hebrew, this vocabulary of physical cleaning is often linked to that of ritual and spiritual purity: to wash is both to clean the body and to restore purity.
H4935.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ezekiel 16:4. It is found in the striking picture of a newborn child completely abandoned: she has not received the basic care of washing, salting, and wrapping that any worthy mother gives to her child. Through this image, the prophet shows how God found Jerusalem in her childhood — left to herself, without protection, without dignity — before raising and elevating her.
H4935.portee: This word emphasizes the importance of caring for the most vulnerable, especially children. It also reminds us that simple gestures of care and dignity — washing, cleaning, dressing — are a form of mercy and love. Through the image of the abandoned newborn, the text also shows how God receives those who are left to themselves and restores them.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Elpaal
H4936.detail: Mischeam is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel. He is the son of Elpaal and is among the many descendants of Shaharaim.
H4936.origine: His Hebrew name מִשְׁעָם (Mischeam) means "purification." He belongs to a well-attested Benjamite lineage in the genealogies of the first book of Chronicles.
H4936.emploi: Mischeam appears only once in the biblical text, in 1 Chronicles 8:12, in the detailed genealogy of the descendants of Benjamin. He is listed among the sons of Elpaal, alongside his brothers Eber, Shemer, and others. These genealogies in the book of Chronicles served to show the continuity and legitimacy of the tribe of Benjamin after the exile, and to document the families that inhabited it.

sens: That on which one leans, what supports
Person or thing one can rely on
Material or moral resource needed for life
H4937A.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: it is that on which one leans to stand or move forward, like a walking stick or a point of support. When David says, "The Lord was my support" in the day of my distress (2 Samuel 22:19), he speaks of God as a strength that supports him, preventing him from falling into misfortune.
2. The support then becomes that which morally or practically sustains us — a person, a presence. It is someone or something on which we count, in whom we trust.
3. Broadly, the word designates any essential resource for life: bread, water, wisdom, counsel. In Isaiah 3:1, the Lord removes from Jerusalem all support and all resource — not only bread and water, but also leaders and wise men, all those who allowed the city to stand.
H4937A.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to lean," "to support." It is literally what serves as a point of support or support. The image is very concrete: one thinks of a stick, a cane, a pillar — anything that prevents one from falling. From there comes the figurative meaning: that which saves us from disaster, that which allows us to live with dignity.
H4937A.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible in three different contexts. In the Psalms and Samuel (Psalms 18:19 and 2 Samuel 22:19, two passages that say the same thing), it designates God as the support of the believer in the day of distress — the one who prevents misfortune from overwhelming us. In Isaiah 3:1, the context changes: the support becomes a resource, a provision. The Lord removes the supports from Jerusalem — that is, the bread, the water, the wise men, the leaders — everything that allowed the nation to survive. The word thus shifts from moral support to material good, but the deep meaning remains the same: it is that without which one cannot live.
H4937A.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the believer going through trial. It reminds us that in distress, the Lord does not leave us without support: He is our support. But it also teaches that no human support, no material resource can truly save us — only God is worthy of that trust. It is a call not to place our hope in visible things, but in the Lord.

sens: that which supports or keeps something upright
that which allows someone to lean on to walk or stand
person or thing on which one relies or depends
material and moral help or support
H4937B.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning: that which physically supports a structure, a person, or an object — a stick, an outstretched arm, a wall. It conveys the idea of a base that keeps something balanced.
2. For a person, it is what allows one to walk or stand upright — a cane, a helping hand. It is the assistance received to move forward despite fatigue or weakness.
3. Figuratively, it is the person in whom one has confidence and on whom one depends — a leader, a reliable friend, someone solid. It is the one on whom one morally leans.
4. It is also any material or moral support: money, advice, comfort, protection. In Isaiah 3:1, the Lord removes from Jerusalem and Judah "all support and all resource" — the bread, the water, the wise leaders, and the warriors — it is the withdrawal of everything that keeps a nation standing.
H4937B.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to lean" or "to incline toward." It expresses the image of a person or thing leaning on a support. It is a variant of another form (mish'an) carrying the same meaning. The family of words conveys the idea of support, assistance, dependence — everything without which one would fall.
H4937B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 3:1, in an oracle of the Lord against Jerusalem. In this major passage, the prophet lists all the "supports" that God will remove from His unfaithful people: not only bread and water (the vital resources), but also the wise, the warriors, the judges — in short, all those on whom the nation relied. It is a language of amplification and accumulation to show the total destruction of the kingdom's support.
H4937B.portee: This word reminds us that all support — material, social, or moral — comes from God and can be withdrawn. It invites us to reflect on what we truly rely on in life. Is it on fragile resources or on God alone? Isaiah shows that losing all earthly "support" can be God's judgment, but also an opportunity to rediscover that God alone is our true support.

sens: That on which one relies to live
Essential material means for subsistence
Concrete support or help
H4938A.detail:
1. The word evokes the idea of leaning on something to stand — just as one leans on a stick or a cane to walk. In Isaiah 3:1, the Lord threatens to remove from Jerusalem "all support and all resource": it refers to the concrete, material means on which the people rely to survive.
2. This word more precisely designates the goods, provisions, and wealth that allow a city or a people to live: the bread and water (as the text explains in detail), but also all the economic means that sustain daily life. Removing the resource means plunging into famine and dependence.
3. Therefore, it is a support or help that one cannot do without — something reliable on which one counts. In the context of divine judgment, the withdrawal of the resource signifies the collapse of the established way of life.
H4938A.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to lean on" or "to make use of." It is related to Hebrew words that denote support, assistance, dependence. The basic image is physical: a stick that supports, something on which one leans to avoid falling. Transferred to the material and economic domain, the resource becomes what "holds" a society, what keeps it standing.
H4938A.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 3:1. The prophet announces a punishment: the Lord will remove from Jerusalem and Judah all that the people rely on to live — support, resource, bread, water. The context shows that it is a judgment against Judah, which depended on its own strength, wealth, and reserves. It is a threat of famine and economic ruin: the resource here designates the entire means of material, military, and food that ensured the survival and stability of the kingdom.
H4938A.portee: This word reminds us that material survival and economic security do not primarily depend on our strength, reserves, or well-being, but on the hand of God. Removing the resource serves to remind a proud people that they are vulnerable. For the Christian reader, it is an invitation not to trust solely in material goods, but to seek first the kingdom of God.

sens: Long, straight wooden object held in hand for walking or support
Instrument used to strike or perform an action
Sign of authority and power
Support, assistance one can rely on
H4938B.detail:
1. The stick is primarily a concrete object: a wooden rod that an injured person holds to walk (Exodus 21:19), or that the elderly use to assist themselves in their movements (Zechariah 8:4). It is a simple everyday utensil.
2. The stick also serves as an active instrument: Elisha uses it to touch the dead child and seek to bring him back to life (2 Kings 4:29), and it can be used to strike or dig (Numbers 21:18 speaks of sticks for digging wells).
3. The stick becomes a symbol of power and authority: the scepter of the great of the people is a stick, and the angel of the Lord carries a stick that manifests his divine power when he touches the offering (Judges 6:21).
4. Figuratively, the stick represents a support on which one leans, as Psalm 23:4 speaks of the rod and staff of the Lord as comfort. But this support can be deceptive: the broken reed of Egypt is a false support that injures the hand of the one who relies on it (2 Kings 18:21 and Isaiah 36:6).
H4938B.origine: The Hebrew word mishénet comes from the root שׁען (shaïn), which means "to lean" or "to rest upon." This is why mishénet primarily designates the object on which one leans to walk. The same root gives rise to words that express the idea of support and dependence. The word has a strong connotation: it is what one needs to stand upright.
H4938B.emploi: This word appears about ten times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives (Samuel, Kings) and the prophets. The usages show a progression: the stick starts as a utilitarian object (support for the sick), then becomes an instrument of action (to touch, to strike), and finally a symbol of divine or human power. But the Bible also emphasizes the danger of taking a false support: when one leans on Egypt instead of God, it is like leaning on a reed that pierces the hand. Psalm 23:4 transfers the image to the relationship with God: His rod and staff comfort the righteous in the valley of the shadow of death.
H4938B.portee: This word invites the believer to reflect on their true supports. In weakness and suffering, the material stick helps the body; but spiritually, only God is a true lasting support. Leaning on wealth, political power, or men is like leaning on a reed that cannot hold. Psalm 23:4 teaches that God's rod comforts in trials: it is a promise of presence and help.

sens: violent pouring of blood, murder
massacre, carnage
bloody injustice, oppressive violence
H4939.detail:
1. The word refers to bloodshed — the violent pouring out of human blood, through murder or violence. In Isaiah 5:7, the prophet reproaches Israel: where God expected justice, He finds instead "bloodshed," meaning murders, violent acts.
2. It can evoke a massacre or carnage — the result of massive, collective violence.
3. Figuratively, it becomes a symbol of bloody injustice, the violent oppression of a people. This is why, in the text of Isaiah, "bloodshed" stands in contrast to "righteousness" and "justice": it is injustice that cries out for vengeance.
H4939.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of spilling or pouring out. It is composed of the idea of "pouring" applied to blood, creating a very concrete image: blood that flows, stains the ground, and cannot be hidden. This image of spilled blood carrying guilt is found throughout the Bible: the innocently shed blood cries out for vengeance to God.
H4939.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 5:7, where the prophet uses it to accuse Israel. God had planted His vineyard — Israel — expecting righteousness and justice; He found "bloodshed" and cries of distress. This unique occurrence makes this passage all the more striking: the prophet employs a rare and powerful word to express divine disappointment at the injustice prevailing in Israel, an injustice so grave that it stagnates and accumulates like spilled blood.
H4939.portee: This word reminds us that God takes human injustice and violence very seriously. It is not just isolated acts: when injustice settles in a society, it becomes a "bloodshed" that soils the land and provokes divine anger. The Christian is called to look around: where is this hidden violence, this injustice that plunges the innocent and weak into misery?

sens: Group of people united by blood, sharing a common ancestor and living under authority.
Subdivision of a tribe, grouping several generations of the same branch.
All the descendants of an ancestor, forming a clan or household.
Natural species or category of living beings.
Professional or corporate group practicing the same trade.
People or nation sharing a common origin.
H4940.detail:
1. The family is the fundamental group of people linked by blood: parents, children, and close relatives living together under the responsibility of a leader. It is the basic unit of Israelite life, as when the sons of Asher are counted "according to their families, according to the houses of their fathers" (Numbers 1:40).

2. A family can also refer to a branch or subgroup of a larger tribe — a "family" of the Zerahites or the Saulites (Numbers 26:13) — sharing a common ancestor but distinct from other branches.

3. The word designates all the descendants of an ancestor, forming a clan or household: the daughters of Zelophehad belong to the "families of Manasseh" (Numbers 27:1), indicating a genealogical lineage.

4. It also applies to natural categories: "All the animals […] according to their kinds came out of the ark" (Genesis 8:19) — each kind of animal forms a "family."

5. The word can refer to a group of workers in the same trade, a guild or professional order, like the families of temple musicians.

6. On the broadest scale, it designates a people or nation — the descendants of a founding ancestor — having a common culture and destiny.
H4940.origine: The Hebrew word mishpakhah comes from a root meaning "to divide" or "to share": a family is what divides or shares the generations of the same stock. It is related to other words denoting division or distribution. The word expresses the idea of a branch that arises from a common root and develops — a coherent but distinct entity.
H4940.emploi: Mishpakhah appears 224 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in the books of Genesis, Numbers, and Chronicles. It is extremely frequent in genealogical lists and censuses: the twelve tribes of Israel are each divided into families (Numbers 1-4), and each family counts its able-bodied men for war. The word is also used for Noah's families and the dispersion of peoples (Genesis 10). Its meaning varies from the intimate setting (the household) to the national setting (an entire people), depending on the context: a "family" can consist of a few dozen people or thousands.
H4940.portee: The biblical notion of family reveals that God organizes His people into natural and responsible human units. Each person belongs to a genealogical chain, affirming the importance of identity, heritage, and the transmission of faith. The family is not an accident but a place of order and blessing intended by God.

sens: Act of rendering a sentence, deciding a matter in justice
Result of this act: the decision, the condemnation or acquittal
Procedure, trial, instance before judges
Law, ordinance, prescription established by authority
Manner of acting in accordance with righteousness, equity
Right, prerogative, what is due to someone
H4941G.detail:
1. Judgment is primarily the act by which a judge or court examines a case and renders a decision. It is the heart of justice: weighing evidence and arguments, then deciding. In Deuteronomy 25:1, "When men have a dispute, they shall come to judgment, and they shall be judged": we see the dispute brought before the competent authority.
2. Judgment also refers to the sentence itself, the decision pronounced: it is the verdict. In 1 Kings 3:28, when Solomon judges the two mothers claiming the child, "all Israel heard of the judgment that the king had rendered" — the people speaks of his renowned decision.
3. It can also mean the trial itself, the entire legal procedure: all the steps through which one is judged. In Numbers 35:24, the elders of the city "shall judge" (literally: shall decide the judgment) between the murderer and the avenger.
4. The word designates the laws and ordinances, that is, the rules established by authority by which one must live. In Exodus 15:25, after the Exodus, "the Lord showed him a tree… And there He gave the people statutes and ordinances": these are the rules for God's people.
5. By extension, judgment refers to justice itself — equity, righteousness — especially when linked to God. In Psalms 1:5, "the wicked will not stand in the day of judgment": it is the day when God renders justice sovereignly and impartially.
6. Finally, the word can mean a right, a prerogative, what is legally due to someone by their status or function. It is the aspect of "what is established, what is due."
H4941G.origine: The Hebrew word mishpat comes from a root that expresses the idea of standing in front of, confronting, hence to judge. It is related to the verb "to judge" (shaphat). The word fundamentally refers to the act of weighing two things, putting them in balance to find the truth. In ancient Hebrew, judgment is never purely abstract: it is always the concrete act of a judge who decides, or the concrete rule that an authority imposes.
H4941G.emploi: This word is one of the most frequent in the Old Testament (208 occurrences). It appears everywhere the Bible speaks of the Law: in the Pentateuch (particularly in Deuteronomy), where Moses enumerates the laws and ordinances of the Lord that the people must keep; in the historical books, where judges and kings render judgments; in the Psalms, where God's judgment is invoked as protection for the righteous. Its meaning varies slightly depending on the context: sometimes it is the procedure ("to go to judgment"), sometimes the verdict rendered ("a just judgment"), sometimes the law itself ("the judgments of the Lord"). But it always unites the idea of established order and equity: judgment is what places each person in their rightful place with righteousness.
H4941G.portee: Judgment, in the Bible, is never a mere technical matter: it is a sacred act, for only God truly judges with perfect justice. For the believer, meditating on judgment reminds us that our actions are seen, that righteousness matters, and that God's laws are good because they order human life according to the wisdom of the Creator. It is also a call to judge with equity when we have the power, and to submit with confidence to the Lord's just judgment.

sens: The act of judging a case, rendering a sentence
The place or court where justice is administered
The quality of one who acts with fairness and righteousness
The legitimate right of someone, what is legally due to them
The ordinance, law, established rule
The just and appropriate way to do something
H4941H.detail: 1. Justice is primarily the act of judging: when a magistrate examines a case and renders a sentence. This is why it is said, "the judgment will be according to justice" (Psalms 94:15) — the judge's decision must be fair. 2. It also refers to the court itself, the place where judgment is rendered: it is the court of justice, the seat of judgment where the case is examined. 3. Justice is also a moral quality: that of one who acts with righteousness, fairness, and uprightness. This is what God possesses perfectly. When one asks, "To justice? Who will make me appear?" (Job 9:19), they invoke fairness as an absolute principle. 4. It refers to the right that someone legitimately possesses — their due, what is rightfully theirs. This is the right of a son to his inheritance or the right of the poor not to be oppressed. 5. Justice is also an ordinance, an established law: "I will establish my law to be a light for the peoples" (Isaiah 51:4), where divine law guides the people. 6. Finally, it can mean the just, suitable, appropriate way to do things — the rule that must be followed.
H4941H.origine: The Hebrew word mish·pat comes from a root that means "to judge," "to decide." It is related to the idea of separating, distinguishing what is just from what is unjust. The word thus primarily designates the action of judging, then extends to the quality of justice and to the law that governs this justice. In the Bible, justice is never abstract: it is the work of God, who judges the whole earth perfectly and establishes just laws for His people.
H4941H.emploi: Mish·pat appears 162 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Psalms, Proverbs, historical and prophetic books. As early as Genesis, Abraham must "practice justice" towards his family (Genesis 18:19), and God Himself judges justly (Genesis 18:25). Under the Law of Moses, justice is expressed through ordinances that protect the weak and the poor (Deuteronomy 10:18, 24:17). Just kings like David "practice justice and equity" (2 Samuel 8:15). In Psalms, justice is the fundamental attribute of God, who "loves justice" (Psalms 33:5, 37:28). Proverbs teaches that justice is the wisdom of good governance and virtuous living. Isaiah announces that divine justice will shine as light upon the nations.
H4941H.portee: The justice of the Bible is not a cold concept of impersonal rules, but the expression of God's just love for His people. It requires that the believer defends the poor, refuses bribes, and judges fairly. By practicing justice, one aligns with God and reflects His character. Divine justice is also a promise: God will ultimately judge all that is unjust and establish His kingdom of justice and peace.

sens: Decision rendered by a judge or court
Sentence, verdict resulting from judgment
Justice, righteousness, what is just and right
Ordinance, prescription, established way of doing
Usage, custom, habitual manner
H4941I.detail:
1. A judicial decision is what a judge pronounces after examining a case: it is the result of judgment, the verdict that determines who is right and who is wrong.
2. The sentence is the concrete application of this decision: it states what must happen, the punishment or compensation ordered (Numbers 29:18 speaks of offerings "according to the established rules," meaning according to what has been ordained).
3. Justice refers to the quality of one who judges with righteousness: it is fairness, uprightness in judgment, the idea that one acts according to what is just and good.
4. An ordinance or prescription is an instruction that states how things should be done: for example, the way to serve God in the temple (2 Kings 17:27 asks to teach "the manner" of serving the god of the land).
5. Usage or custom is the practice established over time: it is "as it is usually done" (1 Chronicles 24:19 mentions "the rule established by Aaron").
H4941I.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to judge, to decide." It evokes the image of someone who separates, discerns, and decides. The same root has given rise to words for "judge," "judgment," "contention." This word is one of the most important in the Old Testament for speaking of God's justice and human rights.
H4941I.emploi: This word appears 15 times in the provided references. It mainly appears in contexts of worship (Numbers 29 and 1 Chronicles 23-24) where it designates the specific rules to follow for offerings and temple service. In 2 Kings 17:27, it signifies the way, the manner of performing a religious rite. In 1 Chronicles 24:19, it refers to the order established long ago by Aaron himself. In all these cases, the word carries the idea of something fixed, prescribed, established once and for all — not an innovation or whim, but an order that deserves obedience.
H4941I.portee: This word teaches that justice and order are not arbitrary human inventions, but are based on an established and just structure. For the believer, this shows that God does not act randomly: His judgments and ordinances are trustworthy because they proceed from His righteousness. Respecting God's "rules" — His ordinances — is not a constraint, but the acceptance of what is just and good.

sens: Act of judging a case, rendering a legal decision
Place or court where justice is rendered
Judicial process, procedure, trial
Sentence or verdict pronounced by a judge
Right, privilege, what is legally due to someone
Habit, custom, usual way of acting
H4941J.detail:
1. The primary meaning is the act of judging: it is the decision that a magistrate or leader renders after hearing a case. In Genesis 40:13, the restoration of the cupbearer to his position means that Pharaoh will render his judgment in his favor.
2. By extension, it is also the physical place where the judgment takes place — the court, the tribunal. It is the place where judges gather and where cases are heard.
3. The word also designates the entire judicial process: the investigation, the hearing of witnesses, the debates, the complete procedure up to the verdict. In 1 Samuel 8:11, God announces to Israel what the "right of the king" will be — that is, the rules, the usages of royal power over his people.
4. It is the sentence itself, the verdict rendered: the conclusion of the judgment that declares someone guilty or innocent, and that decides their punishment or right.
5. The word is used for legal rights, privileges, and shares that are legally due to each person — particularly in the rituals of sacrifice where the priest receives his "portion" (Deuteronomy 18:3).
6. By semantic shift, it eventually comes to mean custom, habit, manner: what "ought" to be done, what is the established usage. In 2 Kings 17:34, Israel follows its old pagan "customs" instead of obeying God's laws.
H4941J.origine: The Hebrew root שׁפט (shapat) means "to judge, to govern." It evokes the image of a leader or magistrate who decides, who makes a ruling. The word in Hebrew thus encompasses the idea of decisive power and governance: the one who judges also directs. Other forms of the same family designate the judge himself (שׁוֹפֵט, shophet), like the judges of Israel in the time of Samson. It is a fundamental word in biblical Hebrew, carrying the idea of social order and authority.
H4941J.emploi: The word מִשְׁפָּט appears 24 times in the Old Testament in various usages. Initially, it primarily denotes the judicial act: the judgment of Pharaoh, the legal procedure in Israel. Very quickly, it takes on a broader and more abstract meaning: the rights of the king, the rights of the priest in worship, the prescriptions that a people must follow. In the wisdom and prophetic books, it increasingly signifies the just order, what is due to each person — which is why it is translated as "right" or "justice." In the books of Kings and in historical narratives, it often refers to the "right" of the king (his powers and his exactions). Habit and custom appear when it comes to established practices, religious or civil, that a people regularly repeat. The word subtly shifts from the particular (a decision) to the general (a rule, a custom).
H4941J.portee: This word shows the reader that in biblical thought, judgment is not an isolated or arbitrary act: it is an established order, an organized justice, based on recognized rights and respected procedures. It reminds us that God Himself is a judge, and that His judgments are not capricious but just, based on an eternal order. For the believer, it is an invitation to respect the established order — whether civil, cultic, or moral — but also to seek true justice, that which gives each person what is due to them, according to the heart of God.

sens: Decision of a judge or authority that establishes the law
Place where justice is rendered
Action of judging, discerning right from wrong
H4941K.detail:
1. Judgment is primarily the decision pronounced by one who has the authority to resolve a dispute or punish an offense: it is the verdict, the sentence that states the law. In 1 Kings 7:7, the "hall of judgment" is the room where King Solomon renders justice, where he pronounces his verdicts.
2. By extension, judgment also designates the physical place where this justice is exercised — the court, the tribunal, the place where judges sit. This meaning appears in the text: Solomon "rendered justice" there.
3. The word can also express the act of judging itself, the activity of discerning, weighing the facts, and deciding according to the law — it is the process rather than its result.
H4941K.origine: The Hebrew word מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat) comes from a root that means "to divide," "to distribute": to judge is to allocate to each what is due to them. This image of fair sharing is found in many words of the same family. In Greek, this word is often translated as "krisis" (judgment, discernment) or "dike" (justice, right).
H4941K.emploi: This word appears only once in the phrase "hall of judgment" (1 Kings 7:7), where it designates the royal room from which the king rendered justice. It is an administrative and political term: it refers to a room in Solomon's palace intended for judicial hearings. The word mishpat, throughout the Hebrew Bible, carries several nuances: sometimes it is the judgment rendered (a sentence), sometimes it is the law itself, sometimes it is the act of judging, and here it is the place where this function is exercised.
H4941K.portee: This hall of judgment reminds us that justice is a sacred function centralized in the kingship of Israel. For the believer, it evokes the importance of justice rendered fairly and publicly, and foreshadows God's final judgment, the supreme judge who will render to each according to their works.

sens: Enclosure or refuge for animals, especially sheep
Place of rest or inactivity, in contrast to action
H4942.detail:
1. The word designates an enclosure, a shelter for flocks of sheep or cattle — a place where animals rest and are protected. In Genesis 49:14, Issachar is compared to "a strong donkey, lying down in the stables": the image evokes a massive animal that prefers to remain comfortably seated rather than work.
2. By extension, the stable symbolizes inactivity or passive rest, often criticized when action is required. In Judges 5:16, the prophet reproaches the tribe of Reuben for remaining "among the stables" listening quietly to the bleating of the flocks, while others fight — the stable becomes a symbol of immobility and detachment in the face of danger.
H4942.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of "home" or "assigned place." Its exact meaning in ancient Hebrew remains debated: some believe it refers to campfires or hearths, others to an enclosure for animals. The biblical context — where it always appears in connection with flocks or a place of rest — strongly suggests that it is a refuge or a sheepfold.
H4942.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, always in a pastoral or resting context. In Genesis 49:14, Moses describes Issachar lying in the stables, highlighting his peaceful and sedentary nature. In Judges 5:16, the same word takes on a critical nuance: remaining in the stables becomes a reproach, a lack of courage at the time of war against Sisera. The contrast between these two usages shows how rest at the fold, natural for animals, becomes a weakness among warriors called to fight.
H4942.portee: For the Christian, these verses invite reflection on the difference between restorative rest and inactivity that paralyzes. Issachar embodies a certain peaceful acceptance of his condition; the warriors of Reuben embody the temptation to remain comfortably aloof when God calls for action. It is a subtle call to examine our priorities: do we seek merely convenience, or are we ready to leave our "stable" when faith demands it?

sens: one who inherits, who receives the property of a father or master
one who will continue the work or lineage
H4943.detail:
1. The heir is one who naturally possesses the property of the father: he receives possession and responsibility after the owner's death. Abram has no child, and his servant Eliezer, in the absence of a son, would therefore become the owner of all his goods (Genesis 15:2).
2. By extension, the heir is also one who continues the work or name of his predecessor, who succeeds him in his function or authority, like a son who takes over the father's business or perpetuates his honor.
H4943.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to possess" or "to acquire." It literally designates one who comes into possession of a property. In biblical culture, the heir is primarily the firstborn son, but the term extends to any servant or relative who inherits the goods of the master or head of the family.
H4943.emploi: The word appears only once in this sense in the Hebrew Bible (Genesis 15:2). In this crucial passage, Abram expresses his anguish: having no child, he fears that his servant Eliezer will become his heir, instead of a son of his own blood carrying his name and promises. This concern shows the critical importance of inheritance in God's plan: a legitimate heir is the key to the perpetuation of the chosen people and divine blessings.
H4943.portee: Genesis 15:2 reveals Abram's anxiety over the absence of a child: he knows that without an heir, all he possesses will disappear. This concern invites the believer to meditate on the question of inheritances in his own heart: what does he truly inherit from the Heavenly Father? The New Testament will teach that all children of God are heirs of His promises (Romans 8:17). Understanding the significance of the word "heir" in this narrative deepens the understanding of the promise made to Abram.

sens: To throw oneself quickly towards something, with an irresistible momentum
To rush en masse, like a swarm or a crowd converging towards a goal
H4944.detail:
1. The word describes the action of rushing, leaping forward with remarkable speed and force of movement. It is the rapid and often impetuous movement of a creature or a mass. In Isaiah 33:4, the locusts rush upon the plunder left on the ground, an image of their sudden and massive descent: they do not crawl, they swoop down like a gust of wind.
2. The figurative sense also emphasizes the notion of a mass in motion: several creatures or people throwing themselves together towards the same object, with a kind of impetuous unanimity. The locusts do not come one by one; they arrive in swarms, sweeping everything away.
H4944.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of rapid movement and charge. This root is related to other Hebrew terms meaning "to run" or "to hasten." The basic image is that of irresistible speed, a flow that progresses with force.
H4944.emploi: The word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Isaiah 33:4. It describes the behavior of locusts rushing upon the scattered plunder. This context is that of a prophetic word of judgment: the riches stolen from the people of God will be devoured as quickly as the locusts devastate the crops, and no one will be able to stop them. The unique usage underscores the intensity of the word, reserved for this dramatic image.
H4944.portee: This verb reminds the reader of the irresistible power of God's judgment: like locusts that no force can hold back, divine justice descends upon ill-gotten gains. For those listening to Isaiah, it is a warning against theft and oppression, with the assurance that God does not leave unpunished the disorder of the order He has established.

sens: Court officer responsible for serving drinks to the king
High-ranking servant with direct access to the sovereign
An honorable and trusted position in royal courts
H4945A.detail:
1. The cupbearer is the officer who fills the cups and serves drinks to the king during meals and banquets. It is a prestigious position: in Genesis 40:13, Joseph promises the chief cupbearer that he will be "restored to your position" and "you will put the cup into Pharaoh's hand, as you used to do." It is a personal, close, and repeated service.
2. Due to his daily proximity to the monarch, the cupbearer enjoys an influential position and great trust. He is important enough for Pharaoh to notice and punish him: in Genesis 40:1-2, the cupbearer and the baker "offended their master, the king of Egypt" and are both thrown into prison. He is a prominent court figure.
3. In 2 Chronicles 9:4, among the splendors of Solomon's palace, "his cupbearers and their garments" are listed, showing that these are servants adorned with visible dignity. It is a coveted position, symbolizing access to power.
H4945A.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root "shaqah" which means "to water, to give to drink." The word "mash.qeh" literally designates one who makes drink, hence cupbearer. It is a compound word that unites the idea of service (to make drink) with an official charge. The role may seem humble — pouring drinks — but the proximity to the king and the trust it implies make it one of the highest functions in the court.
H4945A.emploi: The word is primarily used in the story of Joseph in Egypt (Genesis 40-41), where it refers to the chief cupbearer imprisoned with Joseph and whose dream Joseph interprets. This officer later becomes the medium through which Joseph is brought before Pharaoh to interpret his dreams (Genesis 41:9). The word also appears to describe the prestigious officers of Solomon's courts (1 Kings 10:5) and the king of Persia (Nehemiah 1:11, where Nehemiah himself holds this position). It is always a position of great responsibility and royal proximity.
H4945A.portee: The cupbearer reminds us that God uses everything, even seemingly humble positions, to accomplish His plan. Joseph, a imprisoned servant, interprets the dream of the cupbearer and changes the course of Egyptian history: he teaches us that trust in God is worth more than earthly positions. Being a cupbearer to the King of Kings, serving Him in intimacy, is the highest honor for the believer.

sens: action of watering, irrigating a land
drink, liquid that one drinks
vessel or cup intended for drinking
abundance, fertility (for well-watered land)
H4945B.detail:
1. The beverage primarily refers to the watering, the irrigation of land: it is the water that falls on the soil to make it fertile. When Lot looks at the plain of Jordan, he sees it "watered" (Genesis 13:10), well supplied with water, lush and productive like Egypt.
2. But the word also refers to the drink itself, the liquid consumed to quench thirst. Leviticus specifies that a vessel containing a "beverage" becomes unclean if touched by something unclean (Leviticus 11:34).
3. By extension, it also refers to the vessels themselves, the cups intended for serving or drinking. The "cups" of King Solomon were all made of gold (1 Kings 10:21), a symbol of his wealth and royal splendor.
4. In Ezekiel, we speak of "fat pastures," meaning well-irrigated, rich, and fertile pastures, abundant in grass.
H4945B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to give to drink" or "to pour out liquid." The primary meaning is that of water poured or flowing to water and hydrate. The word has enriched its figurative meanings: from the watering of the soil, it moves to the drink consumed, to the vessels that contain it, and ultimately to the idea of fertility and abundance that good irrigation brings to land.
H4945B.emploi: The word appears six times in the Bible, with nuances of meaning depending on the context. In Genesis 13:10, it describes well-watered, fertile land. In Leviticus 11:34, it refers to the drink itself and its purity rules. In 1 Kings 10:21 and 2 Chronicles 9:20, it designates royal cups, objects of luxury and prestige. Finally, in Isaiah 32:6 and Ezekiel 45:15, it appears in contexts discussing withholding drink from the hungry or of rich and irrigated pastures. The word thus glides from the concrete (the water that waters) to the manufactured object (the cup) and to the figurative (the idea of abundance).
H4945B.portee: This word reminds the reader that the land and life depend on water: it is both what sustains crops and what quenches human thirst. It is a precious resource, to be protected and shared. The image of the "watered" land also invites reflection on divine blessing: a fertile land is a gift from God, and refusing water to one who is thirsty is to refuse to share that gift.

sens: that which makes something heavy, what it measures on a scale
the determined quantity of something
the importance, gravity of something
H4946.detail:
1. Weight is what is measured when something is placed on a scale. In ancient cultures, it was the primary instrument for controlling quantities of food, metals, or any merchandise. In Ezekiel 4:10, the prophet must eat precisely weighed food: twenty shekels (a shekel is a unit of weight-money) each day. This shows that weight serves to set an exact and limited measure.
2. By extension, weight can also refer to the quantity itself, independent of the action of weighing. It is the portion, the determined measure of something: here, the daily quantity of food that the prophet must consume to live day by day.
3. Weight can also take on a figurative sense: that of importance or gravity. A word that "carries weight" is a word that matters, that imposes itself.
H4946.origine: The Hebrew word mišqôl comes from the root שׁקל (shaqal), which means "to weigh" or "to hold in balance." It also gives the name of the shekel (šeqel), the ancient unit of weight and currency in Israel. The root is very ancient and refers to the concrete image of placing something on a scale to measure its mass. The French "poids" comes from the Latin "pensum," the participle of "pendere" (to weigh).
H4946.emploi: The word mišqôl appears once in biblical Hebrew. It is found in Ezekiel 4:10, in a passage where the prophet receives the order to live out a dramatic prophetic act: to eat rationed and inferior quality food to symbolize the siege and famine that will strike Jerusalem. The word here opposes abundance and the freedom to eat: it expresses restriction, imposed measure, strict control of sustenance. The context shows that weight is not neutral, but loaded with prophetic meaning.
H4946.portee: For the reader, this passage reveals how God uses the prophet's actions to speak to the people. The weight of the measured food symbolizes the coming judgment: no abundance, but just and strict sustenance. This reminds us that God controls and orders all things precisely, even famine and trial. It is also a call not to take food for granted, but to see it as a gift from the Lord.

sens: Horizontal beam that overhangs the opening of a door
Symbol of salvation and divine protection
H4947.detail:
1. The lintel is the wooden or stone beam that forms the top of the door frame, resting on the two side posts. In ancient Egypt, it was the most visible architectural structure of a house's entrance. It is on the lintel and the two posts that the Israelites marked the blood of the Passover lamb: "You shall take some of its blood and put it on the two doorposts and on the lintel of the houses where you eat it" (Exodus 12:7).
2. The lintel becomes the visible sign of the saving covenant: the Lord "will see the blood on the lintel and on the two doorposts; the Lord will pass over the door, and will not allow the destroyer to enter your houses to strike" (Exodus 12:23). The lintel marked with blood is thus the visible witness and guarantee of the salvation of the house and its inhabitants in the face of divine judgment.
H4947.origine: The Hebrew word mašqoph comes from the root שׁקף (shaqaph), which means "to look through a window, to lean over" or "to overhang." The lintel is literally what overhangs, what looks down upon the entrance of the house. This image of overhanging and dominance is rich: the lintel dominates the entrance as the divine sign dominates the fate of those who bear it.
H4947.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible, exclusively in the account of the Passover in Exodus 12. It always designates the horizontal beam of the door, a concrete and architectural object. But in this unique context, the lintel acquires theological depth: it becomes the place where the sign of salvation is inscribed. The blood is applied there, then observed by God Himself. The lintel thus transitions from being a simple construction element to a symbolic boundary between judgment and grace, between death and life.
H4947.portee: For the Christian reader, the lintel of the Passover foreshadows the cross of Christ: a visible and concrete sign of salvation, marked with the blood shed to protect us from divine judgment. Just as the Israelites sheltered under this sign, the Christian trusts in the work accomplished by Christ. This word reminds us that faith is never abstract: it is embodied in visible signs and concrete acts.

sens: What makes something heavy, its measured mass
Quantity of a precious material measured in units (shekels, talents)
Action of weighing, determining the mass of something
Load, burden that weighs on someone or something
Figuratively: importance, gravity of a matter
H4948.detail: 1. Weight is the quality that makes an object heavy. Goliath wears a coat of armor weighing five thousand shekels of bronze (1 Samuel 17:5), meaning that its heaviness can be measured in a recognized unit of mass. 2. In transactions and offerings, the word refers to the measured quantity of a metal or commodity: Abraham weighs the exact weight of gold he offers as a gift (Genesis 24:22), and the tables of the Lord for the Temple are specified by their weight in fine gold (1 Chronicles 28:17). 3. The word can also evoke the very action of weighing: God assures Job that the wind is measured and that water is also weighed (Job 28:25), meaning that there is an established measure for everything. 4. In figurative language, weight becomes what burdens or weighs down: in the context of a famine, God reduces the ration of bread to a very light weight (Ezekiel 4:16), symbolizing restriction and suffering. 5. The importance or gravity of a matter can also be expressed by this image of weight that bears heavily.
H4948.origine: The Hebrew word mishqal comes from the root shaqal which means "to weigh." This root evokes the action of placing something on a scale to measure its mass. The family of words includes shéqel (the shekel, unit of weight and currency), qal (light) and its derivatives. In the Septuagint, this word is often rendered by the Greek stathmon or baros, both of which retain the idea of weight and burden.
H4948.emploi: The word mishqal appears 42 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in the historical books (Genesis, Samuel, Kings, Chronicles) and in the instructions of the Law (Leviticus, Numbers). Its most consistent use is that of precise measurement: the offerings of worship are always given with exact weight (the silver dishes and bowls of Numbers), just like the royal ornaments (the crown of Goliath, the crown of the king of Ammon). The word also appears in Job and Ezekiel to evoke more abstract realities: the weight of wind and water in Job (28:25), the reduction of bread in measured weight during the famine in Ezekiel (4:16, 5:1). In Leviticus 19:35, the term serves to remind of the duty of fairness in weights and measures, a fundamental ethical requirement.
H4948.portee: This word reminds Christians that God demands precision and honesty in all material things. Just weights are not merely a commercial convenience, but a moral virtue: cheating in measurements is a sin. More broadly, the image of weight invites reflection on what truly "weighs" in life: the gravity of our actions, the burden of sin and repentance, the grace that lightens this burden.

sens: Instrument to check that something is plumb
Measure, standard of judgment
Straightness, fairness
H4949.detail:
1. The level is the tool that workers use to ensure that a surface is perfectly horizontal or vertical, without tilting to one side or the other. It is a concrete and practical instrument (2 Kings 21:13).

2. By extension, the word denotes a measure, a standard that is applied to judge something. In Isaiah 28:17, God says that He will make justice a "level" — in other words, a perfect criterion for evaluating and correcting.

3. The word also evokes the idea of straightness, of fairness without deviation. When one "applies the level," one corrects what deviates, setting things right according to an unchanging standard.
H4949.origine: The word comes from the root שׁקל (shaqal), which means "to weigh, evaluate." The level is primarily an instrument that weighs and balances; hence the idea of adjustment, of squaring. The family of words from this root always evokes the idea of balance, just measure, and correction.
H4949.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Kings 21:13, King Ahaz uses the level as a construction tool: it is the material instrument of the builder. In Isaiah 28:17, God uses the image of the level metaphorically: His justice will be the leveling that straightens everything that leans toward falsehood and injustice. These two uses show how the concrete meaning (the tool) becomes an image of divine correction and perfect fairness.
H4949.portee: This word helps the reader understand that God acts with absolute and impartial accuracy — there is no deviation or hidden injustice with Him. The image of the level, a builder's tool, also reminds us that God builds His work on straight and lasting foundations. For the believer, this means that divine judgment is always exact and His promises always sure.

sens: Clear and transparent water, without trouble or sediment
Figuratively, what is pure and unmixed
Moral or spiritual purity
H4950.detail:
1. The word denotes water that has clarified, free of the particles that troubled it: it is clear water where one can see the bottom. In Ezekiel 34:18, the shepherd reproaches the greedy sheep for drinking clear water and trampling the rest of the water with their feet, making it muddy for others.

2. Figuratively, this evokes purity and integrity: what has not been mixed or corrupted. The image of clear water extends to everything that is pure, without hidden malice.

3. Spiritually, the clarity of water symbolizes innocence, uprightness, and absence of guilt. The sheep that deliberately muddy the pure water are those who corrupt by their selfishness what was good and accessible to all.
H4950.origine: The Hebrew word מִשְׁקָע comes from a root meaning "to sink" or "to settle" (sediment that settles at the bottom). It thus denotes what has remained clear because impurities have settled. It is a concrete noun, linked to the daily observation of water that becomes clear when allowed to rest.
H4950.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Ezekiel 34:18. The prophet uses it in a word of judgment against the shepherds who oppress God's flock. Clear water symbolizes the goods and resources that God provides for His people, which some corrupt leaders pollute through their injustice. The rarity of the word emphasizes its importance in this passage: Ezekiel insists on the contrast between the offered purity and the trouble caused by evil.
H4950.portee: This word invites the believer to recognize that God offers purity and clarity in communal and spiritual life. It also warns us: those who know what is pure and just, but who muddy it through selfishness or malice, are guilty. It is a call to preserve integrity and not to corrupt what has been purified.

sens: Exercise of authority and power over a territory or a people
Expansion of a reign, increase of a government's power
H4951.detail:
1. The word designates the power to command and govern: it is the authority exercised by a king or a leader over those who are subject to him. In Isaiah 9:5, it is said that "the government will rest on his shoulders" of the Messiah, meaning that he will bear the weight and burden of governance: the image is that of a king who takes upon himself the responsibility of leading his people.
2. The word can also mean the expansion, the enlargement of a reign: it is the development of a government's power. In Isaiah 9:6, the prophet announces that at this "increase" of the Messiah's empire, peace will be without end — his dominion will continue to grow in extent and stability.
H4951.origine: The word comes from a root that means "to keep, to watch over, to dominate." It is formed on a very common action noun pattern in Hebrew. The root evokes the idea of a leader who watches over his people and exercises his authority with vigilance. It is a word specific to government and the exercise of political or royal power.
H4951.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the prophetic passage of Isaiah 9:5-6 announcing the coming of the Messiah. First, the Messiah's dominion is described as resting on his shoulder, emphasizing that he bears personal responsibility for it. Then, this dominion will continually grow, accompanied by eternal peace. These two uses show how the Bible presents the perfect government of the Messiah: a personal authority engaged (resting on his shoulders) and a reign that expands without end (continual increase).
H4951.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that Jesus, the awaited Messiah, does not exercise his authority from a distance or arbitrarily, but he assumes personal responsibility for it ("will rest on his shoulders"). His reign knows no limits: it continually expands in extent and power, bringing with it endless peace. It is a promise that the justice and government of Christ will ultimately triumph.

sens: Beverage obtained by pressing grapes
Product of the fermentation of grapes or grape juice
H4952.detail:
1. It is the liquid extracted by pressing grapes, whether fresh or fermented. In Numbers 6:3, the Nazarite who makes his vow must abstain from any drink "derived" from grapes: fresh juice, wine, vinegar — any liquid form obtained from grapes is forbidden to him. The word concretely designates what is obtained when pressing the fruit.
2. By extension, it also refers to the product of fermentation, the wine itself or any alcoholic beverage derived from grapes. The context of the Nazarite vow shows that the prohibition applies to juice whether it remains fresh or has fermented: the word encompasses all stages of transformation of grapes into beverage.
H4952.origine: The word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "pressing" or "extracting" by compressing. It is a noun formed from the verb meaning to compress or express: the juice is literally what is drawn out by pressing. The word belongs to the vocabulary of winemaking in Israelite culture.
H4952.emploi: This word appears only once in the Old Testament, in Numbers 6:3, in the context of the Nazarite vow. It is a religious law imposing a particular purity: one who commits to being a Nazarite must avoid not only wine but grape juice in all its forms — fresh, fermented, or turned into vinegar. This total prohibition of juice shows that the Nazarite vow demands a radical separation from the vine and its products, symbolizing consecration to God.
H4952.portee: This requirement regarding grape juice forbids the Nazarite and reminds the believer that true consecration to God may require renouncing things that are lawful in themselves. It is a concrete sign of dependence on God and rejection of ordinary comforts or pleasures. It invites us to understand that the consecrated Christian life sometimes involves visible renunciations that testify to our priorities.

sens: wind instrument, pipe for blowing and modulating sound
H4953.detail: 1. It is a pipe pierced with holes, from which sounds are produced by blowing into it — similar to a flute or a simple clarinet. The chalumeau appears in ancient Israel and throughout the Middle East as a popular, lightweight, and portable instrument. In the Bible, it is always mentioned among orchestral musical instruments, never alone: it is a group instrument that adds its voice to that of trumpets, lyres, and harps. In Daniel 3:5, King Nebuchadnezzar orders all peoples to bow down while listening to a symphony where the sound of the chalumeau resounds.
H4953.origine: The Hebrew word mashroqi comes from a root that means "to whistle" or "to produce a high sound." It is an onomatopoeic word: it already imitates the sound of the pipe it designates. In Aramaic, the language in which the book of Daniel is written, this word belongs to the concrete vocabulary of musical instruments, without metaphorical dimension.
H4953.emploi: The chalumeau appears only four times in the Bible, all in the same passage, Daniel 3:5-15, where King Nebuchadnezzar plays orchestral music to announce to the peoples of his empire the order to worship his golden statue. The Greek word that translates it in some versions is "aulos." It is an authentic Eastern instrument from the 6th century BC, and Luke the historian would mention this detail to show his precise knowledge of Babylonian times.
H4953.portee: The chalumeau reminds us that the Bible does not disdain musical instruments — it mentions them without guilt. But this passage also shows the danger: beautiful and captivating music can serve to lead God's people toward idolatry. That is why the three young men, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego, refuse to bow down despite the seduction of this royal symphony.

sens: Descendants of Mishraï, ancestor of one of the four families of Kirjath-Jearim
H4954.detail: 1. The Mischraïens form the fourth clan among the four families descended from Kirjath-Jearim, an important city of Judah. Like the other families mentioned (Jethrites, Puthites, Shumathites), they are identified by their eponymous ancestor, Mishraï.
H4954.origine: The name Mischraïens comes from Mishraï, an ancestor whose patronymic was borne by his descendants. This type of designation by patronymic is typical of Israelite genealogy: those who are descended from an ancestor are called by the name of that ancestor. The precise meaning of the name Mishraï remains uncertain, but it could be related to a root meaning "evil" or "adversity."
H4954.emploi: This name appears only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 2:53. It appears in the genealogical list of the families of Kirjath-Jearim, alongside the three other families from the same city. This mention serves to establish the lineage of the populations settled in this region of Judah before and after the conquest.

sens: A kiln or a hearth where an intense fire burns
A funeral pyre or a place of cremation
A situation of extreme suffering and trial
H4955.detail:
1. The furnace is primarily a kiln, a closed space where a very hot fire burns. In Isaiah 33:12, the prophet compares the peoples to "furnaces of lime": the stone will be cooked there as in a real kiln, to make lime — an image of total destruction.
2. The word also refers to a funeral pyre, where perfumes and goods are burned to honor the dead. In Jeremiah 34:5, God promises Zedekiah that perfumes will be burned in his honor at his death, as for former kings: it is an act of funeral respect.
3. Figuratively, the furnace becomes the biblical image of suffering, of the trial that consumes man as fire consumes wood. It is this image that later inspired apocalyptic texts about judgment.
H4955.origine: The Hebrew word comes from the root שׂרף (saraph), which means "to burn." Mishraphah gathers the idea of burning, of intense and controlled combustion (that of the kiln, that of the funeral hearth).
