The root saraph first evokes the fire that ravages, and then, by extension, any devastating heat that purifies or destroys.
H4955.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two very different contexts. In Isaiah 33:12, it describes the destruction of enemy peoples likened to lime furnaces that collapse into ruins. In Jeremiah 34:5, it refers to the royal funeral rite: perfumes are burned, honoring the dead by fire. These two uses — burning destruction and ritual combustion — show that the mishraphah is always an intense and often inevitable fire.
H4955.portee: The furnace reminds Christians that trials, no matter how overwhelming, are often necessary passages — like fire that refines gold. It also invites respect for what God allows, whether it be judgment on our enemies or death itself, since even death is accompanied by honor and dignity in God's eyes.

sens: city in northern Palestine, near Sidon
H4956.detail: Misrephoth-Maïm is a locality in northern Palestine, located in the coastal region near Sidon. The name literally means "burnings of water" or "hot springs," which may evoke thermal springs or remarkable geological phenomena of the place.
H4956.origine: The Hebrew name is composed of two words: misrephoth ("burnings" or "blazings") and mayim ("waters"). This formation suggests a place known for particular waters — perhaps hot or bubbling springs — that would have captured the imagination of the inhabitants and given its name to the site.
H4956.emploi: Misrephoth-Maïm appears twice in the account of the conquest of Canaan by Joshua. In Joshua 11:8, it is mentioned as the limit of the pursuit of the Canaanite kings defeated by Israel — the pursued warriors fled to this place. In Joshua 13:6, it is listed among the lands that the Lord promises to drive out before Israel, marking a northern boundary of the territory to be conquered, always associated with the region of Sidon. It remains a geographical landmark of the borders of the promised land.

sens: ancient city of Edom, homeland of King Samlah
H4957.detail: Masréka is an ancient city of the kingdom of Edom, located southeast of the Dead Sea. It is the birthplace of King Samlah, one of the ancient Edomite rulers who reigned before the establishment of the Israelite monarchy (Genesis 36:36; 1 Chronicles 1:47).
H4957.origine: The name Masréka literally means "vineyard of noble vines" or "quality vineyard." This etymology evokes a fertile and productive place, a characteristic that the name has retained in biblical tradition to designate this Edomite center.
H4957.emploi: Masréka appears exactly twice in the Bible, both in parallel royal genealogies: in Genesis 36:36 and in 1 Chronicles 1:47. These two passages list the kings of Edom who reigned before the emergence of royalty in Israel. Samlah, originating from Masréka, is presented as the successor of King Hadad in the Edomite royal lineage. The context is purely genealogical: the text simply notes the geographical origin of the ruler without providing further details about the city itself or its political significance.

sens: cooking vessel used to cook food over heat
flat utensil used to sauté or cook food
H4958.detail:
1. A pan is a cooking vessel, generally flat and equipped with a handle, in which food is cooked. In 2 Samuel 13:9, the daughter of King Amnon cooks cakes in it (the text mentions heart-shaped cakes): "then taking the pan, she poured them out before him."
2. This word more broadly designates any cooking utensil over high heat — a shallow dish where food can be sautéed or browned. The image evokes practical and quick cooking, far from large fermentation or storage utensils.
H4958.origine: The Hebrew word מַשְׂרֵת (mas.ret) comes from the root שׂרת (s.ret), which means to spread or lay out. The pan, a flat utensil, is named so because it offers a flat and extended surface for cooking food. This word belongs to a family designating cooking and serving utensils.
H4958.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Samuel 13:9. It designates an ordinary cooking utensil, in the context of food preparation at the royal palace. The unique use of the word does not allow for nuance in its meaning, but it is clearly understood as a domestic or palace cooking vessel.
H4958.portee: This word reminds us that even in the narratives of the Bible, daily life involves simple and practical utensils. It also shows how the Bible does not disdain the concrete details of ordinary life — here, cooking — to tell the story of God with humans.

sens: To touch someone or something with one's hand, to perceive by contact
To grope, to search by feeling in darkness or uncertainty
To rummage, to explore by passing the hand to search
To explore by feeling to verify or inspect
H4959.detail:
1. To touch someone or something with one's hand is the simplest gesture: Isaac asks to feel Jacob by touching him to verify his identity (Genesis 27:22), as he doubts what he hears.
2. To grope describes one who seeks to advance without clear sight: the cursed man in Deuteronomy 28:29 gropes at noon like a blind man in darkness — he walks by groping because the curse removes all clarity and reference points.
3. To rummage means to pass the hands everywhere to explore: Laban rummages through Jacob's tent searching for his stolen gods (Genesis 31:34), passing his hand over all the belongings without finding what he seeks.
4. To explore by feeling means to verify something by touching it methodically: Jacob fears that his father will touch him and discover the deception (Genesis 27:12), as contact reveals the truth.
H4959.origine: The Hebrew verb מָשַׁשׁ (mashash) expresses the action of the hand that feels and explores. The root evokes the natural gesture of one who seeks to know something by touch — hence its use for all senses related to physical contact, from the most direct (touch) to the most uncertain (groping in the dark). This word belongs to the domain of the senses and concrete knowledge, that of the body which verifies and controls.
H4959.emploi: This verb appears about 8 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in Genesis and Exodus. Genesis 27 uses it twice in the episode where Isaac wants to touch Jacob to verify his identity: it is touch as a means of verification. Genesis 31 employs the verb in the sense of rummaging: Laban rummages through Jacob's tents. Exodus 10:21 and Deuteronomy 28:29 describe groping: the plagues of Egypt will make the darkness so dense that it can be touched (Exodus), and the curse will make the Israelite unfaithful like the blind man groping. The context thus varies from simple touch to desperate searching.
H4959.portee: This word teaches that touch is a form of knowledge and verification: Isaac seeks to know the truth through physical contact. It also reminds us that darkness and curse render man powerless, reduced to groping without certainty. For the believer, it is an image of dependence on God and the need for spiritual clarity.

sens: lavish meal gathering several people
rejoicing, celebration through food and drink
drink served or consumed during a meal
food in general
H4960.detail:
1. The feast is a celebratory meal, generally abundant and refined, where several guests gather. It marks a solemn moment or a special occasion. Thus, Lot offers a feast to the angels (Genesis 19:3), King Ahasuerus organizes a grand royal feast (Esther 1:3, 1:5), and Samson receives his guests at the feast (Judges 14:10).
2. The feast is also an occasion for rejoicing and celebration: people gather to honor someone or mark an event. After the death of Saul, David invites Abner and his men to a feast (2 Samuel 3:20), which signifies reconciliation and peace.
3. The word can also refer to the drink itself, the key element of the feast: it is made a day of feasting and joy (Esther 9:18), where the drink flows abundantly.
4. Sometimes it refers to the food and drink offered to the king or an important host (Daniel 1:5, 1:8, 1:10).
H4960.origine: The Hebrew word מִשְׁתֶּה (mish.teh) comes from a root that evokes the idea of drinking together. It is a specifically Hebrew and Aramaic word (there is an identical Aramaic form), very common in the Old Testament to express festive meals. Its root emphasizes the element of shared drink that characterizes the feast, not just a meal, but a convivial celebration.
H4960.emploi: The word appears 43 times in the Old Testament, mainly in Ecclesiastes, Esther, and historical accounts. In the book of Esther, it recurs constantly as the royal palace of King Ahasuerus is the site of sumptuous feasts and intrigues (Esther 1, 5, 7). Feasts mark crucial moments: Samson gives a feast at his wedding (Judges 14), David and Abner reconcile over a feast (2 Samuel 3:20). The book of Job mentions the feasts of Job's sons (Job 1:4, 1:5), showing prosperity. Isaiah 5:12 criticizes those who host feasts while ignoring the work of the Lord. The context shows that the feast is a sign of prosperity, power, or an important moment, but it can also reveal the forgetfulness of God.
H4960.portee: The feast in the Bible is not limited to pleasure: it is a social and spiritual act. Feasts can express joy, reconciliation, gratitude towards God. But Isaiah and Ecclesiastes warn: those who live only for feasts lose sight of the essential and forget the work of God. For the believer, it is about celebrating wisely, without allowing earthly pleasures to distract from the Lord.

sens: lavish and joyful meal where one eats and drinks abundantly
solemn celebration gathering the great ones of the kingdom
moment of relaxation and shared pleasure
H4961.detail:
1. A feast is a grand meal where food and drink flow in abundance, well beyond a simple daily meal. It is an occasion of joy and conviviality where people gather to celebrate. In Daniel 5:10, the queen hurries to join the royal feast where King Belshazzar receives his nobles with grandeur.

2. This word also designates the event itself in its official context: the king's feast is the solemn reception where high dignitaries sit. It is a moment of power and prestige, visible in the grandeur of the invited guests.

3. Figuratively, the feast evokes pleasure, satisfaction, and indulgence in earthly joys. This is why the Bible uses it to depict moments of prosperity or, at times, royal debauchery.
H4961.origine: This Aramaic word is a borrowing or variant of the Hebrew word ‘mishté’ (מִשְׁתֶּה), found in the Old Testament. It likely comes from a root denoting drinking or sitting together. The family of words would include verbs related to consumption and conviviality. The Aramaic shares with Hebrew a notion of joyful gathering around the table.
H4961.emploi: This word appears once in the Bible, in the crucial passage of Daniel 5:10 in Aramaic. It designates the grand feast of King Belshazzar, that nighttime event where the king drinks wine in the presence of his thousand nobles and his wives. It is in the midst of this feast that the mysterious hand appears to write on the wall the divine judgment: ‘Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin’. The royal feast thus becomes the setting for the king's downfall; his moment of earthly glory is also that of his divine humiliation. The word paints the splendor and carelessness of the monarch before his fall.
H4961.portee: This account reminds the believer that no wealth, no earthly power can shield one from God's judgment. The sumptuous feast of King Belshazzar, far from saving him, becomes the witness of his condemnation. This invites the reader to seek first the kingdom of God rather than the fleeting pleasures of the world.

sens: human individual of the male sex
human person in general, without emphasis on sex
small number of people, men
wicked, perverse men
H4962.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a man, a male individual: in Deuteronomy 33:6, one wishes that ‘his men be many’, meaning that Reuben has many male descendants.
2. It can also simply refer to people, without emphasizing sex: it is a generic term for talking about human beings, as in Psalms 26:4 where the psalmist refuses to sit ‘with false men’ — he speaks of people, individuals.
3. The expression ‘small number’ often recurs: in Genesis 34:30, Jacob says ‘I have but a small number of men’, which emphasizes the numerical weakness of his household against the peoples of the land (Genesis 34:30).
4. In a moral context, the word can qualify wicked or perverse men: in Job 11:11, it is written that God ‘knows the wicked’, meaning those who commit iniquity.
H4962.origine: The Hebrew word מַת (mat) belongs to the root that evokes masculinity and male strength. It is related to other terms for ‘man’ or ‘male’ in Hebrew. In the Old Testament, it is mainly used in poetry and archaic narratives to evoke man as a strong and capable being. The word sometimes opposes ‘woman’ (ishsha), but can also refer to humanity more broadly.
H4962.emploi: This word appears 21 times in the Old Testament, mainly in poetic and historical books (Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Jeremiah). It carries three meanings depending on the context. First, it designates men or warriors in number: ‘his men’ (Deuteronomy 33:6), or a group of fighters (Deuteronomy 2:34, 3:6). Secondly, it qualifies a small number: Jacob complains of having ‘few men’ against his enemies (Genesis 34:30). Thirdly, it can evoke morally corrupt men: the ‘false men’ (Psalms 26:4) or the ‘wicked’ (Job 11:11). Thus, the meaning varies between masculine identity, reduced quantity, and moral quality.
H4962.portee: This word reminds us that the believer's strength does not come from the number of men or earthly resources, but from God alone. Like Jacob with his ‘few men’ or the psalmist refusing the company of ‘false men’, the text invites us to seek truth and protection from God rather than relying on human alliances or appearances.

sens: Fibrous residue of grain after threshing
Fragile and contemptible material
That which is crushed or worthless
H4963.detail:
1. Straw is the remainder of the cereal plant (wheat, barley) obtained after separating the grains by threshing. It is a coarse, hollow, and lightweight fiber. In Isaiah 25:10, the straw trampled in a dung pit evokes this substance that can be crushed effortlessly, a concrete and humble image of what is vulnerable.
2. By extension, straw represents what is worthless, fragile, and contemptible. Moab, the enemy of Israel, will be crushed like straw: the image emphasizes its powerlessness against God's might and its inevitable downfall (Isaiah 25:10).
3. In a dung pit, straw takes on an additional dimension: it becomes a symbol of what is defiled, rejected, reduced to nothing. It is an image of dishonor and humiliation for Moab.
H4963.origine: The Hebrew word מַתְבֵּן (matben) comes from the root taban, which denotes the action of beating or trampling grain. The word literally means "that which is beaten," the residue obtained after threshing. The family of the word refers to the idea of separation and reduction to crumbs.
H4963.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 25:10. It is used in a judgment oracle against Moab, an enemy people of Israel. The prophet Isaiah uses the image of straw trampled in a dung pit to describe the humiliation and crushing of this nation. This image contrasts Moab's dignity with its complete humiliation, emphasizing that nothing can withstand the hand of the Lord. The apocalyptic context of the passage accentuates the certainty and inevitability of this judgment.
H4963.portee: This image invites the reader to meditate on God's sovereign power over nations and earthly powers. It teaches that what seems strong or threatening will be brought to nothing before God, and that humility before His will is the only wisdom. For the believer, it is a call not to fear the enemies of God or His people, for their end is sealed.

sens: Metal piece placed in the mouth of an animal to direct it
Means of control or authority over someone
H4964.detail:
1. The bit is the metal equipment that the rider places in the mouth of the horse or donkey to direct and restrain it. It is the instrument that transforms a wild or unruly animal into an obedient creature. In 2 Kings 19:28, the king of Assyria threatens to put "my bit between your lips" to the king of Judah: the image is brutal, lowering the king to the status of a submissive domestic animal.
2. By extension, the bit refers to any means of mastering or controlling someone. In Psalms 32:9, the psalmist exhorts the reader not to be "like a horse or a mule without understanding; they are bridled with a bit and bridle." The warning means: if you refuse divine wisdom, you will have to be forced and constrained like a beast, instead of being directed freely by voluntary obedience.
H4964.origine: The Hebrew word méteg comes from a root that evokes the idea of holding firmly or restraining. It appears infrequently in the Bible (4 times), which shows that it is a strong and precise image. The image of the bit is universal in ancient societies: it was the basic instrument for commanding horses and donkeys, essential animals in pastoral and military life.
H4964.emploi: The word méteg appears only four times in the Hebrew Bible, always in poetic or prophetic texts. It almost always carries a connotation of subjugation or humiliation. In 2 Kings 19:28 and Isaiah 37:29 (two parallel passages), the bit is used as a divine threat against the pride of the Assyrian king: God presents Himself as the one who can reduce the oppressor to the status of an animal. In Psalms 32:9 and Proverbs 26:3, the bit illustrates the necessity of constraining one who refuses wisdom or obedience, an image of divine correction. In all cases, it is an image of servitude and control.
H4964.portee: The bit in the Bible teaches that rebellion against God and refusal of wisdom lead only to slavery. It reminds us that voluntary obedience to God is freedom, while pride and disobedience reduce man to the condition of a beast without understanding. It is an invitation to gentleness and listening rather than to sterile resistance.

sens: Another name for Gath, a Philistine city
H4965.detail: Metheg-Ammah literally means "the bit of the mother" or "the bit of the mother-city." It is another name given to Gath, one of the five major cities of the Philistines. The term evokes the idea of domination or control: the one who holds the "bit" or the "rein" of the mother-city controls it. In 2 Samuel 8:1, this name appears when King David takes this fortress and subdues the Philistines, thus demonstrating his grip on their territory.
H4965.origine: The Hebrew word consists of two elements: "meteg" (מֶתֶג), which means "bit" or "rein" — the object that allows one to direct and master an animal or force — and "ha-amma" (הָאַמָּה), which means "the mother" or "the mother-city." This poetic and evocative name highlights the strategic character of Gath: it was a major city, a "mother-city" among the Philistine cities, and the one who took control of it held the reins of the entire Philistine territory.
H4965.emploi: Metheg-Ammah appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Samuel 8:1, at the heart of the account of King David's victories. At this point in the text, David subdues the Philistines and takes several of their territories. The name Metheg-Ammah is used here as a synonym for Gath to emphasize the strategic importance of this conquest: by taking this mother-city, David establishes his dominance over the entire Philistine people. The choice of this name rather than simply "Gath" reinforces the idea that this victory represents the takeover of Philistine power.
H4965.portee: This name reminds us that King David's victories, granted by God, allowed him to establish order and peace in the territory of Israel by subduing the enemy peoples that threatened it. For the reader, it shows how God honors those who serve Him faithfully and courageously, granting them victory even over the most formidable strongholds.

sens: Having a sweet taste, pleasant to the palate
Pleasing to the senses, charming
Soothing to the soul, comforting
Pleasing to the mind, delightful
H4966.detail:
1. The primary sense is physical: that which is sweet, like honey. In Proverbs 24:13, honey is described as "sweet" to the palate — this is the taste sensation of sweetness. The parallel with Judges 14:18 ("What is sweeter than honey?") shows that it is an image of immediate sensory pleasure.
2. The word expands to encompass everything that is pleasing to the senses. Pleasant words are a ray of "sweet" honey for the soul (Proverbs 16:24) — sweetness extends to moral and spiritual experience. It is a pleasure that envelops and soothes.
3. By extension, "sweet" describes that which deeply comforts. God's commandments are "sweeter than honey" (Psalms 19:11), as they nourish the heart and soul, not just the taste. It is an inner sweetness, a consolation.
4. The word can also describe what pleases the mind, what one desires: in Proverbs 27:7, the hungry person finds "sweet" everything that is bitter, because desire transforms our perception. Sweetness becomes a matter of desire and joy.
H4966.origine: The Hebrew word מָתוֹק (mâtoq) comes from a root that denotes what pleases and attracts. In biblical Hebrew, it is related to the idea of pleasant flavor and that which charms. The word belongs to a family of terms that described sensory and emotional life: that which is good to taste, good to hear, good to live. It is a concrete word at its origin, which has gradually gained figurative meanings.
H4966.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Psalms) and in poetry (Song of Songs). It primarily describes honey and sweet taste (Judges 14:14 and 14:18, Proverbs 24:13), but the Bible quickly uses it in a figurative sense: words (Proverbs 16:24), light (Ecclesiastes 11:7), and especially the divine Word (Psalms 19:11). Ezekiel 3:3 shows the prophet eating a scroll that becomes "sweet as honey" in his mouth — an image of the internalization of the Word. The context changes: sometimes sweet means tasty and attractive (honey, pleasant words), while at other times it means comforting and nourishing (the divine Word). Isaiah 5:20 reverses the image by calling the Jews who "call sweet bitter" — here, sweetness becomes a moral deception.
H4966.portee: This word invites the believer to taste the goodness of God. Just as honey is sweet to the palate, the Word and divine commandments should be sweet to the soul — a flavor to discover and savor, not a burden imposed. But the word also warns: sweetness can deceive those who confuse good and evil. It is an invitation to recognize and cherish what is truly good, and to cultivate a soul capable of tasting divine joy.

sens: Man who lived before the Flood, from the lineage of Cain
H4967.detail: Metuschaël is a human ancestor living in the antediluvian period (before the Flood). He appears in the genealogy of Cain, presented in Genesis 4:18: he is the son of Mehujaël and the father of Lamech. His name means "man of God," suggesting a connection with the divine despite being a descendant of Cain, the first murderer. He represents a link in the chain of primitive human generations, before God sent the Flood to judge the earth.
H4967.origine: The name Metuschaël means "man of God" (composed of the Hebrew word for "who" and "God"). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God. It belongs to the series of antediluvian names, characterized by their length and religious formation. This name reflects the patriarchal tradition of invoking God in the identity of individuals.
H4967.emploi: Metuschaël is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Genesis 4:18. He appears solely as a genealogical link in the lineage of Cain: son of Mehujaël, father of Lamech. The Bible does not report any particular events concerning him, unlike other antediluvian figures such as Enoch or Noah. His role is limited to ensuring genealogical continuity up to Lamech, who himself will live until the Flood.

sens: Man living before the Flood, son of Enoch and father of Lamech
H4968.detail: Methuselah is one of the major figures of the antediluvian Old Testament (before the Flood). He was the son of the prophet Enoch, who "walked with God" (Genesis 5:22), and the father of Lamech. Methuselah is especially famous for having lived longer than any other man in the Bible: nine hundred sixty-nine years (Genesis 5:27). He was born when Enoch was sixty-five years old (Genesis 5:21), and then lived seventy-four generations before the Flood — he thus represents the order and longevity that God granted to men in the antediluvian age. His Hebrew name literally means "man of the dart" or "man of the sent one," possibly symbolizing one who is sent or launched by God. He is mentioned six times in Scripture, notably in the genealogy of Genesis 5 and in that of 1 Chronicles 1, which establishes his place in the lineage leading to Noah and ultimately to Jesus.
H4968.origine: The Hebrew name מְתוּשֶׁלַח (Methuselah) comes from two roots: "meth" (man, mortal) and "shalach" (send, dart, arrow). Literally, it means "man of the arrow" or "man of the dart" — an enigmatic image that some ancients interpreted as prophetic of the Flood: the man through whom God "sent" judgment by the waters. His name in the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) is Μαθουσάλα (Mathousala), and in the New Testament (Luke 3:37), he appears in the genealogy of Jesus as a distant ancestor.
H4968.emploi: Methuselah appears six times in the Bible. He is first named in the genealogy of chapter 5 of Genesis, which lists the antediluvian patriarchs with their ages. In Genesis 5:25-27, we learn that he fathered Lamech at one hundred eighty-seven years, then lived seven hundred eighty-two more years, and died at the exceptionally advanced age of nine hundred sixty-nine years. This genealogy highlights his important place in the chain of descendants from Adam through Enoch to Noah. In 1 Chronicles 1:3, Methuselah is simply listed in the genealogy of Judah, confirming his role as an essential link in the history of salvation before the Flood.
H4968.portee: Methuselah reminds the Christian reader that God granted the early humans extraordinarily long lives, not out of pride or greed, but in a context where obedience and closeness to God (as with his father Enoch) were possible. His exceptional life also illustrates divine patience: nearly a thousand years separate his birth from the Flood, showing the immense delay God granted before judgment. His presence in the genealogy of Christ shows that even the longest of human lives fits within God's plan for redemption.

sens: To stretch, deploy a flexible object forward or sideways
To stretch the heavens, the sky like a veil or a fabric that is opened
To hold something in place by pulling it
H4969.detail:
1. The verb evokes the physical action of deploying or stretching something flexible — fabric, veil, tent — by pulling on it to open or enlarge it. It is a concrete gesture, that of someone who grabs a piece of fabric and pulls it forward or sideways to occupy space.
2. The Bible uses it to describe God's creative gesture: in Isaiah 40:22, the Lord "stretches out the heavens like a light garment" and "spreads them out like a tent." This image compares the celestial vault to a fabric that God spreads above the earth, showing both its apparent lightness and the power of the one who holds it.
3. The word also suggests the idea of holding in place, keeping taut — like a tent that is unfolded and secured to remain stable and useful.
H4969.origine: The Hebrew verb מָתַח (matach) comes from a root that evokes the gesture of pulling or stretching. It belongs to the family of movement and deployment verbs. Its primary image is that of the physical gesture: pulling something to enlarge, open, or set it in place. This stretching particularly applies to flexible objects — fabrics, veils, skins — that lend themselves to being stretched.
H4969.emploi: This verb appears only once in the provided Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 40:22, where it describes God's creative gesture. The context is that of a cosmic hymn: the prophet contemplates Creation and wants to express the absolute dominion of the Lord over heaven and earth. The verb "to stretch" paints God in the act of deployment, the one who masters and orders the universe as one would a simple tent. It is an image of quiet and benevolent power: God does not force, He stretches the heavens with the same ease as a man unfolding a veil.
H4969.portee: This image invites contemplation of God's greatness in Creation. It shows that the entire universe, as vast as it may seem, is for Him only like a tent that He spreads out. For the reader, this becomes a source of comfort: if God holds the heavens with such mastery, we can trust Him with our daily worries. The image also desacralizes the fear of the cosmos: the sky is not a power against us, but a space arranged by our Creator.

sens: At what time? (question about time)
Until what time? (duration, impatience)
How much longer? (exasperation, urgency)
H4970.detail:
1. The word simply poses a question about when something will happen or has happened: "When will I work for my house?" asks Jacob (Genesis 30:30), or "When will he die?" say the enemies of the psalmist (Psalms 41:6). It is a direct inquiry about time.
2. Very often, it expresses impatience: "How long will the wicked triumph?" cries the psalmist (Psalms 94:3), or "How long will you lie down?" asks one of the lazy (Proverbs 6:9). The inquiry concerns the end of a situation that lasts too long.
3. The word can also express exasperation at an unbearable delay: "How long will you delay in purifying yourself?" reproaches God to Jerusalem (Jeremiah 13:27). It is less a question than a complaint: "How much longer?"
H4970.origine: It is a simple interrogative word in Hebrew, formed from an ancient root expressing time and succession. The word can combine with prepositions: "until when" (עַד־מָתַי) to reinforce the idea of duration, "after how long" to point to a delay. In biblical Hebrew, interrogative words like this serve to ask the most fundamental questions about existence and time.
H4970.emploi: This word appears about forty times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Psalms, Proverbs, Jeremiah, and the prophets. It can be a simple question about the future ("When will you stop crying over Saul?" asks God to Samuel in 1 Samuel 16:1), but it most often expresses the impatience or protest of a suffering soul. The Psalms use it abundantly: the believer asks God how much longer his suffering will last (Psalms 6:4, 94:3). It is the cry of one who waits, endures, and pleads with God to act.
H4970.portee: This word reminds us that impatience and the desire for swift action from God are part of authentic prayer. The saints of the Bible do not hide their frustration or the feeling that God is slow to act; it is an act of faith to tell Him so. At the same time, the renewal of this question through the ages shows that waiting on God is at the heart of the believer's life: we always live between the promise and its fulfillment.

sens: Number, quantity, or measure fixed in advance
Ratio established between the parts of a whole
Rule, standard that imposes itself
Recipe, precise formula to follow
H4971.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a determined quantity that must be provided or produced: in Exodus 5:8, Pharaoh imposes on the Israelites to make the same number of bricks as before, no less — this is the "quantity" fixed, the quota that cannot be diminished.
2. It also means the exact ratio between the elements of a mixture or composition: in Exodus 30:32 and 30:37, Moses is ordered to make the sacred perfume exactly according to the "proportions" prescribed by God, a mixture that must neither be added to a man's body nor imitated. It is the formula that must be followed point by point.
3. Applied to measurements, the word describes the rule that must govern the dimensions: in Ezekiel 45:11, the ephah and the bath will have a "measure" "regulated" according to the homer, meaning that a single standard governs them.
H4971.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to measure" or "to trace." It originally designates the act or result of fixing a measure, determining the proportions of something. It is a concrete word, related to the work of the carpenter, jeweler, or chemist — one who manufactures according to precise rules.
H4971.emploi: The word appears about 5 times in the Old Testament, mainly in the books of law and legislation (Exodus, Ezekiel, Chronicles). It applies to very concrete contexts: the production of bricks in Egypt, the composition of the sacred perfume of the tabernacle, the capacity measures for wheat and oil. In each case, it emphasizes the importance of regularity, accuracy, and obedience to a standard that comes from outside — either from Pharaoh or from God Himself. The word never has a purely abstract or spiritual meaning.
H4971.portee: This word reminds the reader that God loves order, precision, and obedience to His ordinances, even in material details: the measurements of the tabernacle are not left to chance, the formula for His sacred perfume must be exact. It is an invitation to respect God's will with attention and faithfulness, without subtracting from or adding to it.

sens: part of the mouth that holds the teeth and can open and close
instrument of power or destruction, compared to a weapon
H4973.detail:
1. The jaw is the part of the mouth, movable or not, that holds the teeth. It is the organ that allows biting and tearing. Job says he "broke the jaw of the wicked" (Job 29:17): he rendered powerless the one who caused harm, depriving him of the ability to do evil, just as one would immobilize a fierce beast.
2. By extension, the jaw becomes the image of the power to devour, conquer, or destroy. An invading people has "the jaws of a lioness" (Joel 1:6), and the teeth of certain men are described as "swords" and their "jaws" as "knives" (Proverbs 30:14): here we see creatures that devour the weak, reduced to machines of death.
H4973.origine: The Hebrew word מְתַלְּעוֹת comes from a root that denotes the action of biting or crushing. The jaw is primarily a physical organ, but biblical language often uses it to speak of the power of a beast or a man to do harm. It is a concrete image: the beast that opens its mouth to seize its prey.
H4973.emploi: This word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts where force or malice is at play. In Job 29:17, it concerns justice: breaking the jaw of the wicked means rendering him harmless. In Proverbs 30:14 and Joel 1:6, the jaw is compared to a weapon or that of a wild animal: it embodies a threat to the weak. The word remains concrete, never abstract; it always paints an image of power or physical destruction.
H4973.portee: The jaw reminds us that the power to do harm is visible and embodied. When Job breaks the jaw of the wicked, he restores justice by depriving the evil one of his weapon. When devouring creatures are described by their jaws, we see that the oppression of the poor is a tangible reality that God sees and for which He demands accountability.

sens: Integrity of the body, absence of disease or injury
Complete state, whole, without defect
Physical and moral well-being
H4974.detail:
1. The word first evokes the health of the body: a state where the flesh is not ravaged by disease or suffering. In Psalms 38:4, the psalmist cries, "There is nothing healthy in my flesh" to express that his entire body suffers under the weight of his sin — every part of him is affected, none brings him relief. It is a lost physical integrity.
2. The word also means wholeness, completeness: nothing is missing, nothing is broken. In Isaiah 1:6, the prophet describes a people sick from head to toe: "From the sole of the foot to the head, there is no soundness" — the image is that of a body whose every part is not spared from the wound. It is a lack of total integrity.
3. More broadly, the word can denote a state of fullness or totality, as in Judges 20:48 where "even the livestock" conveys the sense of completeness: everything, down to the last elements, in all their integrity.
H4974.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of completeness and physical integrity. It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "whole" or "integral." In the Greek Old Testament (Septuagint), this word often translates the Hebrew expressing the fullness of the body or well-being. The basic image is that of a totality without rupture: a body without injury, a preserved integrity.
H4974.emploi: This word is infrequent in the Hebrew Bible: only four occurrences, concentrated in the Psalms and the prophets. It appears mainly when the text describes bodily suffering or physical integrity. In Psalms 38:4 and 8, the word recurs to express the loss of health under the weight of guilt: sin disorganizes the entire body, stripping it of its cohesion. In Isaiah 1:6, it paints the image of Israel as a hopeless sick person: from head to toe, not a part is healthy. In Judges 20:48, the context of war gives the word a nuance of completion and totality: everything that exists has passed through the sword.
H4974.portee: This word speaks to the heart of the Christian reader confronted with suffering and sin. It shows that physical evil and moral evil are linked: sin affects the whole man, body and soul, depriving him of the original integrity that God had given him. In contemplating these texts, the believer understands that healing — in the complete sense — comes only from God alone, and that it restores man in his entirety.

sens: The part of the body between the ribs and the hips
What encircles the body, like a belt or band
Physical strength, vigor of the body
The seat of virility, generative power
Figuratively, the intimate center of being, where deep feelings reside
H4975.detail:
1. The loins are the area of the lower back, between the ribs and the hips. It is an important region of the human body: when Elijah receives God's strength, he "girded up his loins" (1 Kings 18:46), meaning he tucked in his robe to run freely. Similarly, during Passover, the Israelites ate "with their loins girded" (Exodus 12:11), ready to depart in haste.
2. The word can also refer to a belt or band that encircles the body at this height. Ezekiel sees a man "with a writing kit at his side" (Ezekiel 9:11): the Hebrew word denotes the place where one carries attached objects. Warriors and workers would wear "the sword girded on their loins" (Nehemiah 4:18).
3. The loins evoke physical strength and vigor. The Psalm praises the one whose loins are strong, able to endure the trial: "She girds her loins with strength" (Proverbs 31:17) expresses determination and energy.
4. In Hebrew as in many ancient cultures, the loins symbolize generative and virile power. This is why, in genealogies, descendants are spoken of as "coming from his loins." 
5. Spiritually, the loins become the secret place where moral and emotional conscience resides. God "searches the hearts and the loins" (Jeremiah 17:10 implicit in biblical usage), for it is there that the true intentions of a person are tied up.
H4975.origine: The Hebrew word מתנים (motnayim) is linked to the idea of division or the middle of the body: it literally means "that which divides" or "the middle." The word comes from a root that expresses separation or sharing. In Hebrew thought, the loins, like the heart, are not only a physical organ but also the seat of emotions, intentions, and the vital force of man.
H4975.emploi: The word appears 45 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narrative and prophetic books. Its meaning remains stable: it first denotes the anatomical region of the lower back (Genesis 37:34, Exodus 28:42). It is often found in idiomatic expressions: "girding the loins" means preparing for action, effort, or flight (1 Kings 18:46, Ezekiel 1:27). The word is also used to situate an object attached to the body (Ezekiel 9:11, Jeremiah 13:4). In a figurative or poetic sense, the loins become the symbol of virile strength and inner power (Job 40:11, Isaiah 11:5). The prophets mention them to express intense physical or moral pain (Isaiah 21:3, Jeremiah 48:37).
H4975.portee: For the believer, the word "loins" reminds us that God knows man in his entirety, including his most secret intentions and hidden emotions. When the Bible says that God "searches the loins," it affirms that no thought escapes Him. Spiritually, "girding one's loins" becomes an invitation to be ready, both in strength and humility, for the will of God: it is a posture of availability and vigilance. This image also emphasizes that true power does not come from the flesh, but from the divine grace that strengthens us at the very core of our being.

sens: Well offered to someone to honor, entice, or gain a favor
Religious offering brought to the temple or to God
What appeases anger or wins goodwill
H4976.detail:
1. A present is a good or object given to someone to honor them or to obtain a favor. This is what Ephron proposes to Abraham in Genesis 34:12: a substantial dowry and many presents to obtain the young girl in marriage. Proverbs sees the present as a social means: it "opens the way" and grants access to the great (Proverbs 18:16).
2. In a religious context, the present refers to an offering or gift that the children of Israel bring to the temple, presented "by elevation and waving it back and forth" (Numbers 18:11). These offerings belonged to the priests and their families according to God's law.
3. The present has a virtue of reconciliation: a gift given in secret appeases anger and calms violent fury (Proverbs 21:14). It is a tool of peace that often works better than words.
H4976.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to give." Mattan expresses the idea of a voluntary gift, a transfer of property from one person to another, generally for the purpose of relationship or gratitude.
H4976.emploi: This word appears 5 times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in Proverbs (3 occurrences). It refers to both the civil or matrimonial present (Genesis 34:12), the religious offering brought by the people (Numbers 18:11), and the tool of reconciliation or social favor (Proverbs 18:16; 19:6; 21:14). Proverbs particularly emphasizes the effectiveness of the present in human relationships: it opens doors, wins the favor of the powerful, and even appeases anger.
H4976.portee: The present reminds the Christian reader that generosity is a form of practical wisdom. Proverbs shows that a well-placed gift, particularly a discreet one, can transform a situation and bring peace. But it also invites vigilance: while it can serve a just cause, it can also corrupt or entice. It reflects human nature and our connections with one another.

sens: priest of Baal in Jerusalem during the time of Athaliah
H4977G.detail: Matthan was a priest of the god Baal who served in the temple of Baal in Jerusalem. During the religious reform led by the priest Jehoiada at the time of Queen Athaliah, the people destroyed the temple of Baal, overturned its altars and idols, and killed Matthan before these altars (2 Kings 11:18; 2 Chronicles 23:17). He represents the false religion that the people of Israel had adopted and which God caused to disappear by the hand of those who remained faithful to Him.
H4977G.origine: The name Matthan comes from the Hebrew "matane" which means "gift" or "present." It is a common personal name in the Bible, expressing the idea that a child is a gift from God. Several individuals bear this name in the Scriptures.
H4977G.emploi: Matthan is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in relation to the same events: in 2 Kings 11:18 and in 2 Chronicles 23:17. These two parallel passages recount how, under the reign of the young king Joash and under the leadership of the priest Jehoiada, the people of Judah rose up against Queen Athaliah who had imposed the worship of Baal. Matthan, as a priest of Baal, opposed the worship of the true God and was killed during this religious purification. His fate illustrates God's judgment against idolatry.
H4977G.portee: The death of Matthan reminds us that God does not tolerate the mixing of His truth with false religions. His elimination marks the return of the people to true faith and the restoration of the worship of the Lord. For the believer, this event underscores the importance of a clear break with religious compromises.

sens: A man during the time of the divided monarchy
Father of Schephathiah
Official of King Zedekiah's court
H4977H.detail: Matthan is a figure from the time of the division of the kingdom of Israel and Judah. He is the father of Schephathiah, one of the officials of King Zedekiah's court. Matthan appears in Jeremiah 38:1, where his son Schephathiah is among the dignitaries who hear the words of the prophet Jeremiah addressed to the people and react against him.
H4977H.origine: The name Matthan means "a gift" or "a present" in Hebrew, derived from the root that evokes the idea of giving. This theophoric name likely reflects a parental blessing — the received child is a gift from God.
H4977H.emploi: Matthan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 38:1. He is referred to as the father of Schephathiah, one of the princes or officials of King Zedekiah who opposed Jeremiah. It is during a hearing where the prophet declares that those who surrender to the Chaldeans will survive that these dignitaries — including Matthan's son — intervene against the prophet.

sens: Material good offered to someone as a sign of gratitude, honor, or reward
Present or reward given by an authority as a favor
H4978.detail:
1. A gift is a material good that is offered to someone, out of generosity or to honor them. It is a concrete gift, a present. When the king of Babylon promises Daniel "gifts and presents, and great honors" (Daniel 2:6), it refers to tangible wealth intended to reward the one who reveals his dream.
2. It is also a reward or favor granted by one who has authority and power. In Daniel 2:48, the king "made him many and rich gifts" after recognizing in Daniel a wise man sent by God. Daniel later refuses in Daniel 5:17: "Keep your gifts," as he does not want his faithfulness to God to be motivated by material interest.
H4978.origine: This is the Aramaic used in the book of Daniel. It comes from the same root as the Hebrew מַתָּנָה (matana), which also means "gift" or "present." These two words, in Hebrew as well as in Aramaic, express the idea of something given, offered hand to hand.
H4978.emploi: The word appears three times in the Aramaic Vulgate of the book of Daniel, always at the heart of court scenes where royal power distributes rewards or honors. In Daniel 2:6 and 2:48, the gifts are a mark of royal favor. In Daniel 5:17, Daniel rejects the king's gifts, asserting that his wisdom comes from God, not from a desire to enrich himself. The word thus encompasses both the material gift and the act of generosity or favor that accompanies it.
H4978.portee: This word reminds readers that true wisdom and faithfulness to God cannot be bought with gifts or honors. Daniel's example shows that a believer can refuse the world's presents to remain true to his conscience and his God. It is an invitation to examine our own motivations: do we serve out of interest or conviction?

sens: What is given to someone without expecting anything in return, to please them
An offering presented to God, in sacrifice or devotion
A present in money or valuable items
A right or privilege generously granted
What corrupts the heart or diverts from justice when accepted inappropriately
H4979.detail:
1. The gift is the act of giving something to someone without expecting anything in return: it is a gesture of generosity or affection. Genesis 25:6 shows Abraham giving "gifts" to the sons of his concubines before his death, to provide for their future.
2. To God, the gift becomes an offering, a way to express devotion and faith through sacrifices or precious gifts. Numbers 18:7 states that the priesthood itself is a "gift" that the Lord grants to the priests; Leviticus 23:38 speaks of "gifts to the Lord" given voluntarily in addition to prescribed offerings.
3. The gift can be a material present: money, gold, or valuable items, like the considerable "gifts" that the king gives to his sons in 2 Chronicles 21:3.
4. The gift can also be an advantage or privilege granted to someone, like the men "taken as a gift" in Psalm 68:19, meaning granted to God as His portion.
5. Finally, the gift corrupts when offered or accepted to distort justice: Ecclesiastes 7:7 warns that "gifts" corrupt the heart of the wise and divert them from good.
H4979.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to give." It is the same concept that appears in late Aramaic, a language closely related to Hebrew spoken in Babylon, where the word has the same form and meaning: "gift." The family of this word would encompass several verbs and nouns related to the act of giving and receiving.
H4979.emploi: The word "gift" appears 17 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in legal texts (Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy), in historical narratives (Genesis, Chronicles, Esther), and in biblical wisdom (Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes). It is used for royal or personal gifts (Genesis 25:6, 2 Chronicles 21:3), for offerings to God (Leviticus 23:38, Numbers 18:7), and figuratively for a right granted by God Himself (Psalm 68:19). Ezekiel uses it several times to stigmatize gifts offered to idols (20:26, 20:31, 20:39) and to designate lands granted by the prince (46:16, 46:17). The context affects the moral judgment: the gift is commendable when it is generous and just, reprehensible when it corrupts (Ecclesiastes 7:7, Proverbs 15:27).
H4979.portee: The word "gift" reminds the Christian reader that all generosity must come from the heart and glorify God, not corrupt justice. It is also a word that emphasizes divine grace: our privileges and abilities in the service of God are not earned, but given. Finally, in the face of the temptation of moral corruption, the Bible warns us that "gifts" accepted inappropriately shape our spiritual destiny.

sens: Station of the Israelites during their wandering in the desert
Location east of the Jordan, probably southeast of the Dead Sea
H4980.detail:
1. Mattana is a station where the Israelites stopped during their forty years of wandering in the desert, before entering the Promised Land. It appears in the list of stages of the journey (Numbers 21:18-19), as a place of rest and resupply along the long way.

2. This city was located east of the Jordan, probably in the southeastern region of the Dead Sea, in a mountainous and semi-arid territory. It was an important stop on the Israelites' journey before their arrival in Canaan.
H4980.origine: The name literally means "gift of God" in Hebrew (matana = gift, present). The name reflects the belief that this stop, like every stage of the journey, was a gift of divine providence to the Israelites on the move.
H4980.emploi: Mattana appears only twice in the Bible, both in Numbers 21:18-19, in the description of the stations traveled by the Israelites after the battle against the king of Canaan. It is a simple stop listed in the narrative of the desert journey, with no particular event reported.

sens: man of the people of Mithn, or descendant of a lineage called Mithni
H4981.detail: The term refers to Josaphat, one of the elite warriors who served David. He is identified as "of Mithni" (1 Chronicles 11:43), which likely indicates his origin or belonging to a group or family bearing this name. The exact origin of the term remains unknown.
H4981.origine: The name "Mithni" may derive from an ancient Hebrew root designating a people or family, but its exact etymology is not established. It appears only once in Scripture, making the analysis of its origin difficult.
H4981.emploi: Mithni appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:43, where it designates the origin or clan of Josaphat, one of David's thirty mighty warriors. This passage lists the most renowned military leaders of King David. Josaphat is mentioned alongside other warriors like Hanan, son of Maacah, in a list honoring the most faithful and courageous fighters of the kingdom.

sens: Israelite of the time of the return from exile
H4982G.detail: Matthnaï is an Israelite man mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when the exiles return from Babylon. He is among those who, like many others at that time, had married foreign women and had to repudiate his wife to conform to the law of Israel (Ezra 10:33).
H4982G.origine: The name Matthnaï means "gift of Jehovah" in Hebrew (mattân = gift, gift of God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the divine name, expressing gratitude to God or the sacred nature of the child. Several men bore this name at different periods in Israel's history.
H4982G.emploi: Matthnaï appears only once in the scriptures, in Ezra 10:33, in the list of Israelites who repudiated their foreign wives under Ezra's leadership. This passage occurs during the return from Babylonian exile, a crucial period when Israel must purify and spiritually renew itself. Three different men named Matthnaï are mentioned in the Old Testament: one was a priest during the time of Jehoiakim, but here it refers to a layman from the house of Hashum who participated in this reform.

sens: Man of the time of exile and return
One who repudiated his foreign wife
H4982H.detail:
1. Matthnaï is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Judea. His Hebrew name means "gift of God." He is part of the list of those who had married foreign women and who, at the time of Ezra, repudiated them to conform to the law of Israel (Ezra 10:37).

2. His act of renouncing his foreign wife symbolizes the effort of the people returned from captivity to purify themselves and remain faithful to God's covenant. Although little known, this Matthnaï represents one of the many Israelites who had to make a difficult choice between their personal life and obedience to the Torah.
H4982H.origine: The name Matthnaï comes from Hebrew and literally means "gift of Yahweh" or "gift of the Lord": it combines two Hebrew elements that express the idea of a gift granted by God. This type of theophoric name (containing the name of God) was common in Israel and reflected the piety of parents who gave this name to their child, recognizing that life itself was a divine gift.
H4982H.emploi: Matthnaï appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:37. He is mentioned in the context of the religious reform led by the scribe Ezra upon the return from exile. After returning from Babylon, the people had married foreign women, which posed a major religious problem. Ezra convenes an assembly and ensures that all men, including Matthnaï, send away their foreign wives. Matthnaï is one of those ordinary men whose name has been recorded, probably because an official register was drawn up of all those who obeyed this directive.
H4982H.portee: The story of Matthnaï teaches us the cost of obedience to God, even in the most difficult circumstances. His choice to separate from his foreign wife, though painful, illustrates the necessity of remaining separate from the world to maintain communion with God. For today's believer, this account reminds us that faithfulness to God sometimes requires personal sacrifices, and that true piety may demand accepting difficult separations.

sens: priest during the time of Jehoiakim
Israelite during the time of Ezra who repudiated his foreign wife
H4982I.detail: 1. Matthnaï is a priest mentioned in Nehemiah 12:19, son of Jojarib. He is one of the heads of priestly families during the time of Jehoiakim, at the time of the return from exile (Nehemiah 12:19). 2. The name Matthnaï also refers to Israelites during the time of Ezra who had married foreign women and repudiated them (Ezra 10). These individuals share the same name but are not the same person: the Bible lists them separately among those who obeyed Ezra's call to separate from their non-Israelite wives.
H4982I.origine: Matthnaï comes from the Hebrew מַתְּנַי (mattanay), composed of mattan (‘gift’) and the divine suffix yah (abbreviation of Yahweh). The name literally means ‘gift of Yahweh’ or ‘gift of the Lord’. It is a common theophoric name among the Hebrews, expressing gratitude to God for the birth of the child.
H4982I.emploi: Matthnaï appears only once in the Bible in Nehemiah 12:19, where he is mentioned as a priest, son of Jojarib, during the reconstruction of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. Although the Bible also mentions Israelites bearing the same name during the time of Ezra (Ezra 10) who repudiated their foreign wives, the unique reference in Nehemiah 12:19 pertains to the priest. It is a name among the descendants of the priestly families who returned from exile.

sens: Levite responsible for music and singing in the temple of Jerusalem after the exile
Name meaning ‘gift of the Lord’
H4983G.detail: 1. Matthania is a Levite from the time of the exile and return, primarily known as the leader of the praise singing in the temple. His Hebrew name literally means ‘gift of the Lord’ — a beautiful affirmation of trust in God. Several Matthania appear in the lists of Levites from this period, but the one who stands out is the one mentioned in Nehemiah 11:17, son of Micah, who leads the praise in prayer and directs his brothers in the singing of praises (Nehemiah 12:8). He was a Levite from the family of Asaph, a famous lineage of temple musicians established by David to serve in worship.
H4983G.origine: The Hebrew name מַתַּנְיָהוּ (Mattaniah) is composed of two elements: מַתָּנָה (matana, ‘gift’ or ‘present’) and יָהּ (yah, a short form of the divine name YHWH, ‘the Eternal’). It is a theophoric name — a name that contains the name of God — which was common among the Levites and expressed the dedication of the child to the Lord. The word ‘gift’ evokes divine grace.
H4983G.emploi: Matthania appears four times in Scripture, all in texts related to the time of the return from exile (1 Chronicles 9:15; Nehemiah 11:17; 12:8 and 12:25). There are likely several Levites bearing this same name, occupying different roles: some are gatekeepers at the temple gates (Nehemiah 12:25), while others are musicians and singers. The context of 1 Chronicles and Nehemiah shows that Matthania is among those who reorganize worship and singing in the restored temple after the return from Babylon. His role in ‘the singing of praises’ emphasizes that Israel's worship, still wounded by exile, was being rebuilt around singing and prayer.
H4983G.portee: Matthania reminds us that the Lord uses names to express His promise and plan. His name — ‘gift of the Lord’ — suggests that every life, every person, is a gift from God. For Christians who sing praises, Matthania embodies the humble yet noble service of one who helps God’s people worship, a work that the Lord honors.

sens: Son of Heman, Levite of the tribe of Levi, musician of the temple during the divided monarchy
H4983H.detail: Matthania is a Levite from the tribe of Levi, son of the famous musician Heman. He lived during the time of the divided monarchy in Israel and was one of the many musician brothers from Heman's family. According to 1 Chronicles 25:4, he is among the sons of Heman designated for musical service in the temple, in the system organized by King David. The text indicates in 1 Chronicles 25:16 that he led a musical group in the temple composed of himself, his sons, and his brothers, totaling twelve people assigned to the ninth rotation of service.
H4983H.origine: The name Matthania means ‘gift of Jehovah’ in Hebrew. It is composed of two elements: ‘mattan’ (gift) and ‘Yah’ (abbreviation of Jehovah). This name expresses gratitude to God and reflects the piety of the Levite parents who bore it.
H4983H.emploi: Matthania was a Levite musician assigned to the service of the temple during the reign of King David. He was part of the large musical family of Heman, which included many musician brothers. His role was to participate in the celebrations and services of the temple according to a rotation system. Matthania led the ninth group of musicians, composed of twelve members including his sons and brothers.
H4983H.portee: This character illustrates the importance that the Bible places on music and worship in the temple. Matthania and his family belonged to a class dedicated to the service of God, reminding the Christian reader that all forms of ministry — including the arts and music — constitute a sacred service when ordered for the glory of God.

sens: Levite from the family of Asaph, ancestor of Jahaziel
H4983I.detail: Mattania is a Levite belonging to the musical lineage of Asaph. He is mentioned as the ancestor of Jahaziel, a prophet who intervened during the time of King Jehoshaphat (2 Chronicles 20:14). His name means ‘gift of Jehovah’. Although little information is given about him personally, he fits into the history of the tribe of Levi charged with the service of the temple.
H4983I.origine: The name Mattania is composed of two Hebrew elements: ‘mattana’ (mattan), which means ‘gift’ or ‘present’, and ‘Yah’, abbreviation of the divine name Jehovah. Together, the name literally means ‘gift of Jehovah’. This type of theophoric composition is common in the Old Testament to honor God.
H4983I.emploi: Mattania is cited only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 20:14, as the father of Jeiel and ancestor of Jahaziel. He belongs to the musical family of Asaph, a dynasty of Levites responsible for music and prophecy in the temple of Jerusalem. His insertion in this genealogy indicates his role in the transmission of the prophetic and liturgical charge within the temple.
H4983I.portee: This name reminds us that God used family lineages to accomplish His works. Mattania, though obscure in biblical history, produced a prophetic lineage: his great-grandson Jahaziel became God's spokesperson at a critical moment of invasion threat. This shows that faithfulness in ordinary temple service was the foundation for extraordinary prophetic capability.

sens: Descendant of Asaph, Levite of the temple during the reign of King Hezekiah
H4983J.detail: Matthania is a Levite from the family of Asaph mentioned during the purification of the temple under the reign of King Hezekiah (2 Chronicles 29:13). He is among the Levites who received the king's order to sanctify themselves and clean the temple of the Lord, thus participating in a major religious reform in the history of Judah.
H4983J.origine: The name Matthania means ‘gift of Jehovah’ in Hebrew: it is formed from ‘mattan’ (gift) and ‘Yah’ (Jehovah). This name expresses the belief that children are a gift from God, which was common among the Hebrews. Several people bore this name in the Old Testament, including the last king of Judah before the exile (also called Zedekiah).
H4983J.emploi: Matthania appears only once in the Segond, in 2 Chronicles 29:13. This passage lists the Levites who participated in the purification of the temple under Hezekiah, around 715 BC. Belonging to the family of Asaph (whose descendants formed an important lineage of temple musicians), Matthania illustrates the role of the Levites in the reformed worship of Judah.

sens: Man from the tribe of Elam who married a foreign woman during the time of Ezra
H4983K.detail: Matthania is one of the men from the family of Elam who, after the return from exile, had married a non-Israelite woman. During the religious reform led by Ezra, he had to repudiate this wife to restore the purity of God's people according to the Law (Ezra 10:26). His name appears in the list of those who obeyed this difficult order.
H4983K.origine: The name Matthania means "gift of the Lord" in Hebrew: it combines "mattan" (gift) and "yah" (Lord). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in God's generosity. Several biblical figures bore this name at different times in Israel's history.
H4983K.emploi: Matthania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:26, in the context of the return from exile and the religious reform. He is among the descendants of Elam who had married foreign women and who agreed to repudiate them at Ezra's command, in order to preserve the identity and holiness of God's people after the Babylonian captivity.

sens: Man from the family of Zattu who repudiated his foreign wife during the time of Ezra
H4983L.detail: 1. Matthania is a man from the Jewish community that returned from captivity, belonging to the family of Zattu. He appears in the list of men who, under Ezra's leadership, repudiated their foreign wives in order to comply with the Law and purify the people (Ezra 10:27).
H4983L.origine: The name Matthania means "gift of Yahweh" in Hebrew: Matt (gift) and Yah (Yahweh). It is a common theophoric name among the Levites and leaders of Israel, expressing the belief that the child is a gift from God. Several other biblical figures bear this name, including the last king of Judah, Zedekiah, who was originally named Matthania before his name was changed by Nebuchadnezzar.
H4983L.emploi: This Matthania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:27, in the context of the religious reform led by Ezra after the return from exile. He is among the men who agreed to send away their foreign wives, an act aimed at protecting the religious and ethnic identity of God's people. This man remains otherwise unknown: the Bible provides no further details about his life or role in the community.
H4983L.portee: This passage reminds us of the importance of faithfulness to God's covenant and the choice of ritual and spiritual purity for the people. Although Matthania himself is just an anonymous figure in biblical history, his inclusion in this list shows that even difficult acts of repentance — such as repudiation — were undertaken to obey God and restore the integrity of the community of Israel.

sens: Man who repudiated his foreign wife during the time of Ezra
H4983M.detail: Matthania is one of the men from Judah who, upon returning from the Babylonian exile, had married a woman from a foreign nation. During the religious reform led by Ezra, he had to repudiate this woman to comply with the Lord's law and the covenant with the chosen people (Ezra 10:30).
H4983M.origine: The name Matthania means "gift of Jehovah" (from Hebrew "gift" and "Jah", the name of God). It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, common in Israel to express gratitude to the Lord for a child received.
H4983M.emploi: Matthania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the book of Ezra 10:30, among the descendants of Pahath-Moab who repudiated their foreign wives. He is not the only one in the group called this way: several other Matthania are named in the Old Testament (priests and Levites), notably Matthania who became King Zedekiah, but this one is distinct from our man. The context of Ezra 10 shows that the repudiation of these women was an act of repentance and a return to faithfulness to God after the exile.
H4983M.portee: The story of Matthania reminds us that the holiness of God's people requires difficult decisions and concrete breaks with what distances them from God. It is a humble example of repentance and submission to divine will, even at the cost of personal sacrifices.

sens: Biblical character borne by several men during the Exile and the Return
The most well-known: former name of the last king of Judah before captivity, who became Zedekiah
Several Levites of this name, notably from the family of Asaph, musicians in the service of the temple
Ordinary men who repudiated a foreign wife during the time of Ezra
H4983N.detail: 1. Matthania literally means "gift of God" in Hebrew: it was a name borne by several people during the Exile and the Return of Judah. 2. The most famous is the last king of Judah before the Babylonian captivity (2 Kings 24:17): his real name was Matthania, but Nebuchadnezzar imposed the name Zedekiah on him. 3. Several Levites bore this name and served the temple as musicians or singers, notably descendants of Asaph who participated in worship during the reigns of Hezekiah and Jehoshaphat. 4. Other men of the same name are found in Ezra 10:37 among those who repudiated a foreign wife upon returning from the Exile, illustrating the reform of the community that returned to Jerusalem.
H4983N.origine: The Hebrew name מַתַּנְיָ֫הוּ (mattanyahû) consists of two elements: מַתַּן (mattan, "gift") and יָהוּ (yahu, abbreviated form of the divine name). It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God or faith in His gifts. The same root is found in other biblical names like Nathaniel ("God has given").
H4983N.emploi: Matthania is a name borne by at least twelve different characters in the Old Testament. The most important is the last king of Judah (2 Kings 24:17), son of Josiah, whom Nebuchadnezzar renamed Zedekiah during the siege of Jerusalem. Several bearers of the name were Levites: musicians, temple singers, or assistants in worship under David, Hezekiah, and Jehoshaphat. Others appear in Ezra 10:37 as ordinary men who accepted the religious reform that required repudiating foreign wives. This multiplicity of bearers of the name shows its popularity in Israel and its connection to faith in the giving God.

sens: Levitical chief of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
Ancestor in the genealogy of the temple singers
H4983O.detail:
1. Matthania is a Levite from the family of Asaph, mentioned as chief of the Levites in Jerusalem under Nehemiah. He is the father of Micah and the grandfather of Zaccur, forming a lineage of temple servants (Nehemiah 11:22).
2. His name also appears in a genealogy of the priests who played the trumpet during solemn events, confirming his role as a leader in temple worship at the time of the return from exile (Nehemiah 12:35).
H4983O.origine: The name Matthania means "gift of Jehovah" in Hebrew (mattanah = gift, ya(h) = God). It is a common theophoric name in the Bible, expressing gratitude to God for a child received as a blessing. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, particularly among the Levites and priestly families, reflecting the importance of this lineage in the service of the temple.
H4983O.emploi: Matthania appears twice in the text of Nehemiah, at the return from the Babylonian exile (around 445 B.C.). In both passages, he is presented as a Levite from the family of Asaph, the musical branch of the temple clergy. His name appears in the genealogies of worship leaders, indicating that he held a prestigious position among the Levites responsible for music and religious services in the rebuilt temple. No specific event is narrated about him; his mention in these genealogical lists simply underscores his institutional importance for the restoration of worship after the exile.

sens: A Levite during the time of Nehemiah, father of Zaccur
H4983P.detail: Mattania is a Levite mentioned in the Book of Nehemiah as the father of Zaccur. Zaccur himself is the father of Hanan, who was appointed as the treasurer of the temple to oversee distributions to other Levites. This Mattania belonged to a lineage of temple servants known for their faithfulness in fulfilling their duties.
H4983P.origine: The name Mattania means "gift of the Lord" (from the Hebrew "matân" = gift, and "Yah" = the Lord). It was a name borne by several Levites at different periods in Israel's history, notably during the Exile and the return, highlighting the importance of priestly functions in the restored community.
H4983P.emploi: Mattania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 13:13, where he is identified as the ancestor of Hanan. This man was part of the administrative structure of the temple during Nehemiah's time, likely in the fifth century B.C. His mention indicates that his family was known for its loyalty and integrity in the service of the temple and the restored Jewish community.

sens: The original name of the last king of Judah before the Babylonian captivity
A Levite, son of Heman, responsible for sounding the trumpets in the temple
A Levite from the family of Asaph
A Levite who participated in the purification or restoration of the temple
H4983Q.detail: 1. Matthania is the name given initially to the last king of Judah before Babylon destroyed the kingdom and took its inhabitants into exile. In 2 Kings 24:17, the king of Babylon appoints him king in place of Jehoiachin, his nephew, but immediately changes his name to Zedekiah ("The Lord is righteousness"), a name that better suited God's plans for the monarch. 2. Several Levites bear this name in the Old Testament: one of them is the son of Heman and fulfills the role of sounding the trumpets in the temple, a liturgical role established by King David himself. 3. Other Levites named Matthania belong to the family of Asaph, a large family of musicians and singers of the temple. 4. Some of these Levites actively participate in significant moments in Israel's history: the restoration of the temple under Hezekiah, the dedication of the wall of Jerusalem, or reforms under Ezra and Nehemiah.
H4983Q.origine: The name Matthania means "gift of the Lord" or "gift of God" in Hebrew: it comes from the word "mattanah" (gift) and the divine name Yah (God). It is a name from the time of the divided kingdom and the exile, borne by several Levites or servants of worship, as well as by the last king of Judah. The change of his name to Zedekiah shows how foreign powers imposed new names on Israel, marking the end of the people's independence.
H4983Q.emploi: Matthania primarily refers to the last king of Judah before the Babylonian captivity. In 2 Kings 24:17, after Nebuchadnezzar deports King Jehoiachin, he places Matthania, Jehoiachin's uncle, on the throne, but the Babylonian king immediately changes his name to Zedekiah to signify his authority. The name Matthania reappears in several passages as a designation for other figures, notably Levites who play a role in the temple worship (musicians, singers, those responsible for purification or restoration of the temple), or men who, during Ezra's time, had to send away their foreign wives. These various bearers of the name demonstrate the importance of the Levites in Israel's religious life.
H4983Q.portee: The fate of Matthania, whose name is changed upon his inauguration, reminds the reader that the kings of Judah, despite their dignity, remain under the sovereign hand of God. The name change symbolizes the loss of independence of the chosen people and the approach of exile. For the Levites bearing this name, their commitment to restoring temple worship and to religious reforms shows how, even in times of crisis, the servants of the Lord seek to reconnect with faithfulness to His Law.

sens: To become sweet or have a pleasant taste
To have a pleasant, attractive, alluring quality
To evoke tenderness or intimacy
H4985.detail:
1. To become sweet or have a pleasant taste: this is the most concrete and literal meaning. The bitter water of Marah becomes sweet (Exodus 15:25) when Moses throws in the wood that God indicates. It is a physical transformation: what was bitter becomes flavorful.
2. To have a pleasant, attractive, alluring quality: the word expands beyond taste. Evil can be sweet to the mouth of the wicked (Job 20:12), meaning seductive and pleasing, even if it is perverse. Likewise, stolen waters are sweet (Proverbs 9:17), meaning attractive and tempting.
3. To evoke tenderness or intimacy: sweetness can also qualify an affectionate relationship. Living together in sweet intimacy (Psalms 55:15) expresses the warmth of communion. The mother's breast (Job 24:20) refers to the security and natural tenderness of a mother.
H4985.origine: The verb מָתֹק (mataq) comes from a root that evokes the idea of sweet or pleasant to the taste. It is related to other Hebrew words expressing sweetness, and it describes both a real flavor and, by extension, a moral or emotional quality that pleases and attracts. The noun מִתְקָה (mitqa, honey) and מְתָקָה (metaqah, sweetness) belong to the same family.
H4985.emploi: This verb appears 6 times in the Hebrew Bible. Exodus 15:25 uses it in the literal sense: the water becomes sweet after Moses throws wood into it. Job uses the word twice in moral contexts: evil is sweet to the mouth of the wicked (Job 20:12), and the mother's breast represents tenderness (Job 24:20). Psalms and Proverbs apply it to situations where the pleasant or seductive plays a role: the sweet intimacy in the house of God (Psalms 55:15), the stolen waters that seduce by their forbidden allure (Proverbs 9:17). The word thus glides from tangible taste to moral appeal and affection.
H4985.portee: This word teaches that sweetness, whether physical or moral, has a great power of attraction over us. It can be a good — like brotherly communion — or a temptation — like sin that seduces by its allure. It invites the reader to discern what is truly good from what is merely pleasing in appearance, and to seek true sweetness, that which comes from God.

sens: Quality of what is sweet, sweet flavor
Character of being sweet, pleasant to taste or touch
Amiability, kindness in words or feelings
Charm that naturally attracts and pleases
H4986.detail:
1. The concrete meaning of the word is primarily the sweet flavor, what pleases the palate — the image of honey or ripe fruit. But the Bible rarely uses it in the literal sense.

2. The word takes on a personal and moral significance: the sweetness of lips (Proverbs 16:21) refers to pleasant speech, that which is pleasing to hear and persuades without harshness. One who speaks with sweetness is described as wise.

3. In Proverbs 27:9, the affectionate counsel of a friend is described as sweet — here sweetness is no longer the sweet taste, but the quality of what comforts, what does good to the heart like oil or perfume.
H4986.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes honey and the sweetness of taste. It belongs to the family of words that speak of what delights the senses and the soul. In the background is the image of sweet food as something desirable and naturally pleasant.
H4986.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, both in the Book of Proverbs. In these two passages, it describes a moral and emotional quality: the sweetness of speech (Proverbs 16:21) which increases knowledge by persuading without causing offense, and the sweetness of friendship (Proverbs 27:9) which comforts like perfume and oil. It is a word from the wisdom register, praising what pleases, attracts, and builds up.
H4986.portee: Sweetness, in biblical teaching, is not a weakness but a strength: that which truly persuades, heals relationships, and conveys truth without crushing. A Christian who cultivates sweetness of speech and heart imitates Jesus Himself, who spoke with grace and pleaded for the hearts of men without violence.

sens: Quality of what is sweet, pleasant to the taste
Pleasant and benevolent character
Charm, grace in words or actions
H4987.detail:
1. Sweetness primarily denotes the sweet character of something, its pleasant taste. It is the natural nectar of the fruit, which makes it delightful.
