In the parable of the trees in Judges 9:11, the fig tree boasts of its sweetness as its main quality — the sweet honey of its fruit, far more precious than vain agitation.
2. However, the word also extends to what is sweet in heart and speech: kindness, amiability, everything that makes a person or action pleasant. It is a moral sweetness, a grace.
3. Finally, it can denote general charm — the allure and seduction of something — that which pleases and attracts. The fruit of the fig tree gains not only from its sweet taste but also from its overall excellence.
H4987.origine: The Hebrew word מֹ֫תֶק comes from a root that fundamentally evokes sweet taste and pleasantness. In biblical Hebrew, the sweetness of honey and that of sweet fruit are strong images of what delights the senses and the soul. This same root generates related words that retain this idea of pleasure and attraction.
H4987.emploi: This word is rare in the Hebrew Bible: it appears only once, in Judges 9:11, in the fable where the fig tree refuses to leave its post to reign. The fig tree defends its place by emphasizing that it cannot abandon its sweetness — the nectar of its fruit — which makes it useful and precious. Here, sweetness embodies true value, that of one who serves humbly and joyfully rather than aspiring to vain honors.
H4987.portee: This word reminds the reader that true wealth often lies in what brings sweetness to life: kindness, faithfulness to one's vocation, the pleasure one brings to others. The humble and useful fig tree is more honorable than the trees that seek power. For the Christian, it is an invitation to seek the sweetness of heart and faithful service rather than splendor and prestige.

sens: Desert station where the Israelites camped during their exodus from Egypt
H4989.detail: 1. Mithka is the name of a stop along the long journey that the Israelites undertook through the desert after their departure from Egypt. This name appears in the list of resting and camping stations of the people (Numbers 33:28-29), where it is located between Tarach and Hashmonah.
H4989.origine: The name Mithka comes from a Hebrew root meaning "sweetness" or "pleasantness." It evokes an oasis or a place of rest, perhaps characterized by sweet or pleasant water, which would have relieved the desert travelers. The name reflects the importance of finding sustenance and refreshment during the forty years of wandering in the desert.
H4989.emploi: Mithka appears only twice in the Bible, both in chapter 33 of Numbers, which systematically enumerates the forty-two stages of the Israelite journey from Egypt to the plains of Moab. This list shows that, despite difficulties and temptations, God guided and provided for all the needs of His people, station by station. Mithka occupies a modest but real place in this long journey of faith.
H4989.portee: The reminder of the desert stations, including Mithka, invites the reader to meditate on God's faithfulness during long trials. Each station represents a moment when God provided and protected. For a believer, this teaches that the difficult stages of life are never forgotten by God, and that each rest — each "Mithka" — is a gift from His hand.

sens: Treasurer of King Cyrus of Persia
H4990G.detail: Mithredath is the name of a Persian officer, treasurer at the court of King Cyrus. He appears in the account of the return of the Jews from exile: it is he who, at the king's command, hands over the objects of the temple of Jerusalem to the prince Sheshbazzar so that he may bring them back to Judah (Ezra 1:8). His role is that of a trusted intermediary, responsible for royal treasures and precious goods intended for the reconstruction of the temple.
H4990G.origine: The name Mithredath is Persian, formed from two elements: "Mithra" (the god of the sun and justice in ancient Persian religion) and a term meaning "given" — literally "given by Mithra." It is an example of theophoric Persian names, where the name of a deity indicates divine protection over the person.
H4990G.emploi: Mithredath appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 1:8, at the time of Cyrus's decree allowing the exiled Jews to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the temple. He is identified as the treasurer (the one who manages the king's finances and goods) and acts under the direct authority of King Cyrus, executing his order to restore the sacred objects of the temple. He is a minor historical figure but symbolizes how God used even pagan authorities to accomplish His restoration project.
H4990G.portee: Mithredath subtly embodies how God governs history through human authorities, even foreign ones. His existence in this account shows that the return from exile was not only a miraculous act but also the result of a decree from a Persian king and the obedience of his servants. It is a lesson on divine providence that acts through the structures of the world.

sens: Persian officer during the time of Artaxerxes
Man in charge of administrative missions in Samaria
H4990H.detail:
1. Mithredath is a Persian officer mentioned only once in the Bible, during the reign of King Artaxerxes. He appears as one of the correspondents who collectively write to the king to contest the plans of the Jews returned from exile (Ezra 4:7). It is a name that designates an official personality of the Persian administration in the land of Samaria.
2. The name suggests someone holding an important position in the local administration, probably in charge of communications with the central Persian power. He acts in coordination with other officers, indicating his role in the administrative and political affairs of the region.
H4990H.origine: The name Mithredath is of Persian origin and means "given by Mithra." Mithra is a god of Zoroastrian religion, deity of contracts and light. Persian names of this type, composed of the name of a deity followed by a verb, were common among the Persians: they expressed the religious devotion of the parents. This name reflects the Persian religious environment in which these officers lived.
H4990H.emploi: Mithredath appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 4:7, among the Persian officials stationed in Samaria during the time of Artaxerxes I. He is listed alongside other Persian names (Bishlam, Tabeel) as a signatory of a letter addressed to the king of Persia. This letter reports the grievances of the enemies of the Jews against the reconstruction of the temple in Jerusalem. His role in this passage shows that local Persian authorities acted as intermediaries between the local populations and the central power.

sens: Present offered to someone, gift
Reward given for a service or merit
Grace or benefit received from God
Thing one boasts about or takes pride in
H4991.detail:
1. A gift is a present voluntarily offered to someone to please or honor them. In 1 Kings 13:7, the king offers the man of God to come eat at his house and promises him a gift in reward for his visit.
2. A gift can also be a reward given to someone who has accomplished something, a retribution or an honorable salary for a service rendered.
3. It is also, especially in the poetic books, a benefit or grace that God grants: the ability to eat, drink, and enjoy the fruit of one’s labor is a gift from God (Ecclesiastes 3:13; 5:18), meaning a blessing that comes from His generous hand.
4. A gift can also refer to what one boasts about or takes pride in, sometimes inappropriately: Proverbs 25:14 speaks of a man who "boasts falsely" of his gifts, meaning his acts of generosity.
H4991.origine: The word comes from the Hebrew root נתן (natan), which means "to give." Mattan is the nominal form of this verb: it is the act of giving turned into an object, the thing given. The same root is found in other Hebrew words for "gift" and in proper names containing "mattan" (like Mattan, son of Terach). The word emphasizes the idea of transferring something from one hand to another, always with the sense of generosity or kindness.
H4991.emploi: The word mattanah (of which mattan is a variant) appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the wisdom books (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes) and in historical (1 Kings) and prophetic (Ezekiel) narratives. In the wisdom books, the word emphasizes the notion of divine gift: it is a benefit that God gives to men, the pleasure of enjoying the fruit of their labor. In 1 Kings, it refers to a material gift offered by the king to a guest. In Proverbs, it takes on an ironic nuance: boasting about one’s gifts is to boast falsely, it is a form of hollow bragging. The context of the usages always shows a notion of generosity, either divine or human.
H4991.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader see how the Bible distinguishes between giving and boasting about giving. It also invites us to recognize that the goods we possess and enjoy are not merely the fruit of our own efforts, but gifts from God. It is an invitation to gratitude rather than pride: everything we have received comes from His hand.

sens: man of Israel during the Exile and Return
H4992.detail: Matthattha is an Israelite man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile to Babylon. He belongs to the family of Hashum and is among those who had to put away their foreign wives, in accordance with the orders of Ezra who sought to preserve the religious purity of the people after the return from Exile (Ezra 10:33).
H4992.origine: The name Matthattha means "gift of Jehovah" in Hebrew: it combines the word "mattat" (gift) and the abbreviated divine name "Yah." It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing gratitude to God for the gift of life or a blessing.
H4992.emploi: Matthattha appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:33. He is one of the many Israelite men who, after the return from captivity, agreed to send away the foreign wives they had married, to obey the commandments of the Law and restore separation from the idolatrous peoples.

sens: Levite during the Exile and Return
guardian of the baked offerings
H4993G.detail: Matthithia is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe of Levi dedicated to temple service. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:31, where he appears as "firstborn of Shallum the Korahite" and as the one who "was in charge of the baked goods on the griddle" — in other words, he was responsible for preparing the bread offerings for temple worship. His name means "gift of the Lord," which emphasizes that his life and role in temple service are seen as a gift from God to His people.
H4993G.origine: The name Matthithia literally means "gift of the Lord" (מַתָּנָה / matanah = gift; יָהּ / yah = Lord). It is a typical theophoric name from ancient Israel, expressing gratitude to God and the recognition that everything that exists — including each person — comes from His kindness. Similar names, like Jonathan ("the Lord has given") or Nathanael ("God has given"), share this same structure and piety.
H4993G.emploi: Matthithia appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 9:31, a passage that lists the functions of the Levites and priests upon the return from Exile. He is identified as the son of Shallum the Korahite (that is, a descendant of Korah, an important Levitical family) and as the one responsible for the baked goods on the griddle, a specific liturgical task related to the preparation of offerings. This brief but specific mention indicates that he held an important role in the organization of worship at the rebuilt temple.
H4993G.portee: The life of Matthithia reminds the reader that worship of God, in the Old Testament as today, requires dedication and organization — that everyone, in their particular task, contributes to the common worship. His name, "gift of the Lord," also invites us to see our own existence and responsibilities as a gift from God and an opportunity to serve Him.

sens: Levite musician in temple service during the time of King David
Son of the Levite Jeduthun
Leader of one of the classes of musicians in worship
H4993H.detail:
1. Matthithia is a Levite who served as a musician during the transport of the Ark of the Covenant in the time of King David (1 Chronicles 15:18). With his fellow Levites, he played the harp and participated in the sung worship before the Lord.
2. Matthithia is the son of the Levite Jeduthun, who was one of the great musicians and prophets of the temple (1 Chronicles 25:3). He thus belongs to an important family of worship musicians.
3. Matthithia led a class of twelve Levite musicians, among the twenty-four classes organized by King David for temple service (1 Chronicles 25:21). He was responsible for training and leading these singers.
H4993H.origine: The name Matthithia means "gift of the Lord" in Hebrew. It is a compound name: "Matthitta" (gift) and "Yah" (Lord). This name expresses the gratitude of the parents to God for the gift of this child. This type of theophoric name, containing the name of God, was common among the Hebrews to express their faith and gratitude.
H4993H.emploi: Matthithia appears five times in Chronicles, always in the context of temple worship. He is first mentioned in 1 Chronicles 15 as a Levite musician during the ceremony when the Ark was transported to Jerusalem. He played the harp (15:21). In 1 Chronicles 16:5, he is listed among the leaders of the musicians tasked with praising the Lord with instruments. In 1 Chronicles 25:3, we learn that he is the son of Jeduthun and that he prophesied with the harp. Finally, in 1 Chronicles 25:21, he leads the fourteenth class of temple musicians.
H4993H.portee: Matthithia illustrates the importance that the Bible places on sung worship and music in the service of God. He also shows how musical and spiritual talents are passed down within pious families, and how everyone has a role to play, even a humble one, in communal worship. His example encourages believers to see their service, whatever it may be, as a gift received from God.

sens: A man from the tribe of Levi during the time of exile and return to Jerusalem
H4993I.detail: Matthithia is a proper name referring to a man from the tribe of Levi mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of men who had married foreign women and had to repudiate them after the return from exile (Ezra 10:43). Although the name means "gift of the Lord," we have no details about this man's life or personal significance: only his existence and marital situation are recorded.
H4993I.origine: The name Matthithia is composed of two Hebrew elements: "matath" (gift, present) and "Yah" (the name of God, Jehovah abbreviated), which literally means "gift of the Lord." This type of theophoric name (containing the divine name) was common among the Jews and expressed recognition to God for the child received.
H4993I.emploi: Matthithia appears only once in the entire Bible, in Ezra 10:43. He is listed among the descendants of Nebo who had taken foreign wives during or after the Babylonian exile. After the return to Judea, the priest Ezra gathered the people and urged these men to send away their non-Jewish wives to remain faithful to God's covenant. Matthithia obeyed this command, like the other men on the list.

sens: A man from the tribe of Levi at the time of the return from exile
Assistant to Ezra during the public reading of the Law
H4993J.detail:
1. Matthithia is a Levite, meaning a member of the tribe dedicated to the service of the temple and the Law in Israel. He lived at the time of the return from exile when the Jews were rebuilding Jerusalem after the Babylonian captivity.
2. He stands beside Ezra when Ezra solemnly reads the Law to the people, standing at his right on the platform (Nehemiah 8:4). His presence indicates that he was a man of trust and authority, likely tasked with assisting the scribe in this major public reading.
H4993J.origine: The name means "gift of Jehovah" or "gift of the Lord": it combines the Hebrew word "mattan" (gift) and the divine name "Yah." It is a theophoric name, common among the Levites, affirming that the child is a gift from God. Several men bore this name in Israel's history.
H4993J.emploi: Matthithia is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in Nehemiah 8:4. He appears at a crucial moment: the solemn reading of the Law by Ezra before all the people gathered in Jerusalem. This scene marks the reconstitution of the Jewish community after the exile. That Matthithia is named among the seven men standing beside Ezra indicates his importance in this religious restoration.

sens: Particle of entreaty to soften a request, an order, or a question
Marker of politeness and respect addressed to a superior or an equal
Intensive particle that reinforces an affirmation or an exhortation
Marker of urgency or insistence in a supplication
H4994.detail:
1. This is a small particle that the speaker adds to their words to make them softer and more respectful. It essentially says: "I beg you," "Please." Abram uses it in Genesis 12:11 to ask Sarai to tell that she is his sister — it is a delicate request, presented with deference.
2. It expresses politeness towards someone of higher rank or simply towards someone one wishes to honor. It acknowledges the authority or dignity of the person being addressed. In Genesis 18:3, Abraham says to his visitors: "My lord, I pray you" — he adds this particle to show them respect.
3. It can reinforce an affirmation or an exhortation, as in saying: "Truly, I beg you, listen well!" In 1 Kings 17:10, the prophet Elijah says to the widow: "Go fetch me, I pray you, a little water" — this is not a harsh command, but a courteous and insistent request.
4. In supplications addressed to God, it carries a great weight of urgency and humility. In 1 Samuel 23:11, David cries: "O Lord, please reveal it to your servant!" — the particle expresses the urgent need for divine response.
H4994.origine: This is a very ancient Hebrew particle without a true root, used since the oldest biblical texts. It has no "parent" among other words; it is a tool of spoken language, a ready-made formula to polish words. Its usage is nearly universal in biblical Hebrew: it appears as early as Genesis and throughout the historical, prophetic, and poetic books. It reflects the importance that Hebrew culture placed on courtesy and respect, even among friends or family members.
H4994.emploi: This particle appears about 375 times in the Hebrew Bible and is almost always used in direct speech — when someone is speaking to someone else. It is very frequent in Genesis and Exodus, especially in dialogues: it softens the requests of the patriarchs, prayers, commands of kings and leaders. It can accompany a simple request ("Go fetch me some water," 1 Kings 17:10), a supplication to God ("Please reveal to me," 1 Samuel 23:11), a moral exhortation ("Give glory to the Lord," Joshua 7:19), or even a courteous objection ("Why is that?" in Genesis 33:15). It is almost invisible in the French translation — the Segond often renders it with nuances of French or omits it — but it was audible and lively for those who heard Hebrew: it gave the text an intimate, pleading, respectful tone.
H4994.portee: This little word teaches us that the Bible values courtesy even in serious moments: one can ask for something urgent or crucial, but with gentleness and respect. It also shows that biblical prayer is not a harsh demand addressed to God, but a confident and humble supplication. For today's Christian, this reminds us that our requests to God and to others benefit from being accompanied by respect and reverence, not harshness. It is a lesson of heart as much as of style.

sens: Not fully cooked, partially cooked
Refers to meat that is raw or insufficiently cooked
H4995.detail:
1. The word refers to food, especially meat, that has not been cooked all the way through, remaining raw or undercooked. In Exodus 12:9, during the institution of Passover, God expressly forbids eating the "half-cooked" lamb: it must be roasted entirely over the fire, with its head, its legs, and its entrails. This is a matter of ritual cleanliness and respect for the divine command for this central feast.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of incompleteness or insufficiency in the preparation of food. Eating half-cooked meat means consuming something that has not reached its proper state of cooking, which was considered inappropriate and forbidden for the Passover meal.
H4995.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that expresses the idea of "rawness" or lack of complete cooking. It literally describes the state of a substance that has not undergone the necessary thermal treatment to transition from raw to transformed. Cooking was, in antiquity, as today, the means of making food safe and edible.
H4995.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 12:9. It is found in the context of the prescriptions regarding the Passover meal, where Moses communicates to Israel the strict rules for preparing the lamb intended to commemorate the liberation from Egypt. This unique occurrence underscores the importance of detail: the way in which this lamb is prepared is not a matter of taste or common practice, but a precise divine command.
H4995.portee: This prescription reveals that God cares about the details of worship and the lives of His people. It teaches that obeying God means obeying in particular, without doing things halfway. For the believer today, it is a reminder that commitment to God does not tolerate half-measures or partial engagement.

sens: Great city of ancient Egypt, political and religious capital
Prosperous and fortified city, surrounded by waters and militarily powerful
H4996.detail:
1. No is the ancient capital of Egypt, a major city where pharaonic power was exercised. It was here that the great temples were built and where the wealth of the country was concentrated. The prophets refer to it as the heart of Egyptian power, for to dominate No was to dominate Egypt (Ezekiel 30:14-16).
2. The city is described as extraordinarily well protected: it was situated amid the rivers of the Nile, surrounded by water, with the sea as a wall (Nahum 3:8). Its apparent invulnerability symbolized the apparent power of a nation that believes it is safe from God's judgments.
H4996.origine: The Hebrew name No refers to the Greek city known as Thebes (in ancient Egyptian, Wȝset). The prophets trace this judgment back to the omnipotence of the Lord who, despite the beauty and strength of this metropolis, can devastate it. The name carries the idea of "disturbance" or rupture: No will be shattered when judgment comes.
H4996.emploi: No appears five times in the Bible, only in the prophets of the 7th century B.C.: Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Nahum. It is always mentioned as an object of divine judgment: Jeremiah (46:25) associates it with Amon, the Egyptian god, marking it for punishment. Ezekiel (30:14-16) details how it will be conquered, burned, and opened by breach. Nahum (3:8) uses it as an example: even a city so powerful, so well defended, has been brought to nothing. The context is always prophetic and threatening.
H4996.portee: No reminds us that no earthly power, no fortress no matter how impressive, escapes God's judgment. The Bible invites the reader not to be impressed by the appearance of security that wealth or human defenses provide: only obedience to the Lord offers true protection. It is a lesson in humility for peoples tempted by political or religious pride.

sens: Leather container for storing and transporting liquids
Dried skin pouch, image of dryness and fragility
H4997.detail:
1. An outre is a container made from animal skin, sewn to hold liquids: wine, milk, water. A fine example is seen in Joshua 9:4, where the Gibeonites use old, patched wine skins to give the illusion of a long journey. It was the ancient equivalent of our canteens or jugs, practical for traveling and storing liquid provisions.
2. Because an outre ages, dries out, and cracks, the word takes on a figurative value: the skin becomes fragile, wrinkled, brittle. In Psalms 119:83, the psalmist compares himself to an outre in the smoke, symbolizing someone who is drying out due to suffering and trial. It is an image of fatigue, of accelerated aging through sorrow.
H4997.origine: The Hebrew word nod comes from the root that denotes skin and its work. An outre is literally a prepared skin, sewn and filled. The image is very concrete: it is an everyday object in pastoral and nomadic life, where each family carries its provisions. The same root appears in words related to leather and worked skins.
H4997.emploi: The word nod appears six times in the Bible, always in the literal or figurative sense of skin-container. Three occurrences describe actual outres: in Joshua 9, the false Gibeonite ambassadors use old outres to feign a long journey; in Judges 4:19, Jael gives milk to Sisera in an outre; in 1 Samuel 16:20, Jesse sends wine to Saul in an outre. Two occurrences are metaphorical: in Psalms 56:9, tears are collected in God's outre, evoking His tenderness and counting each suffering; in Psalms 119:83, the psalmist likens himself to a dried-out outre in the smoke, an image of fragility and spiritual weariness.
H4997.portee: This concrete word invites the reader to see that God knows our physical and spiritual fragility. When the psalmist compares himself to a dried-out outre, he confesses that prolonged suffering wears down the soul just as time wears down the skin. But the fact that God collects each tear in His outre shows that no trial escapes His attention and compassion. It is an image of vulnerability recognized and preserved by the One who loves us.

sens: To have an attractive, pleasing appearance
To be appropriate, to fit well with something
H4998.detail:
1. To have an attractive, pleasing appearance: this verb expresses physical beauty, that which pleases the eye. In Song of Solomon 1:10, the beloved's cheeks are "beautiful" among her jewels — it is visible beauty, that which strikes the eye and seduces in the moment. It is a simple, human, carnal beauty in the good sense of the term.
2. To be appropriate, to fit well with something: in a figurative sense, the word means that something is conforming, suitable, that it perfectly fits a situation. In Psalms 93:5, "holiness is fitting for your house": this means that holiness is worthy of God's dwelling, that it is His natural adornment, the ornament that suits Him. In Isaiah 52:7, the feet of those who announce good news are "beautiful" upon the mountains — not beautiful physically, but beautiful because they fit this message of salvation, because they are in their place, bearers of a blessed message.
H4998.origine: This verb belongs to the Hebrew root that expresses the idea of what is pleasant to see, of what fits. It is related to words meaning ornament, adornment. In biblical times, beauty was not merely a superficial appearance: it was also a suitability, a harmony between the nature of a thing and its manifestation. A "beautiful" garment for a queen, a "beautiful" word for a king — it is what accords, what is right.
H4998.emploi: This verb appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In the Song of Solomon, it speaks of physical beauty, a central element of the love poem. In Psalms and Isaiah, it takes on a moral or theological dimension: holiness fits the house of God, the feet of the messenger fit his message. The word thus glides from sensible beauty to spiritual suitability, showing that in Hebrew thought, what is true, what is holy, possesses its own beauty.
H4998.portee: This word reminds the believer that beauty is not a vain luxury, but reflects the order, truth, and holiness of God. When the Bible celebrates beauty — that of the beloved, that of God, that of the announcement of salvation — it says that beauty and goodness walk together. Learning to see beauty in what is just and holy is learning to see the world with God's eyes.

sens: Grassy land where herds graze
Plain or meadow, particularly in the desert
Place of habitation or dwelling
Hideout, secret refuge
H4999.detail:
1. It primarily refers to a grassy area where animals live and feed: sheep, goats, herds. Psalm 23 tenderly evokes this when it says that the Lord "makes me lie down in green pastures" — it is an image of peace and provision.
2. The word also designates the plain itself, especially in arid land: a land capable of producing grass and life. Joel depicts the plains of the desert burned by fire (Joel 1:19), then restored (Joel 2:22) — it is the space that greens or dries up.
3. In a broader sense, it is a place of habitation or dwelling — a location where one establishes daily life. Jeremiah speaks of the "peaceful dwellings" destroyed by divine anger (Jeremiah 25:37).
4. The word can also refer to a refuge or hideout: Psalm 74:20 mentions the "hideouts" of robbers hidden in dark places — secret lairs where one takes shelter.
H4999.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root that evokes the idea of remaining, residing, settling in a place. It expresses both rest and establishment: one who has a pasture has a place to live and feed. The same root produces in Hebrew words related to habitation and stable life. The word paints a pastoral picture: green grass, grazing animals, the peace of rest.
H4999.emploi: This word appears twelve times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms and the prophets. It primarily designates the pastures where shepherds lead their flocks (Psalms 23:2, Psalms 65:13). But it broadens: in Jeremiah and Joel, we see it applied to the plains of the desert that suffer from drought or prosper under blessing (Jeremiah 9:10, Joel 1:19, Joel 2:22). It also designates places of human habitation (Jeremiah 25:37, Lamentations 2:2) and even hideouts of robbers (Psalms 74:20). The word thus oscillates between the pastoral image of calm (the shepherd and his sheep) and the broader image of any inhabited or habitable space.
H4999.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God provides for life as a shepherd provides for his flock. It invites trust for one's food and rest. It is also an invitation to see in nature the sign of divine providence — when the plains green or dry up, it is the Lord who acts. The word connects our material well-being to our relationship with God.
